C1.summary_text: The patient's disease control deteriorated despite increasing doses of metformin and gliclazide, and plasma triglycerides increased to 42.6 mmol/L despite concurrent use of rosuvastatin, fenofibrate, and ezetimibe. At 77 years of age, his HbA1c increased to 9.2%. He was admitted for management of severe hyperlipidaemia, with repeat blood tests showing triglycerides 21.2 mmol/L, total cholesterol 10.6 mmol/L, HDL cholesterol 0.5 mmol/L, direct LDL cholesterol 1.7 mmol/L, and apolipoprotein A1 1.11 g/L. Lipoprotein electrophoresis showed type V hyperlipidaemia with dense chylomicron and VLDL lipoprotein bands. Insulin was initiated, which improved both his glycaemic control and lipid profile. He was discharged a week later. C1.summary_text: This case describes a 77-year-old patient with deteriorating disease control [S2|PMC9012948_main|6801]. Despite intensive therapy with metformin, gliclazide, rosuvastatin, fenofibrate, and ezetimibe, HbA1c increased to 9.2% and plasma triglycerides rose to 42.6 mmol/L, prompting hospital admission for severe hyperlipidaemia management [S2|PMC9012948_main|6801], [S3|PMC9012948_main|6801]. Repeat laboratory testing showed triglycerides 21.2 mmol/L, total cholesterol 10.6 mmol/L, HDL cholesterol 0.5 mmol/L, direct LDL cholesterol 1.7 mmol/L, and apolipoprotein A1 at 1.11 g/L [S4|PMC9012948_main|6801]. Lipoprotein electrophoresis confirmed type V hyperlipidaemia with characteristic dense chylomicron and VLDL bands [S5|PMC9012948_main|6801]. Insulin therapy was initiated, resulting in improvement of both glycaemic control and lipid profile [S6|PMC9012948_main|6801], with discharge one week later [S7|PMC9012948_main|6801].

C1.summary_text: This chunk describes a case of severe hypertriglyceridaemia with type V hyperlipidaemia. Lipoprotein electrophoresis demonstrated dense chylomicron and VLDL bands characteristic of type V hyperlipidaemia [S5|PMC9012948_main|6801]. Despite increasing doses of metformin and gliclazide, glycaemic control remained poor (HbA1c 9.2%), and plasma triglycerides reached 42.6 mmol/L despite concurrent rosuvastatin, fenofibrate, and ezetimibe therapy [S2|PMC9012948_main|6801]. Insulin initiation resulted in improvement of both glycaemic control and the lipid profile [S6|PMC9012948_main|6801].

In this regard, HasegawaMurakami et al. analyzed the dermoscopic pattern of the case presented in their paper, pointing out that the lesion presented an aggregation of pink to reddish globules (pink ovoid nests), with each globule separated by white to pink meshes of bands (pink network).
Furthermore, the red/blue globules were seen in pink ovoid nests of the tumor and, also, some very fine linear-irregular disrupted vessels were recognized.

C1.summary_text: EMPSGC lacks a clear clinical profile, leading to differential diagnoses including basal cell carcinoma (BCC), squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC), epidermal inclusion cyst, hidroadenoma, chalazion, or dermatofibroma (DF) [S1]. Dermoscopically, EMPSGC lesions exhibit aggregations of pink to reddish globules forming a pink network, with red/blue globules within pink ovoid nests and fine, disrupted vessels [S2, S3]. Typically, EMPSGC presents as a slowly growing, skin-colored nodule that can be cystic, multiple, or pigmented [S4].

C1.summary_text: EMPSGC typically presents as a slowly growing skin-colored nodule, which may be cystic, multiple, or pigmented. Its clinical profile is not well-defined, leading to differential diagnoses including BCC, SCC, MCC, epidermal inclusion cyst, hidroadenoma, chalazion, or dermatofibroma. Dermoscopic features include pink to reddish globules (pink ovoid nests) separated by white to pink meshes, with red/blue globules and fine linear-irregular vessels observed. These features are characteristic but not specific, complicating clinical recognition.

C1.summary_text: This dermatopathology chunk discusses the clinical and dermoscopic presentation of Eccrine Mucinous Sweat Gland Carcinoma (EMPSGC). The condition lacks a distinctive clinical profile and is frequently misdiagnosed as other skin lesions, including basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, Merkel cell carcinoma, epidermal inclusion cyst, hidroadenoma, chalazion, or dermatofibroma [S1]. Dermoscopic examination reveals characteristic findings: aggregations of pink to reddish ovoid nests (globules) separated by white to pink meshes of bands (pink network), with red/blue globules visible within the ovoid nests and fine linear-irregular disrupted vessels [S2, S3]. Clinically, EMPSGC typically presents as a slowly growing skin-colored nodule that may be cystic, multiple, or pigmented [S4].

C1.summary_text: EMPSGC (ectopic mucinous primary sweat gland carcinoma) has no pathognomonic clinical presentation, making it easily confused with malignant tumours such as BCC, SCC, and MCC, as well as benign entities including epidermal inclusion cyst, hidroadenoma, chalazion, and dermatofibroma [S1|PMC10529628_dermatopathology-10-00035|1768]. Dermoscopically, reported features include aggregations of pink-to-reddish globules forming pink ovoid nests separated by a pink network [S2|PMC10529628_dermatopathology-10-00035|1768], with additional red/blue globules within those nests and very fine linear-irregular disrupted vessels [S3|PMC10529628_dermatopathology-10-00035|1768]. The classic clinical presentation is a slowly growing skin-colored nodule that may be cystic, multiple, or pigmented [S4|PMC10529628_dermatopathology-10-00035|1768].

C1.summary_text: This cohort analysis describes serological patterns in SARS-CoV-2-infected patients [S1|PMC7508500_main|14256]. Eighteen patients demonstrated recent infection, defined by detection of SARS-CoV-2-specific IgM and/or IgA by immunofluorescence assay (IFA) [S1|PMC7508500_main|14256]. Past infection was operationally defined as symptom resolution occurring ≥10 days after first positive nucleic acid testing (NAT) with concurrent absence of IFA-detectable IgM/IgA [S2|PMC7508500_main|14256]. Among two patients with isolated IgG seropositivity, one exhibited a symptom-to-serology interval of 50 days, consistent with past infection [S2|PMC7508500_main|14256]. The second patient with isolated IgG showed evidence of recent infection, inferred from IgG seroconversion preceding the appearance of IgM or IgA [S3|PMC7508500_main|14256].

C1.summary_text: This chunk discusses the clinical implications of nucleocapsid IgM serology testing in the context of COVID-19 travel requirements. With global COVID-19 cases surging due to the Omicron variant [S1|PMC9012948_main|6786], pre-travel serology may yield true-positive IgM results from recent infection rather than vaccination, causing travel delays [S2|PMC9012948_main|6786]. Concerns about false-positive IgM results delaying travel have also been reported by others [S3|PMC9012948_main|6786]. Critically, median IgM seroreversion takes approximately 7 weeks post-infection, and 53% of confirmed cases remain IgM-positive in the 7th week post-illness onset [S4|PMC9012948_main|6786]. Consequently, a large proportion of recently infected but non-infectious travellers are expected to experience significant travel delays if strict IgM-based entry requirements are maintained [S5|PMC9012948_main|6786].

C1.sentence: Molecular data concerning EMPSGC are still limited, although more and more evidence has been published in recent years.
For example, Murshed et al. performed Next Generation Sequencing (NGS) analysis on their case of a 78-year-old man with an EMPSGC of the right inferior eyelid.

The analysis, conducted on genomic DNA of a tumor extracted from formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue, targeting frequently mutated 59 genes (including EGFR, KRAS, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, HRAS, NRAS, NTRK, AKT1, PIK3CA, KIT, and PDGFRA), disclosed no gene mutations or fusions.
On two cases of EMPSGC, Cornejo et al. used NGS with a focused panel of 50 frequently altered genes.
The genes EGFR, KRAS, and GNAS, which are frequently involved in mucinous neoplasms, were not found to have alterations in that study.
AKT1 and PIK3CA gene alterations, which are typically found in papillary carcinomas of the breast, were also not found.
In another two cases of EMPSGC, Qin et al. used array comparative genomic hybridization (aCGH), which revealed a 6p11.2 to 6q16.1 deletion in one of the cases.

Held et al. performed an MYB antibody staining of 10 cases of EMPSGC, revealing that all of the cases displayed significant nuclear MYB expression; furthermore, the expression of MYB was found negative in primary mucinous cutaneous carcinomas and mucin-rich basal cell carcinomas, and, also, they found that MYB might be a helpful surrogate measure, particularly in EMPSGC cases with low mucin levels.
However, the authors underscore that fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) testing on each case in that study came out negative for MYB gene translocation, and amplification is preferable.

C1.summary_text: Molecular data concerning EMPSGC are limited, though increasing evidence is being published. One case of EMPSGC in a 78-year-old man showed no gene mutations or fusions via NGS on FFPE tumor DNA [S2, S3]. Another study using NGS on two EMPSGC cases found no alterations in EGFR, KRAS, GNAS, AKT1, or PIK3CA [S4, S5, S6]. aCGH on two EMPSGC cases revealed a 6p11.2 to 6q16.1 deletion in one case [S7]. MYB antibody staining on 10 EMPSGC cases showed significant nuclear MYB expression, while primary mucinous cutaneous carcinomas and mucin-rich basal cell carcinomas were negative for MYB expression. MYB may serve as a surrogate marker in EMPSGC with low mucin levels [S8]. However, FISH testing was negative for MYB gene translocation, and amplification is preferred [S9].

One case of EMPSGC showed no gene mutations or fusions in 59 targeted genes (including EGFR, KRAS, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, HRAS, NRAS, NTRK, AKT1, PIK3CA, KIT, PDGFRA) via NGS [S3|PMC10529628_dermatopathology-10-00035|1772]. C1.summary_text: This chunk reviews molecular findings in epithelioid mucinous sweat gland carcinomas (EMPSGC). NGS analysis in a single case (78-year-old man) failed to detect mutations or fusions in 59 frequently altered genes including EGFR, KRAS, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, HRAS, NRAS, NTRK, AKT1, PIK3CA, KIT, and PDGFRA [S3]. In two additional cases (Cornejo et al.), NGS with a 50-gene panel found no alterations in EGFR, KRAS, or GNAS—genes frequently involved in mucinous neoplasms [S5]—nor in AKT1 and PIK3CA mutations typical of papillary breast carcinomas [S6]. Qin et al.'s aCGH analysis of two EMPSGC cases revealed a 6p11.2 to 6q16.1 deletion in one case [S7]. MYB antibody staining of 10 EMPSGC cases showed significant nuclear MYB expression in all cases [S8], whereas MYB was negative in primary mucinous cutaneous carcinomas and mucin-rich basal cell carcinomas. MYB may serve as a helpful diagnostic surrogate, particularly in EMPSGC with low mucin content [S8]. However, FISH testing on all 10 cases was negative for MYB gene translocation/amplification [S9].

C1.summary_text: This chunk summarizes molecular and IHC evidence for Ectopic Mucinous Primary Skin Gland Carcinoma (EMPSGC), noting that molecular data remain limited [S1]. NGS on a 59-gene panel in one EMPSGC case found no mutations or fusions in EGFR, KRAS, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, HRAS, NRAS, NTRK, AKT1, PIK3CA, KIT, or PDGFRA [S3]. A separate 50-gene NGS panel in two EMPSGC cases also found no alterations in EGFR, KRAS, or GNAS (genes commonly mutated in mucinous neoplasms) [S4–S5], and no AKT1 or PIK3CA alterations (markers of papillary breast carcinoma) [S6]. aCGH in two additional EMPSGC cases revealed a 6p11.2–6q16.1 deletion in one case [S7]. Importantly, IHC with MYB antibody across 10 EMPSGC cases demonstrated significant nuclear MYB expression in all cases, while MYB was negative in primary mucinous cutaneous carcinomas and mucin-rich basal cell carcinomas, suggesting MYB as a useful surrogate marker especially in low-mucin EMPSGC [S8]. However, FISH for MYB gene translocation was negative in all tested cases, with MYB amplification (rather than translocation) proposed as the more likely mechanism [S9].

C1.summary_text: In a cohort of 444 samples tested with Abbott IgM, 45 (10%) were positive [S1|PMC9012948_main|6781]. Of these Abbott IgM positive samples, 44/44 (100%) returned negative SARS-CoV-2 NAAT results from simultaneously collected nasal and throat swabs, suggesting past infection without active viral replication [S1|PMC9012948_main|6781]. In a smaller cohort of 152 samples tested with Roche Total antibody assay, 4 (3%) were positive [S1|PMC9012948_main|6781]. Concordance between assays was demonstrated by 3/4 (75%) Roche positive samples also testing positive on the Abbott IgM assay [S1|PMC9012948_main|6781]. The positive IgM results from both assays were interpreted as consistent with recent past SARS-CoV-2 infection, with or without recent vaccination [S1|PMC9012948_main|6781].

C1.summary_text: In this SARS-CoV-2 serological study [S1|PMC9012948_main|6781], the Abbott IgM assay returned a positivity rate of 10% (45/444 samples). Notably, all 44 evaluable Abbott IgM-positive samples simultaneously tested negative by SARS-CoV-2 NAAT on nose and throat swabs, suggesting no active infection at the time of sampling. The Roche Total antibody assay showed a lower positivity rate of 3% (4/152 samples). Cross-assay concordance was high: 3 out of 4 (75%) Roche-positive samples were also positive on the Abbott IgM assay, a pattern interpreted as consistent with recent past SARS-CoV-2 infection with or without recent vaccination.

C1.summary_text: This chunk describes circulating cell populations in the context of malignancy and health. Circulating cytokeratin-positive cells appear to represent benign background epithelial cells that are also found in healthy volunteers [S1|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13932]. Circulating megakaryocytes were commonly observed in patients with metastatic carcinoma and were also detected, though less frequently, in healthy volunteers [S2|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13932]. These findings suggest that both cell types have physiological presence in normal circulation but may be enriched or more frequent in the setting of malignancy.

C1.summary_text: This chunk reports two generalizable observations regarding circulating cells in peripheral blood. First, some cytokeratin-positive circulating cells are likely benign background circulating epithelial cells rather than true tumour cells, as they are also detectable in healthy volunteers [S1|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13932]. Second, circulating megakaryocytes are a common finding in patients with metastatic carcinoma but are also present, at lower frequency, in healthy volunteers [S2|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13932]. Both observations highlight important specificity limitations for circulating cell-based diagnostics.

[S1|PMC10529628_dermatopathology-10-00035|1770] From a histopathological point of view, the morphological features of EMPSGC are well delineated, with many scientific papers having clearly and comprehensively described the peculiarities of this neoplasm, focusing, in particular, on the well-circumscribed growth, uninodular or even multinodular, with the possibility of having a solid, cystic, and papillary component.
[S2|PMC10529628_dermatopathology-10-00035|1770] In various case reports, it is emphasized that it is possible to find scattered small cysts, and also cribriform aspects, in which the cells are arranged in a pseudo-rosette and/or lacelike patterns.
[S3|PMC10529628_dermatopathology-10-00035|1770] Cytologically, the cells constituting the tumor are monomorphic, round to oval, and of medium/small size.
[S4|PMC10529628_dermatopathology-10-00035|1770] The nuclei have fine granular or stippled chromatin imparting a 'salt-and-pepper' appearance, and their cytoplasm is large and eosinophilic.
[S5|PMC10529628_dermatopathology-10-00035|1770] In addition, it is important to emphasize the possibility of secreting mucins, both intracellularly and into the extracellular environment, a characteristic that, over time, has suggested a possible placement of EMPSGC in a spectrum of neoplasms that, at the extreme, would have primitive cutaneous mucinous carcinoma (PCMC).

C1.sentence: From a histopathological point of view, the morphological features of EMPSGC are well delineated, with many scientific papers having clearly and comprehensively described the peculiarities of this neoplasm, focusing, in particular, on the well-circumscribed growth, uninodular or even multinodular, with the possibility of having a solid, cystic, and papillary component.
In various case reports, it is emphasized that it is possible to find scattered small cysts, and also cribriform aspects, in which the cells are arranged in a pseudo-rosette and/or lacelike patterns.
Cytologically, the cells constituting the tumor are monomorphic, round to oval, and of medium/small size.
The nuclei have fine granular or stippled chromatin imparting a 'salt-and-pepper' appearance, and their cytoplasm is large and eosinophilic.

In addition, it is important to emphasize the possibility of secreting mucins, both intracellularly and into the extracellular environment, a characteristic that, over time, has suggested a possible placement of EMPSGC in a spectrum of neoplasms that, at the extreme, would have primitive cutaneous mucinous carcinoma (PCMC).

C1.summary_text: From a histopathological perspective, EMPSGC is characterized by well-circumscribed, uninodular or multinodular growth, with solid, cystic, and papillary components. Scattered small cysts and cribriform patterns, where cells form pseudo-rosettes or lacelike structures, can be observed. Cytologically, the tumor cells are monomorphic, round to oval, and medium/small in size, with fine granular or stippled chromatin ('salt-and-pepper' appearance) and large, eosinophilic cytoplasm. EMPSGC can secrete mucins intracellularly and extracellularly, suggesting a possible relationship with primitive cutaneous mucinous carcinoma (PCMC) [S1|PMC10529628_dermatopathology-10-00035|1770, S2|PMC10529628_dermatopathology-10-00035|1770, S3|PMC10529628_dermatopathology-10-00035|1770, S4|PMC10529628_dermatopathology-10-00035|1770, S5|PMC10529628_dermatopathology-10-00035|1770].

C1.summary_text: This chunk provides a comprehensive histopathological overview of ectopic meningothelial-like psammomatoid gangliocytoid cutaneous (EMPSGC) neoplasm. Architecturally, EMPSGC is well-circumscribed with uninodular or multinodular growth and may display solid, cystic, and papillary components [S1]. Scattered small cysts and cribriform patterns with pseudo-rosette and/or lacelike cell arrangements are also described [S2]. Cytologically, tumour cells are monomorphic, round-to-oval, and medium/small in size [S3], with salt-and-pepper nuclear chromatin and large eosinophilic cytoplasm [S4]. A notable feature is the capacity for both intracellular and extracellular mucin secretion [S5], which has led to the suggestion that EMPSGC may occupy a neoplastic spectrum with primitive cutaneous mucinous carcinoma (PCMC) at one extreme [S5].

This chunk describes procedural and operational metrics for a laboratory-based study using the Parsortix™ device and immunohistochemistry (IHC) testing. Key findings include: sample turnaround times varied based on processing delay (samples processed immediately were faster than refrigerated samples) [S2]; refrigerated samples showed increased platelet and white blood cell aggregates that may have interfered with device filtration [S3]; overall device processing time ranged from 1 hour 28 minutes to 5 hours 50 minutes, with typical processing around 3-5 hours [S4]; MNF116 IHC results were available 2-7 days post-sampling [S5]; carcinoma panel IHC results required 6-12 days [S6]; mean cost per case was approximately £316 [S9], which compared favorably to ultrasound- or CT-guided core biopsy at £500+ additional cost [S10]. The authors noted that observed turnaround times were constrained by prioritization of routine clinical work over research priorities [S7], and that faster turnaround times would likely be achievable under equal prioritization [S8].

C1.summary_text: This chunk describes the workflow logistics and costs of a liquid biopsy CTC isolation study using the Parsortix device. Samples arrived in the laboratory within 10–20 minutes of collection [S1]. Immediate processing was faster than overnight refrigeration [S2]; refrigerated samples showed more platelet and WBC aggregates thought to impede filter flow [S3]. Device processing typically required 3–5 hours (range: 1h28m–5h50m) [S4]. MNF116 IHC turnaround was 5–7 days (minimum 2 days) [S5], while sex-specific carcinoma panel IHC required 10–12 days (minimum 6 days) [S6]. Delays were partly attributable to research deprioritisation versus clinical work [S7–S8]. Mean cost per liquid biopsy case was ~£316 [S9], favourably compared to ultrasound- or CT-guided core biopsy which adds ≥£500 [S10].

C1.summary_text: Hornick et al. described 42 cases of benign nerve sheath tumors with hybrid features of perineurioma and schwannoma [S1]. These tumors were architecturally typical of soft-tissue perineurioma, being well circumscribed but unencapsulated, and showed storiform to whorled and lamellar growth patterns [S2]. The cytologic features showed a dominant schwannian component with spindled plump cells having tapering nuclei and palely eosinophilic cytoplasm [S3]. The perineurial component was inconspicuous in most cases [S4], with perineurial cells recognized by their slender elongated bipolar cytoplasmic processes [S5]. Immunohistochemistry revealed dual cell lineages: predominant larger spindled cells were positive for S100 protein, while less conspicuous slender cells were positive for EMA and usually claudin-1 [S6]. Degenerative nuclear atypia was reported in 25% of cases and appeared to have no clinical consequence [S7].

C1.summary_text: Hornick et al. described 42 cases of benign nerve sheath tumors exhibiting hybrid features of perineurioma and schwannoma [S1|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9408]. These tumors are architecturally typical of soft-tissue perineurioma, being well circumscribed, unencapsulated, and displaying storiform to whorled and lamellar growth patterns [S2|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9408]. Cytologically, they show a dominant schwannian component with spindled plump cells, tapering nuclei, and palely eosinophilic cytoplasm [S3|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9408]. The perineurial component is often inconspicuous, characterized by slender elongated bipolar cytoplasmic processes [S4|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9408, S5|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9408]. Immunohistochemistry reveals dual cell lineages, with predominant larger spindled cells positive for S100 protein, and less conspicuous slender cells positive for EMA and usually claudin-1 [S6|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9408]. Degenerative nuclear atypia was reported in 25% of cases but appeared to have no clinical consequence [S7|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9408].

C1.summary_text: Hornick et al. characterized 42 cases of benign nerve sheath tumors with hybrid perineurioma-schwannoma features [S1|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9408]. These tumors exhibit architectural features typical of soft-tissue perineurioma, including well-circumscribed but unencapsulated morphology with storiform to whorled and lamellar growth patterns [S2|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9408]. Cytologically, a dominant schwannian component is present, characterized by spindled plump cells with tapering nuclei and pale eosinophilic cytoplasm [S3|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9408], while the perineurial component is typically inconspicuous [S4|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9408]. Perineurial cells are morphologically distinguished by slender elongated bipolar cytoplasmic processes [S5|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9408]. Immunohistochemically, the dual cell lineages are evident: the predominant larger spindled cells express S100 protein, while the less conspicuous slender cells express EMA and usually also claudin-1 [S6|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9408]. Degenerative nuclear atypia occurs in 25% of cases but appears to have no clinical consequence [S7|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9408].

C1.summary_text: This chunk summarizes a series of 42 benign nerve sheath tumors with hybrid perineurioma-schwannoma features (Hornick et al.) [S1|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9408]. Architecturally, these tumors resemble soft-tissue perineurioma: well circumscribed but unencapsulated, with storiform to whorled and lamellar growth patterns [S2|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9408]. Cytologically, a dominant schwannian component predominates, composed of spindled plump cells with tapering nuclei and pale eosinophilic cytoplasm [S3|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9408], while the perineurial component is inconspicuous in most cases [S4|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9408], identifiable by slender elongated bipolar cytoplasmic processes [S5|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9408]. IHC demonstrates dual cell lineages: S100 protein marks the predominant spindled schwannian cells, while EMA and usually claudin-1 mark the less conspicuous perineurial cells [S6|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9408]. Degenerative nuclear atypia was reported in 25% of cases but appeared to be of no clinical consequence [S7|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9408].

These classical factors have been validated by both RNA and molecular data [S7|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27856].

C1.summary_text: Histological type determination is critical for prognosis and treatment in lung carcinoma, with distinct outcomes for small-cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and large-cell carcinoma [S1|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27856]. Similarly, ovarian carcinoma prognosis and survival vary widely among histological types including high- or low-grade serous carcinoma, endometrioid carcinoma, clear-cell carcinoma, and mucinous adenocarcinoma [S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27856]. C1.sentence: Aims : Invasive cribriform and intraductal carcinoma (IDC) are associated with adverse outcome in prostate cancer patients, with the large cribriform pattern having the worst outcome in radical prostatectomies.
Our objective was to determine the impact of the large and small cribriform patterns in prostate cancer biopsies.
Methods and results : Pathological revision was carried out on biopsies of 1887 patients from the European Randomised Study of Screening for Prostate Cancer.
The large cribriform pattern was defined as having at least twice the size of adjacent benign glands.
The median follow-up time was 13.4 years.
Hazard ratios for metastasis-free survival (MFS) and disease-specific survival (DSS) were calculated using Cox proportional hazards regression.

Any cribriform pattern was found in 280 of 1887 men: 1.1% IDC in grade group (GG) 1, 18.2% in GG2, 57.1% in GG3, 55.4% in GG4 and 59.3% in GG5; the large cribriform pattern was present in 0, 0.5, 9.8, 18.1 and 17.3%, respectively.

In multivariable analyses, small and large cribriform patterns were both ( P < 0.005) associated with worse MFS [small: hazard ratio (HR) = 3.04, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 1.93 -4.78; large: HR = 3.17, 95% CI = 1.68 -5.99] and DSS (small: HR = 4.07, 95% CI = 2.51 -6.62; large: HR = 4.13, 95% CI = 2.14 -7.98).
Patients with the large cribriform pattern did not have worse MFS ( P = 0.77) or DSS ( P = 0.96) than those with the small cribriform pattern.

C1.summary_text: Invasive cribriform and intraductal carcinoma (IDC) are associated with adverse outcomes in prostate cancer patients, with the large cribriform pattern having the worst outcome in radical prostatectomies [S1]. The study analyzed biopsies from 1887 patients from the European Randomised Study of Screening for Prostate Cancer [S3], with a median follow-up of 13.4 years [S5]. The large cribriform pattern was defined as having at least twice the size of adjacent benign glands [S4]. Any cribriform pattern was found in 280 of 1887 men, with IDC prevalence varying by grade group (GG1: 1.1%, GG2: 18.2%, GG3: 57.1%, GG4: 55.4%, GG5: 59.3%) [S7]. The large cribriform pattern was present in 0% of GG1, 0.5% of GG2, 9.8% of GG3, 18.1% of GG4, and 17.3% of GG5 [S7]. Both small and large cribriform patterns were associated with worse metastasis-free survival (MFS) and disease-specific survival (DSS) in multivariable analyses (P < 0.005) [S8]. Specifically, the hazard ratio for MFS was 3.04 for small and 3.17 for large cribriform patterns, and for DSS it was 4.07 for small and 4.13 for large cribriform patterns [S8]. However, patients with the large cribriform pattern did not have significantly worse MFS (P = 0.77) or DSS (P = 0.96) compared to those with the small cribriform pattern [S9]. Hazard ratios were calculated using Cox proportional hazards regression [S6].

C1.summary_text: A retrospective cohort study of 1,887 patients from the European Randomised Study of Screening for Prostate Cancer examined the prognostic impact of cribriform patterns in prostate cancer biopsies [S3]. The large cribriform pattern was defined as glands at least twice the size of adjacent benign glands [S4], with median follow-up of 13.4 years [S5]. Any cribriform pattern was found in 14.9% (280/1887) of patients, with prevalence increasing with grade group: 1.1% in GG1, 18.2% in GG2, 57.1% in GG3, 55.4% in GG4, and 59.3% in GG5 [S7]. The large cribriform pattern was present in 0%, 0.5%, 9.8%, 18.1%, and 17.3% across the same grade groups respectively [S7]. Both small and large cribriform patterns were significantly associated with worse metastasis-free survival (MFS) and disease-specific survival (DSS) in multivariable analysis (P < 0.005) [S8]. Small cribriform pattern showed HR 3.04 (95% CI 1.93–4.78) for MFS and HR 4.07 (95% CI 2.51–6.62) for DSS [S8], while large cribriform pattern showed HR 3.17 (95% CI 1.68–5.99) for MFS and HR 4.13 (95% CI 2.14–7.98) for DSS [S8]. Notably, patients with large cribriform pattern did not have significantly worse MFS (P = 0.77) or DSS (P = 0.96) compared to those with small cribriform pattern [S9].

C1.summary_text: This chunk reports findings from a large cohort study (n=1,887; median follow-up 13.4 years) from the European Randomised Study of Screening for Prostate Cancer [S3, S5|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17550]. Invasive cribriform and IDC patterns are established as adverse prognostic features in prostate cancer [S1]. The large cribriform pattern was specifically defined as glands at least twice the size of adjacent benign glands [S4]. Any cribriform pattern was detected in 280/1,887 men, with prevalence rising steeply from GG1 (1.1%) to GG5 (59.3%); the large cribriform pattern was absent in GG1 and increased to 18.1% in GG4 [S7]. In multivariable Cox regression analyses, both small and large cribriform patterns were independently associated with significantly worse MFS (small: HR=3.04; large: HR=3.17) and DSS (small: HR=4.07; large: HR=4.13), all P<0.005 [S8]. Critically, no statistically significant difference in MFS (P=0.77) or DSS (P=0.96) was found between the large and small cribriform patterns [S9], challenging the assumption that large cribriform morphology confers worse prognosis than small cribriform on biopsy.

C1.summary_text: This chunk classifies common benign nerve sheath tumors and characterizes their cellular composition [S1|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9406]. Schwannomas are composed exclusively of Schwann cells, and perineuriomas exclusively of perineurial cells — both representing monomorphic, single-cell-type tumors [S2|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9406]. In contrast, neurofibromas are heterogeneous, containing Schwann cells, fibroblasts, perineurial cells, and scattered axons [S2|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9406]. The key distinguishing morphological feature is cellular composition: monomorphic in schwannomas/perineuriomas versus pleomorphic/mixed in neurofibromas [S2|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9406].

C1.sentence: From a practical perspective, the distinction between these tumours of the rete testis and metastases, germ cell tumours, or other malignant neoplasms, is seldom problematic, especially when they are entirely cystic.
However, tumours with solid components may show significant overlap with sex cord stromal tumours and may occasionally raise the possibility of metastases to the testis.

In particular, neoplasms within the spectrum of Sertoliform cystadenoma, given their morphologic and immunophenotypic features, may need to be distinguised from Sertoli cell tumor NOS, metastatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the prostate, and papillary renal cell carcinoma, among others.

As shown in this study, the presence of areas of transition between non-neoplastic and neoplastic epithelium within the rete testis can be helpful to support a diagnosis of Sertoliform cystadenoma of the rete testis.
Additionally, positivity for PAX8 and absence of nuclear beta-catenin expression are helpful to distinguish between these neoplasms and Sertoli cell tumor NOS.

In our opinion, the presence of nuclear beta-catenin expression is so consistent among indolent Sertoli cell tumour NOS that, in its absence, this diagnosis should be restricted to cases with prototypical features.

Given that Sertoli cell tumours NOS typically occur within the testis proper, the combination of purely intra-rete growth pattern and the absence of nuclear beta-catenin expression argue against it, even in the presence of SF-1 expression.

C1.summary_text: Distinguishing tumours of the rete testis from other neoplasms is generally straightforward, especially if entirely cystic [S1]. However, solid components can mimic sex cord stromal tumours or metastases [S2]. Sertoliform cystadenoma requires differentiation from Sertoli cell tumor NOS, prostate adenocarcinoma, and renal cell carcinoma [S3]. Areas of transition between non-neoplastic and neoplastic epithelium within the rete testis support Sertoliform cystadenoma [S4]. Positivity for PAX8 and absence of nuclear beta-catenin expression help differentiate these from Sertoli cell tumor NOS [S5]. Nuclear beta-catenin expression is consistent in indolent Sertoli cell tumour NOS, and its absence suggests alternative diagnoses [S6]. While Sertoli cell tumours NOS typically occur in the testis proper, intra-rete growth and absence of nuclear beta-catenin argue against this diagnosis, even with SF-1 expression [S7].

However, tumours with solid components may overlap significantly with sex cord stromal tumours and can raise the possibility of testicular metastases [S2|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15512]. Neoplasms in the Sertoliform cystadenoma spectrum require differentiation from Sertoli cell tumor NOS, metastatic prostatic ductal adenocarcinoma, and papillary renal cell carcinoma [S3|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15512]. The presence of transitional areas between non-neoplastic and neoplastic epithelium within the rete testis supports a diagnosis of Sertoliform cystadenoma of the rete testis [S4|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15512]. PAX8 positivity and the absence of nuclear beta-catenin expression are useful for distinguishing Sertoliform cystadenoma from Sertoli cell tumor NOS [S5|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15512]. Nuclear beta-catenin expression is consistently found in indolent Sertoli cell tumour NOS, and its absence should restrict this diagnosis to prototypical cases [S6|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15512]. Sertoli cell tumours NOS typically occur in the testis proper [S7|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15512]. A purely intra-rete growth pattern and absent nuclear beta-catenin expression argue against a Sertoli cell tumour NOS diagnosis, even if SF-1 expression is present [S7|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15512].

C1.summary_text: This chunk provides diagnostic and immunohistochemical guidance for distinguishing tumours of the rete testis from similar neoplasms. Entirely cystic rete testis tumours are readily distinguished from metastases and germ cell tumours [S1], while solid-component tumours may overlap with sex cord stromal tumours and metastases [S2]. Sertoliform cystadenoma requires distinction from Sertoli cell tumor NOS, metastatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the prostate, and papillary renal cell carcinoma based on morphologic and immunophenotypic features [S3]. Diagnostic support for Sertoliform cystadenoma includes areas of transition between non-neoplastic and neoplastic epithelium [S4]. Key immunohistochemical features include PAX8 positivity and absence of nuclear beta-catenin expression in Sertoliform cystadenoma, which help distinguish it from Sertoli cell tumor NOS [S5]. Indolent Sertoli cell tumour NOS consistently expresses nuclear beta-catenin [S6], and the combination of purely intra-rete growth pattern with absence of nuclear beta-catenin expression argues against Sertoli cell tumor NOS diagnosis, despite possible SF-1 expression [S7]. Sertoli cell tumours NOS characteristically occur within the testis proper rather than the rete [S7].

Key diagnostic features for Sertoliform cystadenoma include the presence of transitional areas between non-neoplastic and neoplastic epithelium within the rete testis [S4|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15512]. PAX8 positivity and absence of nuclear beta-catenin expression are useful IHC markers to distinguish Sertoliform cystadenoma from Sertoli cell tumour NOS [S5|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15512]. Nuclear beta-catenin expression is highly consistent in indolent Sertoli cell tumour NOS, and its absence should restrict this diagnosis to prototypical cases [S6|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15512]. Furthermore, a purely intra-rete growth pattern combined with absent nuclear beta-catenin argues against Sertoli cell tumour NOS even when SF-1 is expressed, given that Sertoli cell tumour NOS typically arises in the testis proper [S7|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15512].

[S1|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10432] Currently, there are no established diagnostic criteria for EGPA with an international consensus.
[S2|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10432] In the past, CSS was defined as a disease characterized by hypereosinophilia (peak blood eosinophil counts exceeding 1.5 /C2 10 9 /L) and systemic vasculitis involving two or more extra-pulmonary organs in patients with asthma and allergic rhinitis.
[S3|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10432] Conversely, four or more of the six items were required to evaluate a given patient with angiitis as having CSS in the subsequent American College of Rheumatology (ACR) 1990 classification criteria.
[S4|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10432] The association with asthma was also specified in the definition of EGPA by the CHCC2012.
[S5|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10432] Accordingly, based on the absence of a history of asthma and satisfying only three of the six ACR criteria, the present case fulfills neither the Lanham diagnostic nor ACR classification criteria nor the definition of EGPA by the CHCC2012.
[S6|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10432] However, it remains to be solved whether the pathological condition in the present case can be interpreted as a spectrum of EGPA even without asthma or another distinct eosinophil-associated disease concept.
[S7|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10432] Another possible interpretation of the histopathologicalfindings is that eosinophils are bystanders intermingled with lymphocytic vasculitis lesions due to peripheral blood hypereosinophilia.

C1.summary_text: This chunk discusses the diagnostic landscape of EGPA (eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis), noting the absence of internationally established diagnostic criteria [S1]. The historical Lanham definition of CSS required hypereosinophilia (>1.5×10⁹/L) and systemic vasculitis of ≥2 extra-pulmonary organs in asthmatic patients [S2], while the ACR 1990 criteria demanded ≥4 of 6 items in patients with angiitis [S3]. The CHCC2012 definition also mandates an asthma association for EGPA [S4]. A case lacking asthma history and satisfying only 3 ACR criteria would not fulfill any of these classification systems [S5]. Whether such a case represents a spectrum of EGPA or a distinct eosinophil-associated disease remains unresolved [S6]. Two interpretations of eosinophilic infiltration in vasculitis lesions are discussed: eosinophils as bystanders secondary to peripheral hypereosinophilia [S7], supported by an existing report of biopsy-proven lymphocytic CNS vasculitis entirely lacking eosinophil infiltration despite severe peripheral hypereosinophilia [S8]. Mechanistically, eosinophils drive tissue inflammation through exocytosis, piecemeal degranulation, and cytolytic degranulation [S9], and lesional eosinophil count may not reliably reflect the true intensity of eosinophilic inflammation [S10].

[S1|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|18993] Although FISH is still considered to be the gold standard for HER2 amplification in the clinical setting, we sought to study our discordant cases (see below) by a third technique.
[S2|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|18993] Real-time quantitative PCR was performed with the LightMix kit HER-2 / neu (Roche Diagnostics, Indianapolis, IN, USA).
[S3|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|18993] A 101-bp fragment of HER2 and a 119-bp fragment of the RPL23 reference gene, both localized on chromosome 17q21, were amplified according to the manufacturer's instructions.
[S4|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|18993] Simultaneous quantification of HER2 and of the reference gene was accomplished by using two different LightCycler hybridization probes (LightCycler Red 640 and LightCycler Red 670, respectively), enabling dualcolour detection in a single test tube.
[S5|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|18993] A colour compensation file generated with the Roche Diagnostics LightCycler Multicolour Compensation Set was used to correct the fluorescence in the duplex reaction.
[S6|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|18993] DNA was extracted from formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tumour tissue with a previously described protocol, and subsequently amplified in triplicate with a LightCycler 480 real-time PCR instrument (Roche Diagnostics).
[S7|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|18993] In each PCR experiment, DNA extracted from tumours with known HER2 amplification status (tumours classified as amplified or non-amplified by both FISH and SISH) was included as a positive control: three samples without amplification and three samples with amplification.
[S8|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|18993] Moreover, each PCR experiment included a non-template control and standards (from 10 1 to 10 6 equivalents per reaction of HER2 DNA and of reference DNA) supplied with the kit.
[S9|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|18993] These standards allow the generation of standard curves for both products to determine the linear range of both PCR reactions and to estimate the quantity of the target sequence in unknown samples.
[S10|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|18993] Briefly, for each reaction, l l of LightCycler HER2 mix, l l of LightCycler reference mix, l l of LightCycler 480 probes master mix and 1 l l of PCR-grade water were combined.

C1.sentence: Although FISH is still considered to be the gold standard for HER2 amplification in the clinical setting, we sought to study our discordant cases (see below) by a third technique.
Real-time quantitative PCR was performed with the LightMix kit HER-2 / neu (Roche Diagnostics, Indianapolis, IN, USA).
A 101-bp fragment of HER2 and a 119-bp fragment of the RPL23 reference gene, both localized on chromosome 17q21, were amplified according to the manufacturer's instructions.

Simultaneous quantification of HER2 and of the reference gene was accomplished by using two different LightCycler hybridization probes (LightCycler Red 640 and LightCycler Red 670, respectively), enabling dualcolour detection in a single test tube.
A colour compensation file generated with the Roche Diagnostics LightCycler Multicolour Compensation Set was used to correct the fluorescence in the duplex reaction.

DNA was extracted from formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tumour tissue with a previously described protocol, and subsequently amplified in triplicate with a LightCycler 480 real-time PCR instrument (Roche Diagnostics).

In each PCR experiment, DNA extracted from tumours with known HER2 amplification status (tumours classified as amplified or non-amplified by both FISH and SISH) was included as a positive control: three samples without amplification and three samples with amplification.
Moreover, each PCR experiment included a non-template control and standards (from 10 1 to 10 6 equivalents per reaction of HER2 DNA and of reference DNA) supplied with the kit.
These standards allow the generation of standard curves for both products to determine the linear range of both PCR reactions and to estimate the quantity of the target sequence in unknown samples.
Briefly, for each reaction, l l of LightCycler HER2 mix, l l of LightCycler reference mix, l l of LightCycler 480 probes master mix and 1 l l of PCR-grade water were combined.

Each cycle consisted of denaturation at 95 /C176 C for 10 s, annealing at 60 /C176 C for 10 s, and extension at 72 /C176 C for 10 s. The fluorescence signals were measured after each annealing step.

For PCR, a 101-bp fragment of HER2 and a 119-bp fragment of the RPL23 reference gene on chromosome 17q21 were amplified [S3|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|18993]. PCR experiments included positive controls with known HER2 amplification status (3 amplified and 3 non-amplified samples) [S7|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|18993]. Non-template controls and standards ranging from 10^1 to 10^6 equivalents per reaction of HER2 and reference DNA were included in each PCR experiment [S8|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|18993]. These standards allowed generation of standard curves to determine the linear range and estimate target sequence quantity [S9|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|18993]. The PCR reaction mix consisted of 11 µl each of LightCycler HER2 mix, LightCycler reference mix, LightCycler 480 probes master mix, and PCR-grade water [S10|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|18993].

[S1|PMC10529628_dermatopathology-10-00035|1767] Epidemiologically, our review of the literature confirms that EMPSGC is more frequent in females, between 60 and 70 years old, with more frequent localization in the peri-ocular region, although there are also reports of other skin sites, such as the cheeks, the scalp, and other very rare localizations such as the skin of the scrotal region, reported in the paper by Shah et al., in which the course of EMPSGC was aggressive, with lymph node, visceral, and bone metastases.

A careful analysis of the literature seems to indicate that, although, initially, the published cases of EMPSGC were of the female sex, in the last 10 years, numerous cases have also been published in the male sex, almost in contrast to previous years.

C1.summary_text: A literature review confirms that epithelioid melanoma of skin with giant cells (EMPSGC) demonstrates a female predominance [S1], with typical presentation in the 60–70 year age range [S1]. The lesion most frequently localizes to the peri-ocular region, though alternative sites including cheeks, scalp, and scrotal skin have been reported [S1]. A case of scrotal EMPSGC presented with aggressive behaviour and metastases to lymph nodes, viscera, and bone [S1]. Notably, while historically the published literature favoured female cases, the past decade has seen increasing reports of EMPSGC in male patients, suggesting a shift in reported sex distribution [S2].

C1.summary_text: In a cohort study, metastasis developed in 7.1% of men after a median of 8.9 years, and 59.5% of patients died, with 11.0% of all deaths being men who died of prostate cancer [S1].  Metastasis and death of disease rates varied by cribriform pattern: 38.3% metastasis and 38.3% death of disease in men with large cribriform pattern (n=47), 25.3% metastasis and 24.9% death of disease in men with small cribriform pattern (n=233), and 3.5% metastasis and 2.9% death of disease in men without cribriform pattern (n=1607) [S2]. Grade group and PSA were independent prognostic parameters for both MFS and DSS [S3]. Radical prostatectomy was the only treatment significantly associated with better DSS (P = 0.004) [S4]. Age, percentage positive biopsies, and tumour length did not significantly impact MFS and DSS [S5]. Patients with the small cribriform pattern had shorter MFS (HR = 3.04) [S6].

C1.summary_text: A prostate cancer cohort (n=1887) was evaluated for prognostic factors associated with metastasis-free survival (MFS) and disease-specific survival (DSS). [S1] At follow-up of median 8.9 years, metastasis developed in 7.1% of men (134/1887), overall mortality occurred in 59.5% (1123/1887), and cancer-specific mortality occurred in 6.5% (123/1887, representing 11.0% of all deaths). [S2] Large cribriform pattern at biopsy was associated with elevated metastasis risk (38.3%, 18/47) and cancer-specific mortality (38.3%), compared to small cribriform pattern (25.3% metastasis, 24.9% DSM) and absence of cribriform pattern (3.5% metastasis, 2.9% DSM). [S3] In multivariable analysis, grade group and PSA were independent prognostic parameters for both MFS and DSS. [S4] Radical prostatectomy was the only treatment significantly associated with improved DSS (p=0.004). [S5] Age, percentage of positive biopsies, and tumour length did not have significant impact on MFS or DSS. [S6] Small cribriform pattern was associated with shorter MFS (HR=3.04, 95% CI not fully stated in chunk).

C1.summary_text: This cohort study of prostate cancer patients reports that 7.1% developed metastasis over a median follow-up of 8.9 years (IQR 5.7–12.8), while 59.5% (n=1123) died overall, with 6.5% (n=123) dying of prostate cancer (11.0% of all deaths) [S1]. Cribriform pattern at biopsy was strongly associated with adverse outcomes: the large cribriform pattern was associated with metastasis and disease-specific death in 38.3% (18/47) each, the small cribriform pattern in 25.3%/24.9% (59/233 and 58/233), versus only 3.5%/2.9% (57/1607 and 47/1607) in patients without cribriform pattern [S2]. In multivariable analysis, grade group and PSA were independent prognostic factors for both MFS and DSS [S3]. Radical prostatectomy was the only treatment significantly associated with improved DSS (P=0.004) [S4]. Age, percentage of positive biopsies, and tumour length did not significantly impact MFS or DSS [S5]. The small cribriform pattern was associated with shorter MFS (HR=3.04; 95% CI truncated at chunk boundary) [S6].

C1.sentence: With a progressive increase in endoscopy procedures, pathologists are bound to see an increased number of duodenal NETs in their routine clinical practice.
The majority of these are non-functional; hence, many are incidentally discovered on endoscopy.

The existing data describe them endoscopically as small, sessile erythematous or pale lesions or submucosal hemispherical or flatly elevated lesions that can be seen in the duodenal cap, bulb, first or second part of the duodenum.
However, in routine clinical practice, we have seen them as lumped together and often described as a mucosal or submucosal nodule.

In addition to NETs, a 'nodular' endoscopic appearance can have varied histological differentials, including benign aetiologies such as Brunner gland hyperplasia, gastric heterotopia, peptic duodenitis and lymphoid hyperplasia, among others.

Once diagnosed there is very limited evidence for a wait-and-watch policy, and it is generally recommended that the tumour be completely excised using endoscopic resection or even local resection, if endoscopic therapy is high risk or unlikely to be curative.
Treatment is based on tumour size, location, histological grade, stage and tumour type.

Given that metastases to lymph nodes and liver from duodenal NET are known to occur and even patients with tumour size ≤ 1 cm have a 40% chance of nodal metastases, an early and accurate diagnosis is essential.
The pathological assessment and grading of duodenal NETs is akin to NETs at other GI sites.

C1.summary_text: The incidence of duodenal NETs is increasing in routine clinical practice [S1|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799]. Most duodenal NETs are non-functional and are incidentally discovered on endoscopy [S2|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799]. Endoscopically, they are described as small, sessile erythematous or pale lesions, or submucosal hemispherical or flatly elevated lesions, often found in the duodenal cap, bulb, or first/second parts of the duodenum [S3|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799]. In routine practice, they are often described as mucosal or submucosal nodules [S4|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799]. A nodular endoscopic appearance can also indicate benign conditions like Brunner gland hyperplasia, gastric heterotopia, peptic duodenitis, and lymphoid hyperplasia [S5|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799]. For duodenal NETs, there is limited evidence for a wait-and-watch policy, and complete excision via endoscopic or local resection is generally recommended [S6|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799]. Treatment decisions are based on tumour size, location, histological grade, stage, and tumour type [S7|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799]. Duodenal NETs are known to metastasize to lymph nodes and liver, with tumours ≤ 1 cm having a 40% chance of nodal metastases [S8|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799]. Pathological assessment and grading of duodenal NETs are similar to NETs at other GI sites [S9|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799].

C1.summary_text: Duodenal neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) are increasingly detected in routine clinical practice due to the rise in endoscopy procedures [S1|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799]. Most duodenal NETs are non-functional and often incidentally discovered during endoscopy [S2|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799]. Endoscopically, these tumors appear as small, sessile erythematous or pale lesions or submucosal hemispherical or flatly elevated lesions located in the duodenal cap, bulb, or first and second parts of the duodenum [S3|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799]. In clinical practice, they are frequently described as mucosal or submucosal nodules [S4|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799]. A nodular endoscopic appearance in the duodenum can also correspond to benign histological differentials such as Brunner gland hyperplasia, gastric heterotopia, peptic duodenitis, and lymphoid hyperplasia [S5|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799]. Treatment generally involves complete excision by endoscopic or local resection, especially since a wait-and-watch approach has limited evidence [S6|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799]. Treatment decisions depend on tumor size, location, histological grade, stage, and tumor type [S7|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799]. Duodenal NETs can metastasize to lymph nodes and liver, with even tumors ≤ 1 cm having a 40% chance of nodal metastases, underscoring the importance of early and accurate diagnosis [S8|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799]. The pathological assessment and grading of duodenal NETs is similar to that of NETs at other gastrointestinal sites [S9|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799].

C1.summary_text: This chunk describes the clinical and pathological features of duodenal neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) [S1]. The majority are non-functional and often incidentally discovered on endoscopy [S2]. Endoscopically, duodenal NETs appear as small, sessile erythematous or pale lesions, or submucosal hemispherical/flatly elevated lesions located in the duodenal cap, bulb, or first/second parts of the duodenum [S3]. The nodular endoscopic appearance can mimic benign conditions including Brunner gland hyperplasia, gastric heterotopia, peptic duodenitis, and lymphoid hyperplasia [S5]. Once diagnosed, complete excision via endoscopic or local resection is generally recommended; wait-and-watch policies have very limited evidence [S6]. Treatment decisions are based on tumor size, location, histological grade, stage, and type [S7]. Notably, even small duodenal NETs (≤1 cm) carry a 40% risk of nodal metastases, and metastases to lymph nodes and liver are known to occur, emphasizing the importance of early accurate diagnosis [S8].

C1.summary_text: This chunk introduces the clinical and pathological landscape of duodenal neuroendocrine tumours (NETs). The majority of duodenal NETs are non-functional and are incidentally discovered on endoscopy [S2|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799]. Endoscopically, they manifest as small, sessile, erythematous or pale lesions, or as submucosal hemispherical/flatly elevated lesions in the duodenal cap, bulb, or first/second part of the duodenum [S3|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799]. The differential diagnosis for a nodular duodenal appearance includes benign entities such as Brunner gland hyperplasia, gastric heterotopia, peptic duodenitis, and lymphoid hyperplasia [S5|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799]. Evidence for a wait-and-watch policy is very limited; complete excision via endoscopic or local resection is generally recommended [S6|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799]. Treatment decisions are driven by tumour size, location, histological grade, stage, and tumour type [S7|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799]. Critically, duodenal NETs metastasise to lymph nodes and liver, and even tumours ≤1 cm carry a 40% risk of nodal metastases [S8|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799]. Pathological grading is performed analogously to NETs at other GI sites [S9|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4799].

C1.sentence: Histological examination of formalinfixed, paraffinembedded sections from the resected specimen on hematoxylin and eosin (HE) revealed perivascular mononuclear cell infiltration containing abundant eosinophils and plasma cells (Fig. 2A).

Transmural mononuclear cell infiltration with destructive or occlusive changes (Fig. 2B) and concentric arrangement of reticularfibers (Fig. 2C) was also noted in the venous vessels, which infiltrated the brain parenchyma together with eosinophils.
Plasma cells of different sizes with occasional binucleation were found in areas distant from the blood vessels (Fig. 2D).

There was no granulomatous inflammation, neutrophil infiltration,fibrinoid necrosis of vessel walls, thrombotic obstruction, or infectious lesions by microorganisms such as bacteria, fungi, parasites, and protozoa.

Immunohistochemically, the infiltrating mononuclear cells consisted of a central area mainly containing CD3-positive T-cells (Fig. 2E) with a subset of CD8-positive cells, surrounded by a peripheral area containing abundant CD138-positive plasma cells (Fig. 2F), a few CD20-positive B-cells (Fig. 2G), and rare CD1a-positive dendritic cells.
These inflammatory cells, including eosinophils, also infiltrated the surrounding brain parenchyma, showing marked reactive astrogliosis and macrophage/microglial infiltration (Fig. 2A, D, H).
Ki-67-positive nuclei were found in both lymphocytes and plasma cells (Fig. 2I).
No immunoreactivity for amyloidβ was observed throughout the specimen.

C1.summary_text: Histological examination revealed perivascular mononuclear cell infiltration with abundant eosinophils and plasma cells, and transmural mononuclear cell infiltration with destructive or occlusive changes in venous vessels, which also infiltrated the brain parenchyma along with eosinophils. Plasma cells showed occasional binucleation. Granulomatous inflammation, neutrophil infiltration, fibrinoid necrosis of vessel walls, thrombotic obstruction, and infectious lesions were absent. Immunohistochemistry showed infiltrating mononuclear cells to be mainly CD3-positive T-cells in the central area, with a subset of CD8-positive cells, surrounded by a peripheral area of abundant CD138-positive plasma cells, few CD20-positive B-cells, and rare CD1a-positive dendritic cells. Inflammatory cells, including eosinophils, infiltrated the surrounding brain parenchyma, showing reactive astrogliosis and macrophage/microglial infiltration. Ki-67-positive nuclei were found in lymphocytes and plasma cells. No immunoreactivity for amyloid-beta was observed. C1.summary_text: The histological examination revealed perivascular mononuclear cell infiltration with abundant eosinophils and plasma cells, transmural infiltration with destructive changes in venous vessels, concentric reticular fiber arrangement, plasma cells with binucleation distant from blood vessels, and absence of granulomatous inflammation, neutrophil infiltration, fibrinoid necrosis, thrombotic obstruction, or infectious lesions. No amyloidβ immunoreactivity was observed. Epstein-Barr virus in situ hybridization was performed.

Inflammatory cells, including eosinophils, infiltrated the surrounding brain parenchyma, which also displayed marked reactive astrogliosis and macrophage/microglial infiltration [S6|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10427]. Ki-67-positive nuclei were present in both lymphocytes and plasma cells [S7|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10427]. C1.summary_text: Histological examination of formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded sections stained with hematoxylin and eosin revealed perivascular mononuclear cell infiltration containing abundant eosinophils and plasma cells. Venous vessels showed transmural mononuclear cell infiltration with destructive or occlusive changes and concentric arrangement of reticular fibers, infiltrating the brain parenchyma together with eosinophils. Plasma cells of different sizes with occasional binucleation were found in areas distant from blood vessels. There was no granulomatous inflammation, neutrophil infiltration, fibrinoid necrosis of vessel walls, thrombotic obstruction, or infectious lesions by microorganisms such as bacteria, fungi, parasites, and protozoa. Immunohistochemistry showed that infiltrating mononuclear cells consisted mainly of CD3-positive T-cells in the central area with a subset of CD8-positive cells, surrounded by a peripheral area containing abundant CD138-positive plasma cells, a few CD20-positive B-cells, and rare CD1a-positive dendritic cells. Inflammatory cells including eosinophils infiltrated the surrounding brain parenchyma with marked reactive astrogliosis and macrophage/microglial infiltration. Ki-67-positive nuclei were found in both lymphocytes and plasma cells. No immunoreactivity for amyloid β was observed throughout the specimen [S1-S8|PMC9541515].

C1.summary_text: This case series analyzed histopathological and immunohistochemical features of a brain lesion specimen. Hematoxylin and eosin staining revealed [S1] perivascular mononuclear cell infiltration with abundant eosinophils and plasma cells, [S2] transmural mononuclear cell infiltration with destructive or occlusive changes and concentric reticular fiber arrangement in venous vessels, and [S3] plasma cells of varying sizes with occasional binucleation in parenchymal areas. [S4] Notably absent were granulomatous inflammation, neutrophil infiltration, fibrinoid necrosis, thrombotic obstruction, and infectious lesions. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated [S5] a spatially organized cellular composition with CD3-positive T-cells (including CD8-positive subsets) in the central infiltrate region, surrounded by abundant CD138-positive plasma cells, few CD20-positive B-cells, and rare CD1a-positive dendritic cells in the periphery. [S6] Eosinophils and macrophage/microglial infiltration extended into brain parenchyma with marked astrogliosis. [S7] Ki-67 positivity indicated proliferative activity in both lymphocytes and plasma cells. [S8] Amyloid-beta immunoreactivity was absent. [S9] Epstein-Barr virus analysis was initiated but incomplete in this chunk.

C1.summary_text: Histological examination (H&E) of the resected brain specimen revealed perivascular mononuclear cell infiltration with abundant eosinophils and plasma cells [S1|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10427]. Venous vessels showed transmural mononuclear infiltration with destructive/occlusive changes and concentric reticular fiber arrangement, with infiltration extending into brain parenchyma alongside eosinophils [S2|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10427]. Plasma cells distant from vessels exhibited size variation and occasional binucleation [S3|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10427]. Importantly, granulomatous inflammation, neutrophil infiltration, fibrinoid necrosis, thrombotic obstruction, and infectious organisms were all absent [S4|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10427]. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated a zonal organization: CD3+ T-cells (with a CD8+ subset) in the central area, surrounded peripherally by abundant CD138+ plasma cells, few CD20+ B-cells, and rare CD1a+ dendritic cells [S5|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10427]. The inflammatory infiltrate extended into brain parenchyma with marked reactive astrogliosis and macrophage/microglial infiltration [S6|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10427]. Ki-67 positivity was observed in both lymphocytes and plasma cells [S7|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10427]. Amyloid-β immunoreactivity was absent throughout [S8|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10427]. Epstein-Barr virus in situ hybridization was performed but the result is truncated at the chunk boundary [S9|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10427].

Overall concordance between the two methods was 96.4% [S1|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|19001]. All six discordant cases were SISH-positive and FISH-negative, yielding sensitivity=1, specificity=0.956, concordance=0.964, and kappa=0.884 [S2|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|19001]. Review of discordant FISH slides revealed polysomy, and real-time PCR confirmed the absence of true amplification in these cases [S3|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|19001]. All SISH concordant cases had ratios >3, with inter-observer medians of 8.1 and 6.02 (ranges 13.66 and 8.02, respectively) [S5|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|19001].

C1.sentence: Adult T cell leukaemia/lymphoma (ATLL) is a T cell malignancy caused by infection with human T cell leukaemia virus type I (HTLV-1).
ATLL exists as four clinical subtypes: smouldering, chronic, lymphoma and acute.
The latter two are considered aggressive and generally show a rapid clinical course.
In contrast, indolent ATLL (smouldering and chronic types) usually progresses slowly and does not require cytotoxic chemotherapy.
Lymphadenopathy is one of the most frequent manifestations of ATLL.
Morphologically, diffuse architectural effacement with proliferation of medium-sized or large pleomorphic cells is usually seen in the aggressive type.
Conversely, HTLV-1-associated lymphadenitis (HAL; morphologically reactive lymphadenitis developing in HTLV-1 carriers) has a good prognosis without treatment.

Although the morphological distinction between overt lymphoma and HAL is usually not difficult, some pathological features, such as dermatopathic reaction, make it hard to accurately evaluate lymph node lesions in HTLV-1 carriers.

C1.summary_text: Adult T cell leukaemia/lymphoma (ATLL) is a T cell malignancy caused by HTLV-1 infection, presenting with four clinical subtypes: smouldering, chronic, lymphoma, and acute. The lymphoma and acute subtypes are considered aggressive, characterized by diffuse architectural effacement and proliferation of medium-sized or large pleomorphic cells, and generally show a rapid clinical course. In contrast, the indolent smouldering and chronic subtypes usually progress slowly and do not require cytotoxic chemotherapy. Lymphadenopathy is a frequent manifestation of ATLL. HTLV-1-associated lymphadenitis (HAL), morphologically reactive lymphadenitis in HTLV-1 carriers, has a good prognosis without treatment. However, features like dermatopathic reaction can complicate the evaluation of lymph node lesions in HTLV-1 carriers. C1.summary_text: ATLL is a T cell malignancy caused by HTLV-1 infection [S1|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21913], presenting as four clinical subtypes: smouldering, chronic, lymphoma, and acute [S2|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21913]. The lymphoma and acute subtypes are aggressive with a rapid clinical course [S3|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21913], while the smouldering and chronic (indolent) subtypes progress slowly without need for cytotoxic chemotherapy [S4|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21913]. Lymphadenopathy is among the most frequent manifestations [S5|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21913]. Morphologically, aggressive-type ATLL shows diffuse architectural effacement with medium-sized or large pleomorphic cells [S6|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21913]. HTLV-1-associated lymphadenitis (HAL), a morphologically reactive lymphadenitis in HTLV-1 carriers, has a good prognosis without treatment [S7|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21913]. While ATLL lymphoma vs. HAL distinction is usually straightforward morphologically, pathological features such as dermatopathic reactions can complicate accurate evaluation of lymph node lesions in HTLV-1 carriers [S8|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21913].

A recent publication reviewed this matter.
An analysis, combining this information with our literature shows that, in 2513 samples, the mean HER2 positivity rate was 16.5% (range 6.9-42.6%), very similar to the results of our series.
Agreement exists that this alteration is associated with GCs of the intestinal type, but it is controversial whether it is homogeneous or focal.

HER2 amplification is more frequent in intestinal-type GC [S4–S5|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|19009], and was found to be heterogeneous in up to 52% of samples [S5|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|19009]. C1.sentence: Central nervous system (CNS) vasculitis can occur as either an isolated lesion or one manifestation of systemic vasculitis.

Clinical signs and symptoms are non-specific in patients with CNS vasculitis, including headache and cognitive decline, and focal neurologic deficits, such as aphasia and paralysis, with the onset of these symptoms varying from acute, subacute, and chronic.
A definite diagnosis of CNS vasculitis usually requires pathological verification by biopsy or surgical resection of the lesion, which may not always be feasible.

The 2012 revised International Chapel Hill Consensus Conference nomenclature (CHCC2012) provided mutually exclusive clinicopathological definitions for primary vasculitides based on the size of affected vessels.

We encountered an elderly patient presenting with slowly progressive hemiparesis associated with a heterogeneously enhanced tumor-like lesion on brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI); histopathological examination of the resected specimen revealed eosinophil-rich lymphocytic vasculitis, requiring differential diagnoses from lymphoma, lymphoproliferative disorders, and other non-neoplastic lesions.
However, the clinicopathological features did not meet any established disease definitions in the present case.

C1.summary_text: Central nervous system (CNS) vasculitis is a heterogeneous condition [S1] that can present as an isolated CNS lesion or as a component of systemic vasculitis [S1]. The clinical presentation is non-specific, including headache, cognitive decline, and focal neurologic deficits such as aphasia and paralysis, with variable onset (acute, subacute, or chronic) [S2]. Definitive diagnosis typically requires pathological verification via biopsy or surgical resection [S3]. On imaging, CNS vasculitis may present as a heterogeneously enhanced, tumor-like lesion on MRI [S5]. Histopathologically, eosinophil-rich lymphocytic vasculitis can be observed [S5], requiring differential diagnosis from lymphoma and other lymphoproliferative or non-neoplastic lesions [S5]. The diagnostic criteria established by the 2012 CHCC nomenclature based on vessel size may not always encompass all clinicopathological presentations [S4, S6].

C1.summary_text: In this chunk [S1|PMC7508500_main|14266], two key observations are reported regarding antibody detection performance. First, there was a positive trend between increasing IgA, IgG, and IgM titres measured by IFA and improved detection rates. C1.sentence: All biopsies were revised by one senior pathologist (G.v.L.) together with a combination of four junior (C.K., I.K., L.R., T.H.) pathologists, who each reviewed a subset of the cases.
In case of discordances, the senior pathologist's assessment was recorded.
The observers were all blinded to clinical information and patient outcome.

For each biopsy we recorded tumour length in millimetres, highest Gleason score/grade group according to the 2014 ISUP recommendations and the presence of invasive cribriform and intraductal carcinoma.

Cribriform carcinoma was defined as a contiguous proliferation of malignant epithelial cells with the majority of tumour cells not being in contact with adjacent stroma and with identifiable intercellular lumina.

A large cribriform pattern was defined as having a diameter of at least twice the size of adjacent benign glands, while the diameter of a small cribriform pattern was smaller than twice the size of pre-existing benign glands (Figure 1).
IDC was distinguished from highgrade prostate intra-epithelial neoplasia (HGPIN) by morphological features as described by Guo et al., and not incorporated into the grade group assessment.
Because their considerable morphological overlap requires basal cell immunohistochemistry for differentiation, invasive cribriform and intraductal carcinoma were analysed as one group (invCR/IDC).
If a case had both large and small invCR/IDC, it was classified as large cribriform in further analysis.

C1.summary_text: All biopsies were revised by pathologists, blinded to clinical information and patient outcome. C1.summary_text: This section outlines the histopathological review methodology and definitions for a prostate cancer biopsy cohort study. All biopsies were revised by one senior pathologist with four junior pathologists [S1|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17558], with observers blinded to clinical data [S3|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17558]. Pathologists recorded tumour length, Gleason score/grade group, and presence of invasive cribriform and intraductal carcinoma [S4|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17558]. Cribriform carcinoma was defined as contiguous malignant epithelial proliferation with tumour cells not in stromal contact and identifiable intercellular lumina [S5|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17558]. Large cribriform patterns were defined as ≥2× the diameter of adjacent benign glands, while small cribriform patterns were <2× the diameter of pre-existing benign glands [S6|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17558]. Intraductal carcinoma was distinguished from high-grade prostate intra-epithelial neoplasia by morphological features [S7|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17558]. Due to considerable morphological overlap, invasive cribriform and intraductal carcinoma required basal cell immunohistochemistry for differentiation and were analyzed as one combined group (invCR/IDC) [S8|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17558].

C1.summary_text: This methods chunk (PMC9321809) describes histopathological assessment criteria for prostate cancer biopsies. Cribriform carcinoma is defined as a contiguous proliferation of malignant epithelial cells, the majority not in contact with adjacent stroma, with identifiable intercellular lumina [S5]. Large cribriform pattern is defined as diameter ≥2x adjacent benign glands, while small cribriform pattern is diameter <2x [S6]. IDC is distinguished from HGPIN by morphological criteria per Guo et al. and is excluded from grade group assignment [S7]. Because invasive cribriform carcinoma and IDC share considerable morphological overlap requiring basal cell IHC for definitive differentiation, they were grouped together as invCR/IDC [S8]. When both large and small invCR/IDC co-existed, the case was classified as large cribriform [S9]. Per biopsy, tumour length (mm), highest Gleason score/grade group (2014 ISUP), and presence of invCR/IDC were recorded [S4].

C1.sentence: Our comprehensive review of the literature confirms the already widely established data regarding the almost non-existent recurrence and/or distant metastasis of EMPSGC, with very few cases of this one.

Interestingly, Froehlich et al. reported a case of EMPSGC of the right eyelid in a patient who had not wanted to undergo surgery after an initial diagnosis and who, upon recurrence, developed a metastasis in 2/9 excised intra-parotid lymph nodes.
It is reasonable to state that this result was not due to the (in itself low) potential of the neoplasm, but to the failure to undergo surgery for therapeutic purposes.

In another paper by Hadi et al., a case is presented of a 66-year-old subject who developed several recurrences of EMPSGC over a period of nine years, with a metastatic lesion on the ipsilateral parotid gland and a rib.

This anecdotal case is of extraordinary importance, as the authors emphasize that the histological and immunohistochemical evaluation of EMPSGC must be very detailed and careful, as potential foci of invasion can easily be overlooked, and not correctly framed within the rarer but aggressive PCMC.

Precisely in this regard, several papers analyzed in the literature have proposed to always perform an immunolabelling with Smooth Actin muscle (SMA), or p63 p CK5/6, to study the continuity of the myoepithelium, similar to what happens in the evaluation of breast cancer.

Although the data presented are in agreement with this solution, in order to understand whether there is reduction/disappearance of the myoepithelium with consequent potential invasiveness of EMPSGC, a paper by Saggini et al. critically addresses the use of IHC markers for the myoepithelium, as they are prone to error.

In particular, referring to the breast, the authors caution against defining as 'invasive' an EMPSGC that, while losing myoepithelial IHC markers, always grows in an expansive pattern in the absence of clear tongues of infiltration.

The neoplasm has low metastatic potential, but failure to undergo surgery can lead to metastasis [S3|PMC10529628_dermatopathology-10-00035|1774]. Histological and immunohistochemical evaluation of EMPSGC must be detailed and careful, as potential foci of invasion can be easily overlooked [S5|PMC10529628_dermatopathology-10-00035|1774]. Caution is advised against defining EMPSGC as 'invasive' if it exhibits an expansive growth pattern without clear tongues of infiltration, even with the loss of myoepithelial IHC markers [S8|PMC10529628_dermatopathology-10-00035|1774].

C1.summary_text: This literature review examines the rarity of recurrence and metastasis in extramammary Paget's disease of sweat gland carcinoma (EMPSGC) [S1]. While recurrence and distant metastasis are characteristically uncommon, two notable anecdotal cases highlight exceptions: one patient with EMPSGC of the right eyelid who declined initial surgery developed metastasis in intra-parotid lymph nodes upon recurrence [S2], and another patient experienced multiple recurrences and metastases to parotid gland and rib over nine years [S4]. These cases are attributed to therapeutic failure or incomplete evaluation rather than inherent neoplastic aggressiveness [S3]. The literature emphasizes the critical importance of meticulous histopathological and immunohistochemical evaluation of EMPSGC to identify potential foci of invasion and avoid misclassification as primary cutaneous myxoid carcinoma (PCMC) [S5]. Multiple studies recommend immunolabelling with SMA, p63, or CK5/6 to assess myoepithelial continuity [S6], though these markers are noted to be prone to interpretive error [S7]. Loss of myoepithelial IHC markers should not alone define EMPSGC as invasive if the lesion exhibits an expansive rather than infiltrative growth pattern [S8].
