C1.summary_text: This chunk from PMC10529628 presents a literature review of EMPSGC (ectopic mammary-like sweat gland carcinoma / eccrine mucinous primary sweat gland carcinoma). The overall prognosis is favourable, with recurrence and distant metastasis being almost non-existent [S1]. However, two illustrative cases highlight exceptions: one case involving metastasis to 2/9 intra-parotid lymph nodes following refusal of surgery [S2], attributed not to inherent neoplasm aggressiveness but to the lack of surgical intervention [S3]; and another with multiple recurrences over nine years and metastasis to the parotid gland and a rib [S4]. The latter case underscores the need for meticulous histological and IHC evaluation to avoid missing foci of invasion and misclassifying lesions within the rarer but aggressive primary cutaneous mucinous carcinoma (PCMC) [S5]. Multiple literature sources recommend immunolabelling with SMA, p63, and CK5/6 to evaluate myoepithelial continuity, analogous to breast cancer evaluation [S6], though these markers are noted to be prone to interpretive error [S7]. Crucially, loss of myoepithelial IHC markers alone should not lead to an 'invasive' designation if the tumour grows in an expansive pattern without clear tongues of infiltration [S8].

[S1|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15509] The current WHO classification of urinary and male genital tumours does include a category for adenomas of the rete testis, but there is no explanation of how these tumours differ from those previously described as 'Sertoliform' cystadenomas in the literature.
[S2|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15509] Hence, the interpretation of what constitutes a Sertoli cell tumour NOS with growth confined to the rete testis and a true adenoma of the rete testis seems entirely arbitrary.
[S3|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15509] Moreover, to the best of our knowledge, there is no convincing documentation of a Sertoli cell tumour with pure intra-rete growth.
[S4|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15509] The present study demonstrates that four lesions within the spectrum of Sertoliform cystadenoma of the rete testis (and originally classified as such) were negative for pathogenic CTNNB1 variants, lacked nuclear expression of beta-catenin, and were positive for PAX8.
[S5|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15509] Additionally, three tumours showed a clear transition between the nonneoplastic rete epithelium and the neoplastic epithelium.
[S6|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15509] These findings argue against the possibility of a Sertoli cell tumour NOS growing into the rete testis, especially considering that over 90% of indolent Sertoli cell tumours show CTNNB1 or APC variants and nuclear beta-catenin expression and are negative for PAX8 nuclear expression.

C1.sentence: The current WHO classification of urinary and male genital tumours does include a category for adenomas of the rete testis, but there is no explanation of how these tumours differ from those previously described as 'Sertoliform' cystadenomas in the literature.
Hence, the interpretation of what constitutes a Sertoli cell tumour NOS with growth confined to the rete testis and a true adenoma of the rete testis seems entirely arbitrary.
Moreover, to the best of our knowledge, there is no convincing documentation of a Sertoli cell tumour with pure intra-rete growth.

The present study demonstrates that four lesions within the spectrum of Sertoliform cystadenoma of the rete testis (and originally classified as such) were negative for pathogenic CTNNB1 variants, lacked nuclear expression of beta-catenin, and were positive for PAX8.

C1.summary_text: This study identifies a distinctive molecular and immunophenotypic profile for Sertoliform cystadenomas of the rete testis that differentiates them from Sertoli cell tumours [S4|S6]. Four cases of Sertoliform cystadenoma lacked pathogenic CTNNB1 variants, lacked nuclear beta-catenin expression, and were PAX8-positive [S4]. Three of these lesions demonstrated clear transitions between nonneoplastic and neoplastic epithelium [S5]. In contrast, >90% of indolent Sertoli cell tumours exhibit CTNNB1 or APC variants, show nuclear beta-catenin expression, and are PAX8-negative [S6]. These contrasting molecular profiles—characterized by the presence of CTNNB1/APC mutations and beta-catenin expression in Sertoli cell tumours versus their absence and PAX8 positivity in rete testis cystadenomas—provide molecular evidence that these are distinct entities rather than variations of a single diagnostic entity [S4|S6].

C1.summary_text: This chunk (PMC12129600) addresses the classification challenge between Sertoliform cystadenoma of the rete testis and Sertoli cell tumour NOS with intra-rete growth. The authors note that the current WHO classification provides no clear criteria to distinguish these entities [S1|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15509], and that no convincing case of a Sertoli cell tumour with pure intra-rete growth exists in the literature [S3|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15509]. In a case series of 4 lesions originally classified as Sertoliform cystadenomas, the tumours were negative for pathogenic CTNNB1 variants, lacked nuclear beta-catenin expression, and were positive for PAX8 [S4|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15509]. Three of four tumours also demonstrated a clear morphological transition between nonneoplastic and neoplastic rete epithelium [S5|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15509]. These IHC and molecular findings sharply contrast with indolent Sertoli cell tumours, of which >90% harbour CTNNB1 or APC variants, show nuclear beta-catenin positivity, and are PAX8-negative [S6|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15509], collectively arguing against reclassifying these rete testis adenomas as Sertoli cell tumours NOS.

C1.summary_text: This chunk describes the molecular genetic diagnosis of lipoprotein lipase (LPL) deficiency as a monogenic cause of severe, treatment-resistant hypertriglyceridaemia [S1|PMC9012948_main|6802]. Sanger sequencing of the LPL gene (NM_000237.2) identified apparent compound heterozygosity for two previously reported pathogenic variants: c.292G>A p.(Ala98Thr) (rs145657341) and c.835C>G p.(Leu279Val) (rs371282890), confirming the diagnosis [S2|PMC9012948_main|6802, S3|PMC9012948_main|6802]. A clinically important treatment note was also extracted: fish oil supplements are contraindicated in lipoprotein lipase deficiency [S5|PMC9012948_main|6802]. Family cascade screening and the discontinuation of fish oil supplements were recommended [S4|PMC9012948_main|6802, S6|PMC9012948_main|6802].

C1.summary_text: Benign peripheral nerve sheath tumors (BPNST) include perineurioma, schwannoma, and neurofibroma. Hybrid BPNST examples such as schwannoma/neurofibroma, neurofibroma/perineurioma, schwannoma/ perineurioma, or schwannoma/perineurioma/neurofibroma have been described. Tumors with divergent neural differentiation, including hybrid schwannoma/neurothekeoma and melanocytic nevus with schwannoma and perineurioma, have also been reported. These tumors typically arise in the skin of the extremities and trunk, with less frequent involvement of extracutaneous sites. Two rare cases of tumors with hybrid features of schwannoma/ perineurioma and schwannoma/neurofibroma were reported, located in the scalp and ankle, respectively.

C1.sentence: Discrepancy between FISH and SISH occurred in six of 166 cases, all of them positive for SISH (all ratios between 2.06 and 2.50) and negative for FISH.
All discrepant cases were polysomic by FISH and negative for HER2 amplification by real-time PCR.
These results are consistent with previous studies reporting on both EGF R and HER 2 brightfield ISH, both using singlecolour and dual-colour approaches.
However, it must pointed out that, in some series, the brightfield ISH results are 'false' negatives, not 'false' positives, and this has potential clinical conse- quences.
Interestingly, polysomy has been reported as the major cause of response to trastuzumab in FISH-negative breast carcinoma patients.
In our series, no cases showing gene amplification by FISH were considered to be negative by SISH.

When we raised the SISH cut-off for amplification ( ‡ 3), the concordance was 100%, demonstrating that SISH is a valid testing method for HER2 testing in GC patients and that a higher cut-off ( ‡ 3) should be considered even for dual-colour SISH, in order to increase the concordance rate.
It is also necessary to take into account that polysomy may be the cause of interobserver differences.

A very recent report on a study using a similar methodogy to the one reported herein (fully automated SISH assay with single-colour locus detection on two separate slides) has arrived at the same conclusions: chromosome 17 counts are the main source of discrepancy between SISH and FISH ratios.
Another potential source of disagreement between ISH techniques is heterogeneity.

C1.summary_text: Discrepancies between FISH and SISH for HER2 amplification occurred in 6 of 166 cases, with SISH being positive and FISH negative [S1]. These discrepant cases were polysomic by FISH and negative for HER2 amplification by real-time PCR [S2]. Brightfield ISH can yield 'false' negatives [S4]. Polysomy is implicated as a cause of response to trastuzumab in FISH-negative breast carcinoma patients [S5] and may also contribute to interobserver differences [S8]. No cases with FISH-detected gene amplification were considered SISH-negative [S6]. Increasing the SISH cut-off for amplification to ≥3 achieved 100% concordance, supporting SISH as a valid HER2 testing method in GC patients, and suggesting a higher cut-off should be considered [S7]. Chromosome 17 counts are identified as the primary source of discrepancy between SISH and FISH ratios [S9], and heterogeneity is another potential source of disagreement between ISH techniques [S10].

C1.summary_text: In a cohort of 166 gastric carcinoma (GC) cases, FISH/SISH discrepancy was observed in 6 cases (3.6%), all of which were SISH-positive (ratios 2.06–2.50) and FISH-negative [S1|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|19007]. These six discrepant cases were polysomic by FISH and lacked true HER2 amplification as confirmed by real-time PCR [S2|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|19007]. No FISH-amplified case was misclassified as SISH-negative, confirming absence of false negatives by SISH [S6|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|19007]. Raising the SISH cut-off to ≥3 achieved 100% concordance with FISH, supporting SISH as a valid HER2 testing modality in GC and suggesting that a higher cut-off (≥3) should be used even for dual-colour SISH [S7|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|19007]. Chromosome 17 polysomy was identified as the principal driver of SISH/FISH discordance [S8|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|19007; S9|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|19007], and tumour heterogeneity was noted as an additional source of inter-technique disagreement [S10|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|19007]. Notably, polysomy has been reported as the major cause of trastuzumab response in FISH-negative breast carcinoma patients [S5|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|19007]. In some brightfield ISH series, false negatives rather than false positives occur, carrying potential clinical consequences [S4|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|19007].

C1.summary_text: This chunk addresses the molecular genetics of lipoprotein lipase (LPL) deficiency. No known genotype-phenotype correlation exists in LPL deficiency [S1|PMC9012948_main|6803]. The LPL Ala98Thr variant decreases both secretion and catalytic activity of LPL, though with some residual activity preserved [S2|PMC9012948_main|6803], whereas the LPL Leu279Val variant almost completely abolishes catalytic activity [S3|PMC9012948_main|6803]. Two additional literature cases carrying the same compound heterozygous LPL Ala98Thr/Leu279Val genotype were identified: one presented with acute pancreatitis during late pregnancy (a state physiologically associated with hypertriglyceridaemia), and the other was diagnosed after three episodes of pancreatitis [S4–S5|PMC9012948_main|6803].

C1.summary_text: Cytological examination of metastatic carcinoma samples [S1|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13928] identified megakaryocytes in 14 of 35 cases. The cytology preparations were complicated by the presence of ambiguous cells that could not be reliably distinguished from circulating tumor cells (CTCs), non-malignant circulating cells (NCCCs), degenerate megakaryocytes, or micromegakaryocytes [S2|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13928]. C1.summary_text: In a case series of metastatic carcinoma, cytology was performed on 35 cases, of which 14 (40%) demonstrated megakaryocytes [S1|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13928]. A subset of cases yielded ambiguous cells that could not be confidently classified as circulating tumour cells (CTCs), non-cancerous circulating cells (NCCCs), degenerate megakaryocytes, or micromegakaryocytes [S2|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13928]. This diagnostic difficulty was attributed in part to prominent cytoplasm stripping artefact affecting many cells [S3|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13928], with only occasional cells being well preserved [S4|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13928].

C1.sentence: The definite diagnosis of central nervous system vasculitis requires pathological verification by biopsy or surgical resection of the lesion, which may not always be feasible.
A 74-year-old woman with a history of allergic rhinitis, but not asthma, presented with slowly progressive left hemiparesis.
Magnetic resonance imaging of the head revealed a heterogeneously enhancing mass involving the right internal capsule and corona radiata.
Histological examination of the resected specimen revealed eosinophilrich non-granulomatous small vessel vasculitis with no neutrophil infiltration or foci of microbial infection.

Epstein -Barr virus in situ hybridization was negative, and polymerase chain reaction tests for both T-cell receptor gamma and immunoglobulin heavy-chain variable region genes did not show rearrangements, excluding the possibility of lymphoma and lymphoproliferative disorders.
Blood hypereosinophilia and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate were observed; however, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were not detected.

C1.summary_text: This case report describes a 74-year-old woman with eosinophilic CNS vasculitis presenting with progressive left hemiparesis [S2|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10417]. Definite diagnosis of CNS vasculitis requires pathological verification by biopsy or surgical resection [S1|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10417]. Histopathology of the resected CNS lesion revealed eosinophil-rich, non-granulomatous small vessel vasculitis without neutrophil infiltration or microbial infection [S4|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10417]. Negative findings included Epstein-Barr virus in situ hybridization, no T-cell receptor gamma or immunoglobulin heavy-chain gene rearrangement (excluding lymphoma), and absence of anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies [S5|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10417, S6|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10417]. Associated laboratory findings included blood hypereosinophilia and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate [S6|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10417]. Cutaneous biopsy from hips and thighs showed perivasculitis with eosinophilic infiltration of the dermis [S7|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10417], and chest CT revealed multiple small lung nodules [S8|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10417]. Corticosteroid administration resulted in resolution of most symptoms except for persistent hemiparesis [S9|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10417]. The clinicopathological features were similar to eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis but did not fully meet its diagnostic criteria [S10|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10417].

C1.summary_text: This case report (PMC9541515) describes a rare presentation of eosinophil-rich non-granulomatous small vessel CNS vasculitis. Definitive CNS vasculitis diagnosis requires pathological biopsy or surgical resection [S1]. Histological examination revealed eosinophil-rich non-granulomatous small vessel vasculitis with absent neutrophil infiltration and no microbial infection foci [S4]. Lymphoma and lymphoproliferative disorders were excluded by absent EBV in situ hybridization and no clonal rearrangements of T-cell receptor gamma or immunoglobulin heavy-chain variable region genes by PCR [S5]. Systemically, blood hypereosinophilia and elevated ESR were present, while ANCA was undetected [S6]. Skin biopsy showed perivasculitis with dermal eosinophilic infiltration [S7], and chest CT demonstrated multiple small pulmonary nodules [S8]. Corticosteroid treatment led to resolution of all symptoms except hemiparesis [S9]. The clinicopathological profile resembled eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) but did not fully satisfy current classification criteria [S10].

This chunk discusses the practical challenges of IgM serology testing in the context of SARS-CoV-2 vaccination and travel screening. The authors note that positive IgM results will become more common among travellers to China due to recent vaccination or infection [S1|PMC9012948_main|6787]. They suggest that nucleocapsid-based assays such as the Roche Total assay may reduce false-positive IgM detection in recently vaccinated individuals [S2|PMC9012948_main|6787], though such assays cannot distinguish between vaccine-induced and infection-induced nucleocapsid antibodies [S3|PMC9012948_main|6787]. The authors describe their laboratory practice of reflex testing with a lateral-flow nucleocapsid-specific IgM assay, which if positive leads to significant travel delays [S4|PMC9012948_main|6787]. They emphasize the substantial practical and economic burden of IgM testing requirements on international travellers [S5|PMC9012948_main|6787] and advocate for reliance on nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) alone [S6|PMC9012948_main|6787].

C1.summary_text: This concluding passage addresses the practical limitations of IgM-based SARS-CoV-2 serology in the travel context, particularly for travellers to China [S1|PMC9012948_main|6787]. The Roche Total nucleocapsid-based assay is proposed as a screening tool that may reduce false-positive IgM rates among recently vaccinated travellers, since it does not detect vaccine-induced spike IgM [S2–S3|PMC9012948_main|6787]. However, individuals previously infected with SARS-CoV-2 will have detectable nucleocapsid antibodies with this assay; in the described laboratory workflow, these are subsequently tested with a lateral-flow nucleocapsid-specific IgM assay, and a positive result is likely to cause significant travel delays [S3–S4|PMC9012948_main|6787]. The authors highlight that IgM testing pitfalls carry major practical implications, including inconvenience and cost from postponed travel and additional testing, a situation expected to persist [S5|PMC9012948_main|6787]. Ultimately, NAAT alone is advocated as the most reliable indicator of infection risk in travellers, with the "dual-test" (IgM + NAAT) requirement considered problematic [S6|PMC9012948_main|6787].

C1.sentence: Currently, precision oncology is based on the existence of alterations in certain specific therapeutic targets regardless of tumour location or type.

Tumours with somatic mutations such as BRAF, EGFR or gene rearrangements such as ALK are considered therapeutic options regardless of tumour type or location, and tumours may even be characterised as BRAFomas or ALKomas.

However, some clinical data have shown that, while BRAF inhibitors are effective in melanoma, the same inhibitors of the same BRAF mutations in colorectal cancer induce feedback loops in signalling pathways that can have a detrimental effect.
Cell signalling pathways are also highly regulated, often dependent on numerous positive and negative feedback loops, which are specific to the cell type and tumour environment.
For this reason, BRAF inhibition in colorectal cancer indirectly results in EGFR receptor activation and subsequent PI3K -Akt pathway activation.
Similarly, ALK alterations and their inhibitors do not have the same clinical response in lung tumours as in neuroblastomas.
Further examples are inhibitors of EGFR, HER2 and HER3, depending on the tumour type and location.

In a recent basket clinical trial, not all tumours were affected by the same HER mutations, and response to the HER2 inhibitor (neratinib) varied in different tissues: for example, colorectal or bladder cancer with HER2 mutations did not respond.
In summary, specific drug treatment depends on the tissue context.

C1.summary_text: Precision oncology currently relies on identifying alterations in specific therapeutic targets, irrespective of tumour location or type, such as somatic mutations (BRAF, EGFR) or gene rearrangements (ALK) which are considered therapeutic options [S2]. However, the effectiveness of targeted therapies can be influenced by the tumour environment and cell type. For instance, BRAF inhibitors are effective in melanoma but can have detrimental feedback effects in colorectal cancer by activating EGFR and the PI3K-Akt pathway [S3, S5]. Similarly, the clinical response to ALK alterations and their inhibitors varies between lung tumours and neuroblastomas [S6]. Inhibitors of EGFR, HER2, and HER3 also show context-dependent efficacy based on tumour type and location [S7]. A basket trial indicated that colorectal or bladder cancers with HER2 mutations did not respond to the HER2 inhibitor neratinib [S8]. Ultimately, specific drug treatment is contingent on the tissue context [S9].

C1.summary_text: Precision oncology is based on alterations in specific therapeutic targets [S1|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27837]. Tumours with somatic mutations like BRAF or EGFR, or gene rearrangements like ALK, are considered therapeutic options [S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27837]. Such tumours may be characterized as BRAFomas or ALKomas based on their mutations [S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27837]. While BRAF inhibitors are effective in melanoma, in colorectal cancer, they induce feedback loops in signalling pathways that can have a detrimental effect [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27837]. This is because BRAF inhibition in colorectal cancer indirectly activates EGFR receptors and the PI3K-Akt pathway [S5|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27837]. Cell signalling pathways are highly regulated and depend on positive and negative feedback loops, which are specific to cell type and tumour environment [S4|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27837]. ALK inhibitors for ALK alterations do not yield the same clinical response in lung tumours as in neuroblastomas [S6|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27837]. Similarly, the effectiveness of EGFR, HER2, and HER3 inhibitors depends on tumour type and location [S7|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27837]. A basket clinical trial showed that not all tumours were affected by the same HER mutations, and response to the HER2 inhibitor neratinib varied across tissues; for instance, colorectal or bladder cancer with HER2 mutations did not respond [S8|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27837]. Overall, specific drug treatment is dependent on the tissue context [S9|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27837].

C1.summary_text: This chunk addresses tissue context-dependent treatment response in precision oncology. While somatic mutations such as BRAF, EGFR, ALK, and HER2 are often considered therapeutic targets independent of tumour type or location [S1, S2], clinical evidence demonstrates significant variation in drug efficacy based on tissue environment. BRAF inhibitors are effective in melanoma [S3] but ineffective in colorectal cancer with BRAF mutations, where they induce detrimental feedback loops [S3] and subsequently activate EGFR receptors [S5] and the PI3K-Akt pathway [S5]. Similarly, ALK inhibitors show different clinical responses in lung tumours compared to neuroblastomas [S6]. In a recent basket clinical trial, HER2 inhibitor neratinib demonstrated tissue-dependent response, with colorectal and bladder cancers harbouring HER2 mutations showing no response [S8]. The underlying mechanism is rooted in cell type-specific signalling pathways that are regulated by feedback loops specific to the tumour environment [S4]. This evidence underscores that specific drug treatment depends on tissue context [S9].

C1.summary_text: This chunk discusses tissue-context dependency in precision oncology. BRAF inhibitors are effective in BRAF-mutant melanoma [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27837] but induce detrimental feedback loops in colorectal cancer [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27837], specifically by indirectly activating EGFR and the downstream PI3K-Akt pathway [S5|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27837]. ALK inhibitors yield different clinical responses in lung tumours compared to neuroblastomas [S6|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27837]. In a basket clinical trial, neratinib (HER2 inhibitor) showed variable responses across tumour types, with colorectal and bladder cancers harbouring HER2 mutations failing to respond [S8|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27837]. The overarching conclusion is that specific drug treatment depends on tissue context [S9|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27837].

C1.sentence: Four cases showed morphologic features compatible with so-called 'Sertoliform adenoma/cystadenoma' of the rete testis.
More specifically, these tumours were solid (one case) or solid and cystic (three cases), and well-circumscribed.
Confinement within expanded profiles of the rete testis was clearly identifiable in three tumours.
Architecture was tubulo-papillary (three tumours, Figure 1A -C), or tubular and trabecular (one tumour, Figure 1D,E), reminiscent of a Sertoli cell lesion.
Tubules were elongated and branching, often showing continuity with papillary structures.
Papillae were slender and showed occasional branching; in one case, the fibrovascular cores showed prominent hyalinization consistent with deposits of abundant basement membrane material.
One tumour was solid, with tubular and trabecular growth patterns.
In this lesion, trabeculae showed a parallel arrangement of epithelial cells, focally resembling a 'tram track', with prominent intratumoral lymphocytes and occasional hyaline globules.
Tumour cells were eosinophilic, cuboidal to columnar with minimal to mild atypia; nuclei were oval, elongated, or slightly irregular containing fine chromatin.
Nucleoli were inconspicuous, and mitotic activity was consistently low ( < 1 mitotic figure per 10 high-power fields).

C2.sentence: Necrosis, invasive growth, or angioinvasion were not identified.

In three of these tumours, areas of transition between the flat nonneoplastic epithelium of the rete and the neoplastic epithelium of the adenoma were clearly identifiable (Figure 2A -C), arguing against a Sertoli cell origin of these lesions.
Immunohistochemistry demonstrated that all of them expressed PAX8 diffusely (Figure 3A).
Expression of beta catenin was restricted to the cytoplasmic membrane in all cases (4/4; Figure 3B), with no tumour

C1.summary_text: Four cases exhibited morphologic features compatible with 'Sertoliform adenoma/cystadenoma' of the rete testis. These tumours were solid or solid and cystic, and well-circumscribed [S2]. Confinement within expanded rete testis profiles was identifiable in three tumours [S3]. The architecture was tubulo-papillary (three tumours) or tubular and trabecular (one tumour), reminiscent of a Sertoli cell lesion [S4]. Tubules were elongated and branching, often showing continuity with papillary structures [S5]. Papillae were slender and showed occasional branching [S6]. In one case, fibrovascular cores showed prominent hyalinization consistent with abundant basement membrane material [S6]. One tumour was solid with tubular and trabecular growth patterns [S7]. In this lesion, trabeculae showed a parallel arrangement of epithelial cells, focally resembling a 'tram track', with prominent intratumoral lymphocytes and occasional hyaline globules [S8]. Tumour cells were eosinophilic, cuboidal to columnar with minimal to mild atypia; nuclei were oval, elongated, or slightly irregular containing fine chromatin [S9]. Nucleoli were inconspicuous, and mitotic activity was consistently low (< 1 mitotic figure per 10 high-power fields) [S10].

C1.summary_text: Four cases exhibited morphologic features consistent with 'Sertoliform adenoma/cystadenoma' of the rete testis [S1|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504]. These tumours were well-circumscribed [S2|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504], with one case being solid and three cases being solid and cystic [S2|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504]. Confinement within expanded rete testis profiles was seen in three tumours [S3|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504]. Architecture was tubulo-papillary in three tumours and tubular and trabecular in one, reminiscent of a Sertoli cell lesion [S4|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504]. Tubules were elongated, branching, and often continuous with papillary structures [S5|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504]. Papillae were slender and occasionally branched; one case showed prominent hyalinization in fibrovascular cores, consistent with abundant basement membrane material deposits [S6|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504]. One tumour was solid with tubular and trabecular growth patterns [S7|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504], where trabeculae showed a parallel arrangement of epithelial cells, focally resembling a 'tram track', along with prominent intratumoral lymphocytes and occasional hyaline globules [S8|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504]. Tumour cells were eosinophilic, cuboidal to columnar, with minimal to mild atypia; nuclei were oval, elongated, or slightly irregular, containing fine chromatin [S9|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504]. Nucleoli were inconspicuous, and mitotic activity was consistently low (< 1 mitotic figure per 10 high-power fields) [S10|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504].

C1.summary_text: Sertoliform adenoma/cystadenoma of the rete testis presents morphologically as solid or solid and cystic tumours that are well-circumscribed and mostly confined within expanded profiles of the rete testis. The architecture is predominantly tubulo-papillary in most cases, with some showing tubular and trabecular patterns. Tubules are elongated and branching, often continuous with papillary structures. Papillae are slender and occasionally branching, with fibrovascular cores that can show prominent hyalinization consistent with abundant basement membrane material. Some tumours show solid growth with tubular and trabecular patterns, trabeculae with parallel epithelial cell arrangement resembling a 'tram track', prominent intratumoral lymphocytes, and occasional hyaline globules. Tumour cells are eosinophilic, cuboidal to columnar with minimal to mild atypia, oval to slightly irregular nuclei with fine chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli, and consistently low mitotic activity (<1 mitotic figure per 10 high-power fields) [S1-S10|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504].

C1.summary_text: This case series of four Sertoliform adenoma/cystadenoma of the rete testis presents detailed morphologic characterization [S1]. The tumours demonstrated a predominantly solid or solid-and-cystic architecture with well-circumscribed borders, with three showing clear confinement within expanded rete testis profiles [S2, S3]. Architecturally, the lesions exhibited either tubulo-papillary patterns (three cases) or mixed tubular and trabecular patterns (one case), with resemblance to Sertoli cell lesions [S4]. Tubules were characteristically elongated and branching with continuity to papillary structures [S5]. Papillae appeared slender with occasional branching; in one case, fibrovascular cores demonstrated prominent hyalinization consistent with abundant basement membrane material [S6]. One solid variant displayed trabecular architecture with parallel epithelial cell arrangement resembling 'tram track' pattern, featuring prominent intratumoral lymphocytes and occasional hyaline globules [S7, S8]. Cytologically, tumour cells were eosinophilic with cuboidal to columnar morphology and minimal to mild atypia; nuclei were oval, elongated, or slightly irregular with fine chromatin [S9]. Importantly, nucleoli were inconspicuous and mitotic activity remained consistently low at less than 1 mitotic figure per 10 high-power fields [S10].

C1.summary_text: This chunk describes 4 cases of 'Sertoliform adenoma/cystadenoma' of the rete testis [S1|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504]. Grossly, tumours were solid (1 case) or solid and cystic (3 cases) and well-circumscribed [S2|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504]; 3/4 showed clear confinement within expanded rete testis profiles [S3|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504]. Architecturally, 3 tumours were tubulo-papillary and 1 was tubular-trabecular, all reminiscent of a Sertoli cell lesion [S4|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504]. Tubules were elongated and branching with continuity to papillary structures [S5|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504]; papillae were slender with occasional branching, and one case showed fibrovascular core hyalinization from basement membrane material deposits [S6|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504]. The solid tumour displayed a 'tram-track' trabecular pattern, prominent intratumoral lymphocytes, and occasional hyaline globules [S7–S8|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504]. Cytologically, tumour cells were eosinophilic, cuboidal to columnar with minimal-to-mild atypia; nuclei were oval/elongated/slightly irregular with fine chromatin [S9|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504]. Nucleoli were inconspicuous and mitotic activity was uniformly low (<1/10 HPF) [S10|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15504].

Using the LightMix HER-2/neu kit (Roche Diagnostics), positive control samples (amplified by both FISH and SISH) were confirmed as amplified by PCR [S2]. Conversely, samples negative by both FISH and SISH yielded a normalized HER2/RPL23 ratio of ~1 (range 0.836–1.0), well below the cut-off of 2, confirming non-amplification [S3]. After normalization of the target/reference gene ratio, all tumours in the discordant cohort had ratios <2, confirming FISH-based classification [S4].

In-house validation demonstrated high specificity for both assays — 99.5% for Roche Total and 98.9% for Abbott IgM — values comparable to manufacturer-stated specificities of 99.8% and 99.56%, respectively [S2|PMC9012948_main|6776]. However, in-house sensitivity at 8–14 days post symptom onset in confirmed COVID-19 cases was 67% for both assays, substantially lower than the manufacturer-stated sensitivity of 85% [S3|PMC9012948_main|6776].

C1.summary_text: Four different point-of-care tests (POCTs) for SARS-CoV-2 antibodies were evaluated: OnSite COVID-19 IgG/IgM Rapid Test, 2019-nCov Antibody Test, SARS-CoV-2 Antibody Test Strip, and Standard Q COVID-19 IgM/IgG Duo/Combo Test. All are lateral flow assays designed to detect IgG and IgM antibodies in whole blood, plasma, or serum [S1, S2]. The OnSite, Innovita, and Standard Q Combo tests utilize separate lines for IgG and IgM detection, whereas the Sinocare test uses a single line for both [S3]. The Standard Q Duo tests feature separate devices for IgG and IgM but are functionally similar to the Combo test [S4]. A valid test requires the development of a control line [S5]. These POCTs are marketed for use by healthcare professionals, with regulatory restrictions limiting their application to medical practitioners [S6].

All are lateral flow assays that detect IgG and IgM antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 in whole blood, plasma, or serum [S2|PMC7508500_main|14252]. The OnSite, Innovita, and Standard Q Combo tests feature separate lines containing anti-human IgG and IgM monoclonal antibodies, while the Sinocare test employs a single line with both antibodies [S3|PMC7508500_main|14252]. The Standard Q Duo tests are available as separate individual devices for IgG and IgM detection [S4|PMC7508500_main|14252]. All tests include a control line that must develop colour for the test to be considered valid [S5|PMC7508500_main|14252]. These tests are promoted for use by healthcare professionals, with the TGA restricting their use to medical practitioners [S6|PMC7508500_main|14252].

C1.sentence: Malignant tumours show a marked degree of morphological, molecular and proteomic heterogeneity.
This variability is closely related to microenvironmental factors and the location of the tumour.
The activation of genetic alterations is very tissue-dependent and only few tumours have distinct genetic alterations.
Importantly, the activation state of proteins and signaling factors is heterogeneous in the primary tumour and in metastases and recurrences.

The molecular diagnosis based only on genetic alterations can lead to treatments with unpredictable responses, depending on the tumour location, such as the tumour response in melanomas versus colon carcinomas with BRAF mutations.

Therefore, we understand that the correct evaluation of tumours requires a system that integrates both morphological, molecular and protein information in a clinical and pathological context, where intratumoral heterogeneity can be assessed.

Thus, we propose the term 'tissunomics', where the diagnosis will be contextualised in each tumour based on the complementation of the pathological, molecular, protein expression, environmental cells and clinical data.

C1.summary_text: This introductory section establishes the concept that malignant tumours exhibit marked morphological, molecular, and proteomic heterogeneity [S1|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27814], a variability closely related to microenvironmental factors and tumour location [S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27814]. Genetic alterations show tissue-dependent activation, with only a minority of tumours possessing truly distinct genetic alterations [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27814]. Critically, the activation state of proteins and signalling factors is heterogeneous not only within primary tumours but also across metastases and recurrences [S4|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27814]. This heterogeneity has direct clinical implications: molecular diagnosis based solely on genetic alterations can lead to unpredictable treatment responses that vary by tumour location—exemplified by the differential BRAF mutation response in melanomas versus colon carcinomas [S5|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27814]. The authors advocate for integrated assessment of morphological, molecular, and protein information within clinical and pathological context to account for intratumoral heterogeneity [S6|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27814], proposing the term 'tissunomics' as a diagnostic framework incorporating pathological, molecular, protein expression, environmental, and clinical data [S7|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27814].

C1.summary_text: This chunk (PMC6851567) establishes the conceptual basis for a multimodal tumour evaluation framework. Malignant tumours display marked morphological, molecular, and proteomic heterogeneity [S1], driven by microenvironmental factors and tumour location [S2]. Genetic alterations are tissue-dependent in their activation, with few tumours possessing truly distinct alterations [S3], and protein/signaling factor activation states are heterogeneous across primary tumours, metastases, and recurrences [S4]. Relying solely on genetic alterations for molecular diagnosis can yield unpredictable treatment responses depending on tumour location [S5] — exemplified by divergent BRAF mutation responses in melanoma versus colon carcinoma [S5]. Accordingly, correct tumour evaluation is proposed to require integrated morphological, molecular, protein, and clinical assessment that accounts for intratumoral heterogeneity [S6]. The authors propose the term 'tissunomics' to describe this context-specific, multi-domain diagnostic approach [S7].

C1.sentence: The study set out to assess the feasibility of using this method to diagnose metastatic carcinoma.
While cost and turnaround times are potentially an improvement on alternatives such as an ultrasound and computed tomography- guided core biopsy, the sensitivity was suboptimal.
Many of the patients with metastatic carcinoma did not have detectable CTCs using this method.

In addition, the specificity of this approach is constrained by the observation that some patients with metastatic carcinoma had circulating cytokeratin- positive cells that were probably benign NCCCs and these were also found in healthy volunteers.

It might be possible to increase the volume of the blood sample and this is likely to increase the yield of circulating epithelial cells, but in order to increase the volume substantially, one would prob -ably have to resort to a recirculation method such as diagnostic leukapheresis.
In this method, up to 2.5 L of blood may be sampled 8 and returned to the patient.
However, such a specialist technique would increase the complexity and cost of the method described above, and so make it a less compelling alternative to routine biopsy methods.
In some patients with clinically suspected metastatic malignancy, there is no obvious target mass for biopsy on imaging and so leukapheresis might be a useful strategy.
Another approach would be to screen all carcinoma patients to find those that had CTCs, and for those patients use repeat testing to monitor treatment and progression.

C1.summary_text: This feasibility study assessed circulating tumor cell (CTC) detection for diagnosing metastatic carcinoma [S1]. While the method showed potential advantages in cost and turnaround time compared to ultrasound and CT-guided core biopsy [S2], it demonstrated significant diagnostic limitations. Sensitivity was suboptimal, with many metastatic carcinoma patients showing no detectable CTCs [S3]. Specificity was constrained by the presence of benign cytokeratin-positive non-circulating cells (NCCCs) in both carcinoma patients and healthy volunteers, creating false-positive results [S4]. The authors suggested increasing blood sample volume through diagnostic leukapheresis, which can sample up to 2.5 L per procedure [S5, S6]. However, this specialist technique would increase complexity and cost, making it less practical than routine biopsy [S7]. Leukapheresis might be useful in cases of clinically suspected metastatic malignancy where no imaging target is available for conventional biopsy [S8]. An alternative proposed strategy would involve screening all carcinoma patients for CTCs and using repeat testing in positive cases to monitor treatment response and disease progression [S9].

C1.summary_text: This chunk discusses the feasibility and limitations of a CTC-based liquid biopsy method for diagnosing metastatic carcinoma [S1|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13931]. The method's sensitivity was found to be suboptimal [S2|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13931], with many metastatic carcinoma patients lacking detectable CTCs [S3|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13931]. Specificity was also constrained by the presence of circulating cytokeratin-positive benign NCCCs in both metastatic carcinoma patients and healthy volunteers [S4|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13931]. Increasing blood sample volume could improve CTC yield [S5|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13931]; diagnostic leukapheresis allows up to 2.5 L of blood to be sampled [S6|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13931], but adds complexity and cost relative to routine biopsy [S7|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13931]. Leukapheresis may nonetheless be valuable where no imageable biopsy target exists [S8|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13931]. A proposed strategy is to screen all carcinoma patients for CTCs, then use repeat testing to monitor treatment and progression in CTC-positive individuals [S9|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13931].

C1.sentence: Certain genetic alterations are only observed in the context of specific cell or tissue types; 34 for example, alterations in the APC gene in colorectal cancer, CDH1 (E-cadherin) in gastric carcinoma, the VHL gene in renal carcinoma or BCR/ABL in leukaemia.
These specific genetic alterations demonstrate that tissue type plays a role, which is currently not well understood and is under intensive investigation.
The higher incidence of certain somatic mutations in some cell types might be explained by a cell- or tissue-specific chromosome disposition during interphase.

This, along with epigenetic imprinting, may serve as a mechanism of gene regulation and allow differential access of carcinogens to certain DNA regions, resulting in a higher probability of mutations and specific rearrangements in some cells but not others.
Similarly, the accessibility of certain chromosomal regions might explain cell-type-specific chromosomal translocations such as BCR/ABL in leucocytes or VHL mutations in renal cell carcinoma.

Some mutations and genetic alterations are uniformly present in the entire organism, such as germline mutations, BRCA1 and BRCA2, VHL in Von Hippel Lindau syndrome and as many as 30 others, but they are usually only associated with tumours in specific tissues, such as BRCA1/2 in breast and ovarian tumours.
This clearly indicates that driver, trigger or passenger mutations only exert an effect in certain tissues.

C1.summary_text: This chunk discusses tissue-specific genetic alterations and their role in cancer development. Several key genetic alterations show tissue-specific patterns: APC mutations are characteristic of colorectal cancer [S1], CDH1 alterations occur in gastric carcinoma [S1], VHL gene mutations are specific to renal carcinoma [S1], and BCR/ABL translocations are found in leukaemia [S1]. The authors explain that this tissue specificity may be explained by cell- or tissue-specific chromosome disposition during interphase, combined with epigenetic imprinting, which regulates differential access of carcinogens to certain DNA regions [S3, S4]. Cell-type-specific chromosomal translocations include BCR/ABL in leucocytes and VHL mutations in renal cell carcinoma [S5]. Notably, some germline mutations such as BRCA1/2 and VHL are uniformly present throughout the organism but are typically associated with tumours in specific tissues—for example, BRCA1/2 mutations predispose to breast and ovarian tumours [S6]. This pattern demonstrates that driver, trigger, and passenger mutations only exert their effects in certain tissues [S7].

C1.summary_text: This chunk discusses tissue- and cell-type specificity of genetic alterations in cancer. Specific examples cited include APC mutations in colorectal cancer [S1], CDH1 (E-cadherin) in gastric carcinoma [S1], VHL in renal carcinoma [S1|S5], and BCR/ABL translocation in leukaemia/leucocytes [S1|S5]. The authors propose that higher incidence of somatic mutations in certain cell types may stem from cell-specific chromosomal disposition during interphase [S3] and epigenetic imprinting that modulates carcinogen access to DNA [S4]. Germline mutations such as BRCA1/2 and VHL (Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome), among ~30 others, are organism-wide yet predominantly tumourigenic in specific tissues (breast/ovary for BRCA1/2) [S6]. The conclusion is that driver, trigger, or passenger mutations exert oncogenic effects only in specific tissues [S7].

C1.summary_text: This chunk addresses the etiology and management of EA (epidermal acanthoma) in relation to HPV and other proposed causes. Molecular studies have consistently failed to detect a viral genome in EA, and p16 immunostaining is uniformly negative in both solitary and multiple lesions [S2|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7712]. Epidemiologically, EA occurs in patients without prior sexually transmitted diseases or risky sexual behavior, further arguing against an HPV-driven etiology [S3|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7712]. Trauma/chronic scratching and immunosuppression have been proposed as alternative etiological factors, though supporting evidence is weak [S4–S5|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7712]. From a treatment perspective, no intervention is required; however, options including surgical excision, cryotherapy, and topical immune modulators are available for cosmetically bothered patients, with variable response rates [S6|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7712].

DNA was extracted following standard laboratory protocols; sequencing was performed at the Solid Tumour Molecular Pathology Laboratory at the University of Bologna Medical Center using three different laboratory-developed panels that analyse the genomic regions reported in Table S1 (human reference sequence hg19/GRCh37).

Briefly, ~ 30 ng of DNA was used per each panel to amplify sequencing libraries using the AmpliSeq Plus Library Kit 2.0, according to the manufacturer's recommendations (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA).
Sequencing was performed on an Ion S5 Prime machine (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and the results were analysed with the Ion Reporter tool (v5.20 -Thermo Fisher Scientific).
As described in the validation study, single nucleotide variants / Indels present in at least 5% of the generated reads and observed in both strands were considered for variant calling.
Sequencing results were further assessed for clinical and biologic relevance by one of the authors with expertise in molecular pathology (D.dB.).

C1.summary_text: This chunk describes microscopic and molecular features of mixed tumours with extreme histological diversity. Biphasic synovial sarcoma, carcinosarcomas, and some mesotheliomas are identified as prototypic examples of such extreme diversity [S1–S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27836]. Carcinosarcomas—variously termed metaplastic carcinoma, sarcomatoid carcinoma, or carcinosarcoma depending on organ—are characterised by a malignant epithelial component that gives rise to mesenchymal elements and may exhibit fully developed sarcomatoid features such as malignant skeletal muscle, cartilage, or bone [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27836]. Integration of molecular data into the microscopic context is emphasised as essential for understanding these tumours and accurately assessing prognosis [S4|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27836].

C1.sentence: The main differential diagnosis for hybrid BPNST includes other BPNST and low-grade malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNST).
The composite nature of these lesions could be easily overlooked if only limited immunohistochemistry is performed (for example only S100 protein or EMA).
As nuclear atypia could be seen in the hybrid tumors, a low-grade MPNST might be considered.
However, MPNST show variation in cellularity and a mitotic activity that is generally either very low or absent in hybrid BPNST.
The atypia seen in hybrid tumors are of a degenerative nature similar to that seen in other benign nerve sheath tumors (i.e., smudged chromatin, nuclear pseudoinclusions).

C1.summary_text: Hybrid BPNST can be distinguished from other BPNST and low-grade MPNST in differential diagnosis [S1]. Limited immunohistochemistry, such as only S100 protein or EMA, may overlook the composite nature of these lesions [S2]. While hybrid tumors can show nuclear atypia, it is of a degenerative nature, similar to that seen in other benign nerve sheath tumors, characterized by smudged chromatin and nuclear pseudoinclusions [S3, S5]. In contrast, MPNST exhibit variation in cellularity and generally very low or absent mitotic activity compared to hybrid BPNST [S4].

C1.summary_text: Hybrid benign peripheral nerve sheath tumors (BPNST) are characterized by variable cellularity and absent or very low mitotic activity [S4], which distinguishes them from low-grade malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNST) [S4]. Nuclear atypia in hybrid BPNST is degenerative in nature, manifesting as smudged chromatin and nuclear pseudoinclusions similar to other benign nerve sheath tumors [S5]. Diagnostic recognition of the composite nature of hybrid BPNST requires comprehensive immunohistochemistry beyond single-marker analysis; limited S100 protein or EMA staining alone may fail to identify this composite architecture [S2]. The differential diagnosis between hybrid BPNST and low-grade MPNST is critical, as both may show nuclear atypia, but MPNST exhibit greater cellularity variation and mitotic activity that is typically either very low or absent in hybrid BPNST [S3, S4].

C1.summary_text: This chunk addresses the differential diagnosis of hybrid benign peripheral nerve sheath tumors (BPNST). The primary differentials include other BPNSTs and low-grade malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNST) [S1|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9410]. The composite nature of hybrid BPNST can be missed when only limited IHC markers (e.g., S100 protein or EMA alone) are used [S2|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9410]. Nuclear atypia is present in hybrid BPNST and may raise concern for low-grade MPNST [S3|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9410]; however, MPNST is distinguished by variation in cellularity, whereas mitotic activity is generally very low or absent in hybrid BPNST [S4|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9410]. Importantly, the atypia in hybrid BPNST is degenerative in character—manifesting as smudged chromatin and nuclear pseudoinclusions—analogous to that seen in other benign nerve sheath tumors [S5|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9410].

C1.summary_text: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) is crucial for diagnosing EMPSGC. Published literature indicates high concordance for Cytokeratin AE1/AE3, CAM 5.2, CK7, EMA, GCDFP-15, and E-cadherin. Additionally, at least one neuroendocrine marker (Synaptophysin, Chromogranin A, Neuron-specific Enolase, CD56) is typically expressed. Estrogen Receptors (ER) and Progesterone Receptors (PgR) are also expressed in the vast majority of cases [S1|PMC10529628_dermatopathology-10-00035|1771, S2|PMC10529628_dermatopathology-10-00035|1771, S3|PMC10529628_dermatopathology-10-00035|1771]. A specific case demonstrated expression of CK8/18, partial expression of CK7, diffuse and strong expression of Synaptophysin, focal expression of Chromogranin A, and nuclear expression of ER and PgR [S4|PMC10529628_dermatopathology-10-00035|1771].

The entity consistently expresses epithelial markers including Cytokeratin AE1/AE3, CAM 5.2, CK7, and EMA, along with GCDFP-15 and E-cadherin [S2]. At least one neuroendocrine differentiation marker is present, typically Synaptophysin, Chromogranin A, Neuron-specific Enolase, and/or CD56 [S2]. Notably, EMPSGC expresses both Estrogen Receptors (ER) and Progesterone Receptors (PgR) in the vast majority of cases [S3]. A representative case demonstrated diffuse and strong expression of Synaptophysin, focal Chromogranin A positivity, and nuclear expression of both ER and PgR, with partial CK7 expression and consistent CK8/18 positivity [S4].

C1.summary_text: In a cohort of 50 carcinoma patients, cytokeratin-positive circulating cells were detected in 19 cases (38%) [S1|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13912]. Of these, 8 cases showed circulating cytokeratin-positive cells with an immunoprofile concordant with the primary carcinoma as identified on conventional biopsy or cytology [S2|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13912]. Some carcinoma patients also harboured circulating cytokeratin-positive cells considered likely benign epithelial cells, as well as circulating megakaryocytes [S3|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13912]; notably, both cell types were also identified in healthy volunteers, highlighting a specificity challenge [S4|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13912]. The assay demonstrated practical utility: processing and initial examination were achievable within 2 days [S5|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13912] at a full processing cost of approximately £316 per case [S6|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13912].

C1.summary_text: This chunk characterises two overlapping hypertriglyceridaemia entities. Severe hypertriglyceridaemia (plasma TG >10 mmol/L) is primarily polygenic, with multiple acquired contributing factors including diet, obesity, alcoholism, diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, paraproteinaemia, and drugs [S1|PMC9012948_main|6797]. Familial chylomicronaemia syndrome (FCS) is a group of rare hypertriglyceridaemia disorders, the most common subtype being lipoprotein lipase deficiency (LPL deficiency; MIM #238600), caused by pathogenic variants in the LPL gene (MIM *609708) and estimated to occur at a prevalence of 1 in 1,000,000 [S2|PMC9012948_main|6797]. LPL deficiency follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern and is characterised by impaired plasma clearance of both chylomicrons and very low-density lipoproteins (VLDL) [S3|PMC9012948_main|6797]. Clinically, the majority of patients present before 10 years of age with recurrent pancreatitis secondary to severe hypertriglyceridaemia [S4|PMC9012948_main|6797].

C1.summary_text: This chunk evaluates commercial point-of-care test (POCT) IgG and IgM assays against immunofluorescence assay (IFA) as the reference standard [S1|PMC7508500_main|14264]. All POCTs demonstrated poor sensitivities for both IgG and IgM, despite maintaining relatively high specificities [S2|PMC7508500_main|14264]. Notably, the evaluated sensitivity was significantly lower than the manufacturer-stated performance for every POCT examined [S3|PMC7508500_main|14264]. Regarding false positives, the only false positive IgG result using the OnSite assay originated from a patient with a known positive [condition; text truncated at chunk boundary] [S5|PMC7508500_main|14264].

C1.sentence: The median age of the patients ( n = 1887) at time of diagnosis was 67.3 years [interquartile range (IQR) = 63.7 -70.9] and median PSA level was 4.6 ng/ml (IQR = 3.4 -7.1).
Of all patients, 1116 (59.1%) had grade group 1, (23.5%) grade group 2, (8.6%) grade group 3, (4.4%) grade group 4 and 81 (4.3%) grade group 5 cancer.
In total, 1479 (78.4%) patients received active treatment, while 407 (21.6%) patients were monitored by watchful waiting/active surveillance.
In total, (35.1%) patients underwent radical prostatectomy, (41.9%) patients had radiotherapy and 44 (2.3%) received endocrine treatment.
Grade group was positively correlated with age ( P = 0.004), PSA level ( P < 0.001) and percentage of positive biopsy cores ( P < 0.001) (Table 1).
Patients with a higher grade group more often received radiotherapy ( P < 0.001) and endocrine treatment ( P = 0.006) and less often watchful waiting/active surveillance ( P < 0.001).
The median follow-up time with censoring of deaths was 13.4 years (IQR = 10.6 -17.1) and 12.5 years (IQR = 8.9 -16.5) without censoring.

C1.summary_text: The study included 1887 patients with a median age of 67.3 years and a median PSA level of 4.6 ng/ml [S1]. The distribution of grade groups was: grade group 1 (59.1%), grade group 2 (23.5%), grade group 3 (8.6%), grade group 4 (4.4%), and grade group 5 (4.3%) [S2]. [S2|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17556] In earlier studies, different-sized thresholds have been used for cribriform pattern definition.
[S3|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17556] For instance, Iczkowski et al. required the presence of more than 12 luminal spaces in a cribriform structure, while Trudel et al. included lesions exceeding the size of an average benign gland and Van Leenders et al. did not set a specific size limitation.
[S4|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17556] Furthermore, Hollemans et al. found that grade group 2 patients with large cribriform structures exceeding twice the size of adjacent benign glands at radical prostatectomy had shorter BCRFS than men with small cribriform glands.

C1.sentence: Because the reporting of cribriform architecture is important for clinical decision-making, details on the definition of cribriform pattern and its distinction from potential mimickers are coming to attention.
In earlier studies, different-sized thresholds have been used for cribriform pattern definition.

For instance, Iczkowski et al. required the presence of more than 12 luminal spaces in a cribriform structure, while Trudel et al. included lesions exceeding the size of an average benign gland and Van Leenders et al. did not set a specific size limitation.

Furthermore, Hollemans et al. found that grade group 2 patients with large cribriform structures exceeding twice the size of adjacent benign glands at radical prostatectomy had shorter BCRFS than men with small cribriform glands.
It is currently unknown whether large cribriform structures at diagnostic biopsies are also associated with worse outcome compared to small cribriform glands.

The objective of the current study is to determine whether large cribriform structures have independent adverse predictive value for clinical outcome compared to small cribriform architecture in a large cohort of prostate cancer biopsies with long-term follow-up.

C1.summary_text: This introductory section establishes that cribriform architecture reporting is clinically important for prostate cancer [S1|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17556]. However, prior studies used inconsistent thresholds for defining cribriform patterns: Iczkowski et al. required >12 luminal spaces [S3|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17556], Trudel et al. used size relative to benign glands [S3|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17556], and Van Leenders et al. did not set size limitations [S3|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17556]. A key prior finding by Hollemans et al. demonstrated that grade group 2 patients with large cribriform structures (exceeding twice the size of adjacent benign glands) at radical prostatectomy experienced shorter biochemical recurrence-free survival (BCRFS) compared to men with small cribriform glands [S4|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17556]. Critically, it remains unknown whether this adverse prognostic association extends to large cribriform structures identified at diagnostic biopsies [S5|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17556]. The study aims to determine whether large cribriform structures have independent adverse predictive value in a large cohort of prostate cancer biopsies with long-term follow-up [S6|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17556].

C1.summary_text: This chunk introduces the clinical relevance of cribriform architecture in prostate cancer and the heterogeneity in its histological definition across studies [S1|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17556]. Three distinct size-based definitional thresholds have been applied historically: Iczkowski et al. required >12 luminal spaces, Trudel et al. required lesion size exceeding that of an average benign gland, and Van Leenders et al. imposed no size limitation [S3|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17556]. Hollemans et al. demonstrated that grade group 2 patients with large cribriform structures (>2× the size of adjacent benign glands) at radical prostatectomy had shorter biochemical recurrence-free survival (BCRFS) compared to those with small cribriform glands [S4|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17556]. Whether this size-dependent prognostic difference extends to diagnostic biopsies remains unknown [S5|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17556], motivating the current study to evaluate large versus small cribriform architecture as an independent predictor of clinical outcome in a large biopsy cohort with long-term follow-up [S6|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17556].

Notably, no pathogenic variants were identified across the series; specifically, no pathogenic CTNNB1 or KRAS variants were detected in Sertoliform adenomas/cystadenomas, and no pathogenic BRAF variants were found in benign cystadenomas [S2|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15507]. The low lesional cellularity characteristic of most mucinous tumours — a consequence of their morphologic features — necessitated manual review for variant detection [S3|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15507].

C1.summary_text: This study demonstrates that circulating tumour cells (CTCs) can be successfully extracted from the blood of metastatic carcinoma patients using routine formalin-fixed cell-block immunohistochemistry [S1]. The extracted CTCs exhibit morphological features similar to those observed in the primary tumour biopsy [S1]. Processing and examination can be completed within 2 days using standard laboratory techniques in a district general hospital setting [S2], at a cost of approximately £316 per case [S3]. Future work is planned to extend CTC capture methodology to patients with large cell lymphoma [S5].

C1.summary_text: This summary chunk (PMC6899935) presents conclusions from a study on circulating tumour cell (CTC) extraction and characterisation in metastatic carcinoma. CTCs can be extracted from the blood of some patients with metastatic carcinoma, and formalin-fixed cell-block IHC can demonstrate that these CTCs share features with the primary tumour biopsy [S1|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13940]. The workflow is practically feasible in an NHS district general hospital laboratory using standard biopsy techniques, with a turnaround time of 2 days when prioritised [S2|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13940] and a processing cost of approximately £316 per case [S3|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13940]. Importantly, the study identified a potential confound: benign cytokeratin-positive cells and megakaryocytes are detectable in the blood of both metastatic carcinoma patients and healthy volunteers [S4|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13940], representing a diagnostic pitfall in CTC isolation. A follow-on study targeting CTCs in large cell lymphoma is planned [S5|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13940].

Clinically, it presents as a skin-colored or whitish papule with a verruciform surface. EA occurs in a wide age range, from children to the elderly, with a male predominance. Lesions are found on the genitalia (scrotum and vulva), trunk, and extremities, and can be solitary or multiple. The cause is generally unknown, and human papilloma virus (HPV) presence has not been proven. Treatment is typically not necessary unless symptoms or cosmetic concerns arise. Additionally, the sensitivity rate of specimens collected more than 14 days post-symptom onset was compared [S5].

Additionally, sensitivity rates were compared for specimens collected more than 14 days after symptom onset [S5|PMC7508500_main|14259].

C1.summary_text: This chunk describes the methodological framework used to evaluate SARS-CoV-2 point-of-care tests (POCTs). Following Tang et al.'s distinction [S1], the study separately quantifies (1) **analytical sensitivity/specificity** — the ability to detect SARS-CoV-2-specific IgG and IgM versus IFA as comparator [S2], and (2) **clinical sensitivity** — defined as detection of any antibody in any sample from a patient to reflect overall immune status [S3], with corresponding clinical specificity also assessed [S4]. Additionally, sensitivity rates were compared specifically for specimens collected more than 14 days after symptom onset [S5].

C1.summary_text: This concluding chunk (PMC7383570) summarises key findings and clinical recommendations regarding nodal lesions in HTLV-1 carriers [S1]. HTLV-1 carriers present with a spectrum of nodal lesions accompanied by dermatopathic reaction [S1]. HAL-D and ATLLD share overlapping features, and careful assessment of atypical lymphoid cell infiltration, abnormal T cell immunophenotype, and clonality rearrangement is required to distinguish reactive from neoplastic conditions [S2]. Once overt lymphoma has been excluded, HAL-D follows an indolent clinical course [S3]. Treatment of HAL-D should consist of topical therapy, and cytotoxic chemotherapy should be avoided to prevent overtreatment [S4].

C1.sentence: Benign neoplasms of the rete testis comprise a spectrum of predominantly cystic or solid and cystic lesions that have been classified as different entities.
A subset of them was formerly called 'Sertoliform cystadenomas' of the rete testis due to their partial resemblance to Sertoli cell lesions.

The latest WHO classification of urinary and male genital tumours has excluded this entity under the assumption that it comprises examples of Sertoli cell tumour with intra-rete growth, but evidence to support this decision was lacking.

Most of the remaining benign neoplasms of the rete testis are benign cystadenomas and have been historically thought to represent testicular counterparts of Mullerian tumours with similar morphology to those of the ovary.
Data for these tumours were also limited and, therefore, the hypothesis that they may represent counterparts of Mullerian neoplasms of the ovaries was largely based on assumptions.

C1.summary_text: This chunk introduces the classification landscape of benign rete testis neoplasms [S1|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15508]. A subset was historically termed 'Sertoliform cystadenomas' on the basis of partial morphological resemblance to Sertoli cell lesions [S2|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15508]. The latest WHO classification of urinary and male genital tumours eliminated this entity, assuming such cases represent Sertoli cell tumours with intra-rete growth, although the supporting evidence for this decision was acknowledged as lacking [S3|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15508]. The majority of remaining benign rete testis neoplasms are cystadenomas, traditionally regarded as testicular counterparts of Müllerian ovarian tumours based on shared morphology [S4|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15508]; however, this hypothesis rested largely on assumptions given limited data [S5|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15508].

C1.summary_text: Four SARS-CoV-2 point-of-care antibody tests (POCTs) were evaluated. Manufacturer-listed sensitivities were 96.9% (OnSite) [S1|PMC7508500_main|14270], 87.3% (Innovita) [S1|PMC7508500_main|14270], 96.3% (Sinocare) [S1|PMC7508500_main|14270], and 99.1% (Standard Q) [S1|PMC7508500_main|14270]. However, independent findings contradicted these claims: all four POCTs demonstrated unacceptably low analytic and clinical sensitivity for SARS-CoV-2-specific antibodies, with a notable delay in antibody detection [S2|PMC7508500_main|14270]. Although sensitivity improved in specimens collected more than 14 days post-onset of symptoms, this improvement was insufficient to reach acceptable performance levels [S2|PMC7508500_main|14270].

C1.summary_text: The methodology for investigating HER2 copy number using FISH is described, involving the PathVysion HER2 DNA probe kit and the Dako Histology FISH Accessory kit [S1]. Modifications were made to the Dako Histology kit's instructions to optimize the technique and decrease laboratory processing [S2]. The process included overnight incubation of sections at 56°C, deparaffinization with xylol, and rehydration with ethanol [S3]. Slides were pretreated with Pre-treatment Solution at 97°C for 10 minutes in a water bath [S4]. Enzymatic digestion was performed using Ready-to-Use Pepsin for 3 minutes at room temperature for endoscopic biopsies or 6 minutes at 37°C for surgical specimens [S5]. Following dehydration, the HER2/CEP17 probe mix was applied to tissue sections [S6]. Slides and probes were denatured at 80°C for 5 minutes and hybridized at 37°C overnight in a Dako Hybridizer [S7]. Sections were then washed with Stringent Wash Buffer at 65°C for 10 minutes [S8]. Finally, slides were dehydrated, and fluorescence mounting medium containing DAPI was applied [S9].

C1.summary_text: This chunk evaluates the diagnostic performance of point-of-care tests (POCTs) for SARS-CoV-2 antibodies [S1]. The analysis reveals uniformly low analytic sensitivity (27.3–58.2%) across all POCTs, with acceptable specificity (88.3–100%) [S1]. Clinical sensitivity is similarly low (45–65%), while clinical specificity remains acceptable (87.3–100%) [S1]. A key finding is that POCT sensitivity improves when specimens are collected more than 14 days after symptom onset [S2]. Comparative testing demonstrates that POCT-based antibody detection lags behind the indirect fluorescence antibody (IFA) reference standard by 0–9 days [S3]. While POCTs offer the advantage of rapid, point-of-care antibody screening [S4], their poor sensitivity and delayed detection kinetics make them unsuitable for standalone diagnostic or screening applications [S5].

C1.summary_text: This chunk reports performance characteristics of point-of-care tests (POCTs) for SARS-CoV-2 antibodies [S1|PMC7508500_main|14240]. Analytic sensitivity was low (27.3%–58.2%), analytic specificity was 88.3%–100%, clinical sensitivity was 45%–65%, and clinical specificity was 87.3%–100% [S1|PMC7508500_main|14240]. Sensitivity improved when specimens were collected more than 14 days after symptom onset [S2|PMC7508500_main|14240]. POCT-based antibody detection lagged behind immunofluorescence assay (IFA) by 0–9 days after disease onset [S3|PMC7508500_main|14240]. Due to poor sensitivity and delayed antibody detection, POCTs are considered unsuitable as a standalone diagnostic or screening tool for SARS-CoV-2 [S5|PMC7508500_main|14240].

They seem to be more common in patients with advanced malignancy than early stage malignancy and benign conditions.
Megakaryocytes are commonly seen in pulmonary capillaries.
It is possible that other researchers have found megakaryocytes while looking for CTCs but have not recognised them.

C1.summary_text: Megakaryocytes are known to be present in the peripheral blood of patients with myeloproliferative disorders, carcinoma, non-neoplastic disorders, and even in healthy subjects [S1, S2]. They are commonly found in pulmonary capillaries [S4]. Megakaryocytes appear to be more frequent in advanced malignancy compared to early-stage malignancy and benign conditions [S3]. In a current study, megakaryocytes were found to be more common in patients with carcinoma than in healthy volunteers [S7]. A significant observation was that many megakaryocytes appeared to have lost their cytoplasm, a feature also noted when enzymatic streptolysin O haemolysis was employed for cell separation [S8, S9].

C1.summary_text: This chunk summarizes observations on peripheral blood megakaryocytes across patient populations. Megakaryocytes are well-established in myeloproliferative disorders [S1] but are also found in carcinoma, non-neoplastic conditions, and healthy subjects [S2]. They appear more frequent in advanced malignancy compared to early-stage or benign disease [S3], and the current study confirms they are more prevalent in carcinoma patients than healthy volunteers [S7]. Anatomically, megakaryocytes are commonly found in pulmonary capillaries [S4]. A notable morphological feature observed is cytoplasmic loss [S8], which was seen with both Parsortix filtration and enzymatic streptolysin O haemolysis, suggesting this is not purely an artefact of one method [S9]. The authors also note that megakaryocyte-like cells may have been inadvertently captured in prior circulating tumour cell (CTC) studies without recognition [S5, S6].

The technique is positioned as relevant for identifying actionable genomic alterations and therapeutic targets, monitoring treatment response, predicting disease progression, and identifying resistance mechanisms in early-stage and metastatic disease contexts [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27863]. Pilot study data from early-stage NSCLC indicates that liquid biopsy provides additional insights into intratumoural heterogeneity [S4|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27863].

C1.summary_text: This chunk describes the utility of liquid biopsy in oncology. Liquid biopsy analytes — including CTCs, cfDNA, RNA, and circulating tumour exosome DNA — enable global, location-independent assessment of the tumour mutational landscape and are emerging as an alternative to tissue biopsies when these are difficult to obtain [S1–S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27863]. Key clinical applications include identification of actionable genomic alterations and therapeutic targets, monitoring treatment response, predicting disease progression ahead of clinical/radiological confirmation, and characterising resistance mechanisms, particularly in early-stage and metastatic disease [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27863]. Additionally, a pilot study in early-stage NSCLC patients demonstrated that liquid biopsy provides supplementary insight into intratumour heterogeneity (ITH) [S4|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27863].

A good business plan aligned with the local environment and long-term vision can lead to success even in small pathology departments [S8|PMC4035753_pthy-46-165|5951].

This chunk discusses the organizational and implementation aspects of electronic synoptic reporting in pathology, focusing on the successful adoption in Ontario, Canada (S3), and the importance of organizational planning and stakeholder engagement in implementing such systems. The text emphasizes that while electronic synoptic reporting offers qualitative and efficiency benefits over traditional narrative reporting (S1), significant organizational hurdles exist during implementation (S2). The authors note that successful implementation requires careful planning, engagement with stakeholders, and compulsory organizational adoption with monitoring (S3), but acknowledge that not all settings can replicate Ontario's comprehensive framework (S4). They argue that organizations can still achieve quality improvements through sound local planning and strategic vision, regardless of resource constraints (S6, S7, S8). The content is primarily about implementation methodology and organizational change management rather than medical/clinical findings.

C1.sentence: Automated SISH was performed on a Ventana Benchmark XT (Ventana Medical Systems, Tucson, AZ, USA).
INFORM HER2 DNA Probe and INFORM Chromosome 17 Probe were visualized on the same slide, following the manufacturer's protocols, with a few variations.
Assay conditions were modified for optimal results.
The entire assay procedure (deparaffinization, pretreatment, hybridization, stringency wash, signal detection and counterstaining) was fully automated.
Pretreatment was performed with Reaction Buffer and enzyme digestion with ISH Protease 3 for 12 min.

HER2 probe was denatured at 95 /C176 C for 15 min and hybridized at 56 C for 6 h. Chromosome 17 centromere probe was denatured at 95 C for 12 min and hybridized at 44 /C176 C for 3 h. Stringency washes for HER2 probe were performed at 72 /C176 C for 8 min (three steps) and incubated with anti-dinitrophenol (DNP) antibody for 20 min.
Then, tissue sections were incubated with horseradish peroxidase-conjugated anti-rabbit anti- revealed by sequential silver reactions (Silver C incubation time, min).
For chromosomal 17 centromere probe, three stringency washes were performed at 59 /C176 C for 8 min.

C1.summary_text: This chunk presents concluding findings on the prognostic significance of cribriform growth patterns in prostate cancer. Both small and large cribriform patterns are independently associated with shorter metastasis-free and disease-specific survival [S1|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17575]. Consequently, men harboring a cribriform growth pattern should not be considered candidates for active surveillance [S2|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17575]. The first biopsy concluded a CA and the patient was treated with cryotherapy, with no significant benefit.
During the last physical examination in September 2018, whitish papules of the glans penis were still present (Fig. 1).
The differential diagnosis was clinically CA versus intraepithelial neoplasm versus psoriasis.
The patient had stopped his treatment of adalimumab 6 months previously and in spite of that, the psoriasis was clinically mild with a PASI score of 2.5.
A new biopsy of the penis was performed.
Histologically, dysplasia could be excluded.
Acanthosis and hyperkeratosis with variable degree of papillomatosis were present (Fig. 2a).
The keratinocytes of the granular and spinous layer showed cytoplasmic vacuolization, coarse keratohyaline granules, and eosinophilic inclusions, consistent with EA (Fig. 2b, c).
The review of the first biopsy in 2008 diagnosed as CA showed the same histological image and allowed the same conclusion.

Initial treatment with cryotherapy for a presumed CA showed no benefit [S2]. In September 2018, whitish papules persisted [S3]. Differential diagnoses included CA, intraepithelial neoplasm, and psoriasis [S4]. The patient had stopped adalimumab 6 months prior, with his psoriasis remaining mild (PASI 2.5) [S5]. A new biopsy excluded dysplasia [S7] and revealed acanthosis, hyperkeratosis with variable papillomatosis [S8], and keratinocyte changes including cytoplasmic vacuolization, coarse keratohyaline granules, and eosinophilic inclusions, consistent with EA [S9]. Review of the initial biopsy confirmed the same histological findings [S10].
