C1.summary_text: This case describes a 51-year-old male with psoriasis on adalimumab (discontinued 6 months prior) who presented with persistent whitish papules of the glans penis [S1, S3]. Initial biopsy in 2008 was inconclusive; cryotherapy provided no significant benefit [S2]. Re-biopsy in 2018 revealed generalizable histopathological features of Erythema multiforme (EM): acanthosis and hyperkeratosis with variable papillomatosis [S8], cytoplasmic vacuolization of granular and spinous layer keratinocytes with coarse keratohyaline granules and eosinophilic inclusions [S9], and absence of dysplasia [S7]. These morphological findings are consistent with Erythema multiforme rather than condyloma acuminatum or intraepithelial neoplasm. The review of the initial 2008 biopsy confirmed the same histological pattern [S10].

C1.summary_text: This chunk describes a case of epidermolytic acanthoma (EA) of the glans penis in the context of adalimumab-treated psoriasis. Key generalizable histopathological facts: EA histologically demonstrates acanthosis, hyperkeratosis with variable papillomatosis [S8], and characteristic keratinocyte changes in the granular and spinous layers including cytoplasmic vacuolization, coarse keratohyaline granules, and eosinophilic inclusions [S9]. Dysplasia is absent on histology [S7], and these features are reproducible across biopsies over time [S10]. Clinically, EA of the penis enters differential diagnosis with condyloma acuminatum (CA), intraepithelial neoplasm, and psoriasis [S4]. Cryotherapy administered under the initial (incorrect) diagnosis of CA yielded no significant benefit [S2].

C1.sentence: Although skin is one of the most frequently affected organs in ATLL and may be involved in up to 50% of cases, the detailed clinicopathological findings of ATLL and HAL cases with dermatopathic reaction remain unclear.
To address this issue, we carried out a comparative clinicopathological analysis of lymph nodes with dermatopathic reaction in 18 HTLV-1-infected cases with or without ATLL.

The majority of these cases were considered to be reactive lesions showing an indolent clinical course, while three cases with definitive involvement by tumour cells showed a relatively poorer prognosis.
These findings highlighted the disease spectrum from benign to malignant status in dermatopathic reaction of lymph nodes of HTLV-1 carriers.

C1.summary_text: In case 14, focal proliferation of EBV-infected large B cells was observed, while definitive clonal T cell proliferation or abnormal T cell immunophenotype was not seen [S1]. This finding is described in several lymphomas and reflects an immunodeficient local environment created by tumour cells [S2]. The proliferating cells were uniformly CD20 positive, focally CD30 positive, and CD15 negative, distinguishing this case from the Hodgkin lymphoma-like variant with incipient ATLL [S3]. EBV-positive B cell lymphoproliferative disorders are associated with age-related immune deficiency and span a spectrum from benign to malignant [S4]. HTLV-1 infection-induced immunosuppression may also contribute to EBV-infected cell proliferation [S5]. ATLL tumour cells and HTLV-1-infected cells often exhibit a regulatory T cell phenotype, including CD4, CD25, and forkhead box P3 expression [S6]. EBV-positive cell proliferation with dermatopathic reaction can mimic lymphoma-type ATLL, posing a diagnostic pitfall [S7].

C1.summary_text: This case series (case 14 from a larger cohort) describes an unusual clinical presentation combining focal EBV-infected B cell proliferation with absence of clonal T cell proliferation or abnormal T cell immunophenotype [S1]. The EBV-infected B cell findings reflect an immunodeficient local environment, a pattern observed in multiple lymphomas including angioimmunoblastic T cell lymphoma [S2]. The proliferating cells in case 14 exhibited a distinct immunophenotype: uniform CD20 positivity, focal CD30 positivity, and CD15 negativity, distinguishing this case from Hodgkin lymphoma-like variants associated with incipient ATLL [S3]. EBV-positive B cell lymphoproliferative disorders represent a spectrum of diseases associated with age-related immune deficiency, ranging from benign to malignant [S4]. HTLV-1 infection can create an immunosuppressive environment contributing to EBV-infected cell proliferation [S5]. ATLL tumour cells and HTLV-1-infected cells characteristically exhibit a regulatory T cell phenotype, including expression of CD4, CD25, and forkhead box P3 [S6]. EBV-positive cell proliferation combined with dermatopathic reaction presents a diagnostic challenge as it can mimic lymphoma-type ATLL [S7].

C1.summary_text: This chunk describes diagnostic and immunophenotypic features of a case (case 14) involving focal proliferation of EBV-infected large B cells in the setting of ATLL. The proliferating B cells were uniformly CD20+ [S3], focally CD30+ [S3], and CD15– [S3], distinguishing this from the Hodgkin lymphoma-like variant of incipient ATLL. No definitive clonal T cell proliferation or abnormal T cell immunophenotype was identified [S1]. EBV-positive large B cell proliferation is a recognised feature in several T cell lymphomas including angioimmunoblastic T cell lymphoma, attributed to an immunodeficient local tumour microenvironment [S2]. HTLV-1-induced immunosuppression may further facilitate EBV-infected cell outgrowth [S5]. ATLL tumour cells and HTLV-1-infected cells characteristically express a regulatory T cell phenotype (CD4, CD25, FoxP3) [S6]. EBV-positive B cell lymphoproliferative disorders encompass a spectrum from benign to malignant and are linked to age-related immune deficiency [S4]. Importantly, EBV-positive cell proliferation combined with dermatopathic reaction can mimic lymphoma-type ATLL and represents a diagnostic pitfall [S7].

ITH of oestrogen receptors, which may be positive in just 1% of cells, has been associated with the long-term risk of fatal breast cancer [S2]. Other examples include heterogeneous expression of cyclin D1 in mantle cell lymphomas, which typically have a homogeneous CCND1-IGH translocation, and HER2+ breast or gastric tumours, where positive cells can range from 10% to 100% [S3].

Examples of ITH include oestrogen receptors, which can be positive in as few as 1% of cells, and this ITH is associated with a long-term risk of fatal breast cancer [S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27849]. Other instances are the heterogeneous expression of cyclin D1 in mantle cell lymphomas, despite these lymphomas carrying a homogeneous CCND1-IGH translocation [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27849]. Additionally, HER2+ breast or gastric tumours can show a wide range of positivity, from 10% to 100% of cells [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27849].

C1.sentence: In cases with HAL-D, lymph node tissue architecture was preserved, and proliferation of transformed large lymphoid cells as well as aggregates of interdigitating dendritic cells, Langerhans cells and macrophages forming mottled clear foci was observed in the paracortex (Figure 1A,B).
Transformed large lymphocytes with prominent nucleoli were detected in all cases.
Numerous CD25-positive cells distributed in the expanded paracortex were observed in all cases by immunohistochemistry (Figure 1C).
The number of CD30-positive cells varied, and there was no clear correlation between the number of positive cells in neoplastic and reactive lesions (Figure 1D and Table 2).
No HRS-like cells or CD15-positive large cells were observed in the present series.
Although one patient (case 2) showed T cell monoclonality by PCR for TCRc, the definitive atypical tumour cells or phenotypical abnormalities of T cell markers were not identified.
No clonal rearrangement was recognised in the other samples (polyclonal pattern in 12 cases and not evaluable in three cases).
All lymph node samples of HAL-D showed a normal T cell phenotype by flow cytometry analysis (Figure 3 and Supporting information, Table S1) and/or immunohistochemistry.

C1.summary_text: In cases with HAL-D, lymph node tissue architecture was preserved, and proliferation of transformed large lymphoid cells and aggregates of interdigitating dendritic cells, Langerhans cells, and macrophages forming mottled clear foci were observed in the paracortex [S1]. Transformed large lymphocytes with prominent nucleoli were detected in all cases [S2]. Numerous CD25-positive cells were observed in the expanded paracortex in all cases by immunohistochemistry [S3]. The number of CD30-positive cells varied, with no clear correlation between the number of positive cells in neoplastic and reactive lesions [S4]. No HRS-like cells or CD15-positive large cells were observed [S5]. One patient (case 2) showed T cell monoclonality by PCR for TCRc, but definitive atypical tumor cells or phenotypical abnormalities of T cell markers were not identified [S6]. No clonal rearrangement was recognized in the other samples (polyclonal pattern in 12 cases and not evaluable in three cases) [S7]. All lymph node samples of HAL-D showed a normal T cell phenotype by flow cytometry analysis and/or immunohistochemistry [S8].

C1.summary_text: In cases of HAL-D, lymph node tissue architecture was preserved, and proliferation of transformed large lymphoid cells, as well as aggregates of interdigitating dendritic cells, Langerhans cells, and macrophages forming mottled clear foci, were observed in the paracortex [S1|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21924]. Transformed large lymphocytes with prominent nucleoli were detected in all HAL-D cases [S2|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21924]. Immunohistochemistry revealed numerous CD25-positive cells distributed in the expanded paracortex in all HAL-D cases [S3|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21924]. The number of CD30-positive cells varied, and no clear correlation was found between the number of positive cells in neoplastic and reactive lesions [S4|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21924]. HRS-like cells and CD15-positive large cells were absent in HAL-D cases [S5|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21924]. Definitive atypical tumour cells or phenotypical abnormalities of T cell markers were not identified in HAL-D cases [S6|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21924]. No clonal rearrangement was recognized in 12 HAL-D samples, which showed a polyclonal pattern for TCRc clonal rearrangement [S7|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21924]. All HAL-D lymph node samples exhibited a normal T cell phenotype by both flow cytometry analysis and immunohistochemistry [S8|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21924].

C1.summary_text: This case series describes the histopathological and immunophenotypic features of Hydroa Actinica-Like Dermatitis (HAL-D) in lymph node tissue. HAL-D shows preserved lymph node architecture [S1|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21924] with proliferation of transformed large lymphoid cells and characteristic aggregates of dendritic cells, Langerhans cells, and macrophages in the paracortex, forming mottled clear foci [S1|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21924]. All cases showed morphologically prominent transformed large lymphocytes with prominent nucleoli [S2|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21924]. Immunohistochemically, numerous CD25-positive cells were observed in the expanded paracortex in all cases [S3|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21924], while CD30-positive cells showed variable numbers with no clear correlation between neoplastic and reactive lesions [S4|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21924]. HRS-like cells and CD15-positive large cells were absent [S5|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21924]. Molecularly, only one case showed TCRc monoclonality; however, no definitive atypical tumour cells or T cell phenotypical abnormalities were identified [S6|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21924]. The remaining 12 evaluable cases showed polyclonal pattern with no clonal rearrangement [S7|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21924]. Flow cytometry and immunohistochemistry confirmed a normal T cell phenotype in all HAL-D lymph node samples [S8|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21924]."

C1.summary_text: In HAL-D, lymph node tissue architecture is preserved, with paracortical expansion featuring proliferating transformed large lymphoid cells and aggregates of interdigitating dendritic cells, Langerhans cells, and macrophages forming mottled clear foci [S1]. Transformed large lymphocytes with prominent nucleoli are a universal finding [S2]. CD25-positive cells are numerous throughout the expanded paracortex in all cases by IHC [S3], while the number of CD30-positive cells varies without clear correlation between neoplastic and reactive lesions [S4]. HRS-like cells and CD15-positive large cells are consistently absent [S5]. TCR clonal rearrangement analysis shows a polyclonal pattern in 12 cases, not evaluable in 3 cases, with T-cell monoclonality detected by PCR in only 1 case (case 2), though no definitive atypical tumour cells or T-cell phenotypical abnormalities were identified in that case [S6, S7]. All HAL-D lymph node samples demonstrate a normal T-cell phenotype by flow cytometry and/or IHC [S8].

C1.summary_text: Medulloblastomas comprise four distinct molecular subtypes with clear clinical differences: group 1 (WNT-activated), group 2 (SHH-activated), group 3 (GABAergic), and group 4 (glutaminergic) [S1|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27844]. These molecular subtypes can be identified and assessed using immunohistochemistry or FISH methodologies [S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27844]. C1.sentence: Abstract: (1) Background: Endocrine Mucin-Producing Sweat Gland Carcinoma (EMPSGC) is a rare, low-grade, neuroendocrine-differentiated, cutaneous adnexal tumor, officially recognized by the World Health Organization (WHO) Skin Tumors Classification in 2018 as a separate entity and homologue of endocrine ductal carcinoma in situ (eDCIS)/solid papillary carcinoma of the breast.

Although it is more frequent in the female sex, between 60 and 70 years old, in the peri-orbital region, EMPSGC has also been described in the male sex, in subjects under 60 and over 80, and in extraeyelid localizations (cheek, temple, scalp), but also in extra-facial localizations (chest and scrotum).
(2) Methods: We present the clinical case of a 71-year-old woman with an undated lesion of the scalp, which presented as a nodule, skin-colored, and 2.5 cm in maximum diameter.

We also conduct a comprehensive literature review from 1997 to the end of 2022, consulting PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science (WoS), and Google Scholar using the following keywords: 'Endocrine mucin-producing sweat gland carcinoma' and/or 'EMPSGC' and/or 'skin' and 'cutaneous neoplasms'.
In addition, we followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines.
A total of 253 patients were recorded; 146 were females (57.7%) and 107 were males (42.2%).

The vast majority of the lesions were in the eyelids (peri-ocular region), and only a minority of cases involved the cheeks, supra-auricular, retro-auricular, and occipital region, with very rare cases in the scalp, to which the present is also added.

(4) Conclusions: The morphological and immunophenotypical features are essential both for the correct diagnosis and to be able to classify this lesion among the corresponding eDCIS/solid papillary carcinoma of the breast, with neuroendocrine differentiation.
Recent papers have attempted to shed light on the molecular features of EMPSGC, and much remains to be conducted in the attempt to subtype the molecular profiles of these entities.
Future studies with large case series, and especially with molecular biology techniques, will be needed to further add information about EMPSGC and its relationship in the PCMC spectrum.

C1.summary_text: Endocrine Mucin-Producing Sweat Gland Carcinoma (EMPSGC) is a rare, low-grade, neuroendocrine-differentiated, cutaneous adnexal tumor, recognized by the WHO in 2018, and is a homologue of eDCIS/solid papillary carcinoma of the breast [S1]. It is more frequent in females between 60-70 years old, primarily in the peri-orbital region, but has also been described in males, younger than 60, older than 80, and in extra-facial locations including the cheek, temple, scalp, chest, and scrotum [S2]. A literature review identified 253 patients, with 146 females (57.7%) and 107 males (42.2%) [S6]. The majority of lesions are in the eyelids, with a minority in the cheeks, supra-auricular, retro-auricular, and occipital regions, and very rare cases in the scalp [S7]. Morphological and immunophenotypical features are essential for diagnosis [S8]. Molecular features of EMPSGC are being investigated, with future studies using molecular biology techniques expected to provide more information on EMPSGC and its relationship within the PCMC spectrum [S9, S10].

[S2|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17573] Multivariable analysis in the radical prostatectomy study of Hollemans et al. showed that the large cribriform pattern was the only significant predictive variable for BCRFS, while the small cribriform pattern lost its significance.
[S3|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17573] Therefore, we hypothesise that the large cribriform pattern is clinically important but that its recognition is seriously hampered by sampling artefacts inherent to biopsies.
[S4|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17573] This finding is in line with the grade group 2 biopsy study by Flood et al., who found that small and large cribriform patterns, as distinguished by ≤ 12 and > 12 punched-out lumina, respectively, were both significantly associated with upgrading and extraprostatic expansion at subsequent radical prostatectomy.
[S5|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17573] Together, this underscores the importance of multimodal risk stratification of prostate cancer management; for instance, by including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) results or molecular companion diagnostics.

C1.sentence: As far as we are aware, two studies have specifically compared the outcome of large and small cribriform pattern in grade group 2 prostate cancer patients.

Multivariable analysis in the radical prostatectomy study of Hollemans et al. showed that the large cribriform pattern was the only significant predictive variable for BCRFS, while the small cribriform pattern lost its significance.
Therefore, we hypothesise that the large cribriform pattern is clinically important but that its recognition is seriously hampered by sampling artefacts inherent to biopsies.

This finding is in line with the grade group 2 biopsy study by Flood et al., who found that small and large cribriform patterns, as distinguished by ≤ 12 and > 12 punched-out lumina, respectively, were both significantly associated with upgrading and extraprostatic expansion at subsequent radical prostatectomy.

Together, this underscores the importance of multimodal risk stratification of prostate cancer management; for instance, by including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) results or molecular companion diagnostics.
Patients with cribriform carcinoma at radical prostatectomy tend to have a higher PiRADS score than those without the cribriform pattern.

C1.summary_text: This chunk (PMC9321809) compares the prognostic significance of large versus small cribriform patterns in grade group 2 prostate cancer. Multivariable analysis (Hollemans et al., radical prostatectomy cohort) showed large cribriform pattern was the only significant predictor of BCRFS, while small cribriform pattern lost significance [S2]. Clinically, cribriform carcinoma at radical prostatectomy is associated with higher PiRADS scores on MRI [S6]. C1.summary_text: This prostate cancer biopsy cohort study examined the prognostic significance of cribriform architecture [S4]. Both small and large cribriform carcinomas demonstrated independent predictive value for metastasis-free survival (MFS) and disease-specific survival (DSS) [S4]. Contrary to prior literature suggesting large cribriform patterns drive adverse outcomes [S2], patients with large cribriform structures did not experience worse clinical outcomes compared to those with small cribriform carcinoma [S5]. The study aimed to evaluate whether cribriform pattern-related prognostic effects observed in earlier work were reproducible in a large, long-term follow-up prostate cancer biopsy cohort [S3].

C1.summary_text: This chunk from PMC9321809 reports findings from a large cohort study of prostate cancer biopsies with long-term follow-up. Prior evidence suggested the large cribriform pattern is mainly responsible for adverse outcome rather than any cribriform pattern per se [S2]. However, the current study demonstrates that both small and large cribriform carcinomas on prostate biopsies carry independent predictive value for metastasis-free survival (MFS) and disease-specific survival (DSS) [S4]. Notably, patients with large cribriform structures did not have a worse outcome compared to those with small cribriform carcinoma [S5], challenging the assumption that size of the cribriform pattern differentially stratifies prognosis.

[S1|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17572] The current findings in biopsy specimens are not in agreement with our previous study among 420 grade group 2 radical prostatectomy specimens.
[S2|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17572] In the prostatectomy cohort, we found that grade group 2 patients with the large cribriform pattern had significantly more frequent extraprostatic expansion and pelvic lymph node metastasis as well as shorter BCRFS than those with the small pattern.
[S3|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17572] This discrepancy can have several causes.
[S4|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17572] First, recognition of the large cribriform pattern at biopsy seems less reliable than on surgical specimens.
[S5|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17572] We defined the large cribriform pattern as a malignant cribriform lesion having at least twice the size of adjacent preexistent glands.
[S6|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17572] While cribriform size is easily visualised in radical prostatectomy, it can be less well appreciated in 1-mm thick biopsy specimens which will only sample a part of a large cribriform lesion.
[S7|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17572] This is reflected by the frequency of the large cribriform pattern.

C1.summary_text: This chunk compares the diagnostic reliability of large cribriform pattern (LCP) identification in prostate cancer biopsies versus radical prostatectomy specimens. The authors define LCP as a malignant cribriform lesion ≥2× the size of adjacent preexistent glands [S5]. In a prior cohort of 420 grade group 2 radical prostatectomy specimens, LCP was associated with significantly increased extraprostatic expansion, pelvic lymph node metastasis, and shorter biochemical recurrence-free survival compared to small cribriform patterns [S2]. However, recognition of LCP is substantially less reliable in biopsy specimens than surgical specimens [S4], primarily because cribriform size is poorly appreciated in 1-mm thick biopsy cores that sample only part of a lesion [S6]. This is reflected in markedly different prevalence: LCP occurred in 8.1% (34/420) of prostatectomy specimens but only 0.5% (2/444) of biopsies in the current study [S8]. Supporting data from three studies shows low sensitivity but high specificity for cribriform pattern identification in matched biopsy–prostatectomy pairs [S9]. In a prior cohort of 420 radical prostatectomy specimens, grade group 2 patients with the large cribriform pattern showed significantly more extraprostatic extension, pelvic lymph node metastasis, and shorter BCRFS than those with the small pattern [S2]. C1.sentence: The processing through the Parsortix™ device and the formation of a cell- block has been described in detail previously.
Briefly, as the blood was processed through the Parsortix™ device, cells larger than approximately 6 μ m were retained by the filter cassette.
These were then recovered by a phosphate buffered saline back wash of the cassette, yielding 90 μ L extract.
Next, a 40 μ L droplet of plasma was placed at the centre of a clean glass microscope slide.
The plasma was derived from the patient's own blood sample.

A 12- mm Cytofoam Disc was placed on top of the droplet on the slide and the 90 μ L phosphate buffered saline extract containing the recovered cells was added to the centre of the top face of the disc.
A further 40 μ L of plasma was then added.
The surface of the disc was then prodded with a micropipette tip 30 times to encourage mixing of the fluids.
A 500- mL plastic histology specimen container was then prepared with a folded paper towel across its floor that was soaked with 5 mL of neutral buffered formalin.
The glass slide was then placed flat on top of this with the Cytofoam Disc uppermost.

C2.sentence: The container's lid was closed and left at room temperature for 24 hours for the sample to fix in the formalin vapour.
The slide was then removed from the container and the Cytofoam Disc prised from the surface of the slide with the edge of a scalpel.
The disc was then wrapped in tissue paper and paraffin processed as for a biopsy specimen.
This method was designed to minimise the loss of cells during processing with recovery of the cells directly into the CytoFoam Disc cell- block matrix.

C1.sentence: Breast carcinoma.
According to the mRNA expression profile, six molecular subtypes are described: luminal A, luminal B, HER2 +, basal-like, claudin-low and normal breast-like.

However, RNA signatures can vary dramatically between patients with the same molecular subtype 69 and, with the exception of the basal subtype, are not highly reproducible for diagnosis on microarray analysis.
A high degree of ITH has been described, as assessed by immunohistochemical (IHC) studies, array-CGH studies 71 and massive parallel sequencing technologies.

Given these problems in the exact diagnosis of breast cancer subtype by molecular characterisation, IHC-based characterisations are recommended as a diagnostic approach in most of the consensus oncology guidelines.
Additional IHC staining helps to distinguish luminal A and B subtypes, such as GATA3 and FOXM.
CK5 and EGFR expression define the basal subtype of breast cancer, and CD44 and Snail expression determine the claudin-low subtype.

C1.summary_text: This chunk reviews the molecular and IHC classification of breast carcinoma. Six molecular subtypes are defined by mRNA expression profiling: luminal A, luminal B, HER2+, basal-like, claudin-low, and normal breast-like [S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27839]. C1.sentence: The paradigm of cancer as a genetic disease has existed since the early 1970s.
For the last 50 years, cancer has been explained according to the somatic mutation theory (SMT), which states that genetic mutations accumulate in cells by inducing clonal expansion.
Following Darwinian-type evolution, an initial clone accumulates multiple mutations, resulting in malignant transformation characterised by growth independence and resistance to apoptosis.
These clones have trunk and branch mutations, and may also have driver and passenger mutations.
-18 During tumour progression and after chemotherapy or radiotherapy, genetic alterations accumulate to select for the bestadapted clone.
Molecular heterogeneity has been described in renal adenocarcinoma, breast cancer and glioblastoma, among others.
It is thought that these clones with greater proliferative advantages and resistance to local stresses then predominate.

C1.summary_text: This chunk presents the foundational somatic mutation theory (SMT) of cancer as a genetic disease [S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27819]. Cancer arises through clonal expansion driven by accumulation of somatic mutations, with clones undergoing Darwinian-type evolution and accumulating both trunk and branch mutations, as well as driver and passenger mutations [S3, S4|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27819]. Malignant transformation is characterized by growth independence and resistance to apoptosis [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27819]. During tumour progression and after exposure to chemotherapy or radiotherapy, genetic alterations accumulate to select for best-adapted clones [S5|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27819]. Molecular heterogeneity has been documented across multiple cancer types including renal adenocarcinoma, breast cancer, and glioblastoma [S6|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27819]. Clones with greater proliferative advantages and resistance to local stresses are thought to predominate [S7|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27819].

C1.summary_text: This chunk introduces the somatic mutation theory (SMT) as the dominant paradigm for cancer biology since the early 1970s [S1–S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27819]. Under SMT, accumulating genetic mutations drive clonal expansion and ultimately malignant transformation, characterised by growth independence and apoptosis resistance [S2–S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27819]. Tumour clones are further distinguished by trunk/branch and driver/passenger mutations [S4|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27819]. Genetic alterations continue to accumulate during tumour progression and in response to chemotherapy or radiotherapy, selecting for the best-adapted clone [S5|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27819]. Molecular heterogeneity—a key consequence of this Darwinian evolution—has been documented in renal adenocarcinoma, breast cancer, and glioblastoma [S6|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27819], with clones bearing proliferative and stress-resistance advantages ultimately predominating [S7|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27819].

C1.summary_text: Microscopic analysis of this dermal lesion [S1] revealed a well-circumscribed but unencapsulated growth covered by normal-appearing skin [S1]. The lesion exhibited a biphasic architecture: cellular areas centrally and hypocellular-to-myxoid areas peripherally [S1]. The central zone displayed alternating hyper- and hypocellularity resembling Antoni A and Antoni B patterns [S2], with spindle cells showing abundant fibrillary cytoplasm, plump nuclei, and coarse chromatin [S3]. The peripheral myxoid zone contained slender spindle cells with delicate nuclei and elongated bipolar cytoplasm [S4]. Notably, no atypia or mitotic figures were identified [S5], consistent with a benign spindle cell proliferation.

C1.summary_text: Protein expression within a tumour can be influenced by local environmental factors like hypoxia, nutrient starvation, or oxidative stress, irrespective of the cell's genetic makeup [S1]. These environmental cues can modify entire signalling pathways downstream of oncogenic alterations [S2]. While tumours may possess activating mutations in upstream signalling elements (e.g., RAS, EGFR, HER2), the phosphorylation of downstream factors (e.g., MAP-kinases, mTOR) can be inhibited by environmental factors [S3]. Consequently, even if specific driver genetic alterations are targeted, no effect may be observed in cells where these signalling pathways are inhibited by such factors [S3].

C1.summary_text: Gleason score 7 prostate cancer is characterized by a mix of Gleason pattern 3 and 4 glands [S1|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17555]. Gleason pattern 4 encompasses poorly formed, fused, glomeruloid, and cribriform growth patterns [S2|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17555]. The presence of an invasive cribriform pattern is associated with worse biochemical recurrence-free survival (BCRFS), metastasis-free survival (MFS), and disease-specific survival (DSS) compared to its absence, observed in both prostate biopsies and radical prostatectomies [S3|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17555]. Intraductal carcinoma (IDC) is defined as malignant epithelial cell proliferation within ducts and acini, often accompanying invasive prostate carcinoma [S3|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17555]. Both invasive cribriform carcinoma and IDC are adverse prognostic factors that enhance the predictive accuracy of models incorporating other clinicopathological parameters [S4|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17555]. Consequently, the 2019 ISUP and GUPS consensus recommend reporting the presence or absence of invasive cribriform and intraductal carcinoma in all prostate cancer pathology reports [S5|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17555].

C1.summary_text: Gleason score 7 prostate cancer is defined morphologically as a mixture of well-differentiated Gleason pattern 3 glands interspersed with Gleason pattern 4 structures [S1]. Gleason pattern 4 cancer comprises multiple growth patterns including poorly formed, fused, glomeruloid, and cribriform types [S2]. The presence of invasive cribriform pattern is strongly associated with adverse outcomes: worse biochemical recurrence-free survival (BCRFS), metastasis-free survival (MFS), and disease-specific survival (DSS) compared to tumours lacking invasive cribriform architecture, across both prostate biopsies and radical prostatectomies [S3]. Intraductal carcinoma (IDC) is characterized as proliferation of malignant epithelial cells confined to distended pre-existent acini and prostatic ducts, and is predominantly accompanied by invasive prostate carcinoma [S3]. Like invasive cribriform carcinoma, IDC is an adverse prognostic factor and both entities significantly increase the discriminative power of prediction models in prostate cancer prognosis [S4]. The 2019 ISUP consensus meeting and GUPS therefore recommend routine documentation of invasive cribriform pattern and intraductal carcinoma in all prostate cancer pathology reports [S5].

C1.summary_text: This chunk summarises key histopathological and prognostic features of Gleason score 7 prostate cancer and its subpatterns [S1|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17555]. Gleason pattern 4 is categorised into four growth subtypes: poorly formed, fused, glomeruloid, and cribriform [S2|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17555]. Multiple studies demonstrate that the invasive cribriform pattern is independently associated with worse BCRFS, MFS, and DSS compared to non-cribriform architecture, in both biopsies and radical prostatectomy specimens [S3|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17555]. Intraductal carcinoma (IDC) is defined as malignant epithelial proliferation confined to distended acini/prostatic ducts, typically co-existing with invasive carcinoma [S3|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17555]. Both IDC and invasive cribriform carcinoma are adverse prognostic factors that significantly improve prediction model performance [S4|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17555]. Consequently, the 2019 ISUP consensus and GUPS recommend mandatory reporting of invasive cribriform and IDC in all prostate cancer pathology reports [S5|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17555].

C1.summary_text: This methods chunk (PMC7383570) describes the histopathological and immunohistochemical workup for HAL-D and ATLL-D cases. FFPE tissue was used throughout [S1]. Haematoxylin and eosin staining was the primary histological method [S2]. HAL-D was diagnosed per prior published criteria [S3], while ATLL-D was defined by significant atypical lymphocyte infiltration [S4]. A seven-marker IHC panel—CD3 and CD8 (Agilent), CD4, CD5, CD25, and CD30 (Roche), and CD7 (Abcam)—was run on the Benchmark ULTRA platform [S5]. One case (Case 14) additionally underwent EBER in-situ hybridisation (Dako) to assess EBV involvement [S6]. IHC data from cooperating institutions were incorporated into the overall analysis [S7].

C1.sentence: The strength of this study is the use of a large well-characterised prostate biopsy cohort with longterm clinical follow-up of more than 13 years.
This allows for the analysis of detailed pathological features with strong and relevant clinical endpoints such as occurrence of metastasis and disease-specific death.
One inherent disadvantage of the use of samples with such long-term follow-up is that, at that time, stateof-the-art clinical practice was different from the present.
In the 1990s standard sextant biopsies were used, while current biopsy schemes often apply more systematic biopsies as well as MRI targeted biopsies.
Together, this might have led to an underestimation of the presence of the large cribriform pattern in the current study.
Furthermore, treatment modalities have been modified over the years with more common use of active surveillance in low-risk patients who received active treatment two decades ago.

Although the large cribriform architecture is believed to have a worse outcome than the small cribriform pattern, there is no consensus on the distinguishing features of large and small cribriform structures.
In this study we defined large cribriform pattern as those structures exceeding twice the size of adjacent pre-existent glands, which we also applied in our previous radical prostatectomy study.
This threshold is easy to apply, but is subjective.

Application of other definitions of the large cribriform pattern, such as an exact-sized cut-off in l m or number of punched-out lumina, will probably result in different distributions and clinical outcomes.

C2.sentence: Furthermore, interobserver variability on assessment of the cribriform pattern could also affect the outcome of different studies.

Finally, we did not perform basal cell immunohistochemistry in each cribriform biopsy to distinguish invasive from intraductal carcinoma, which might have affected definitive grade group assignment in a 31

C1.summary_text: This study utilized a large, well-characterized prostate biopsy cohort with over 13 years of clinical follow-up, allowing for the analysis of detailed pathological features against clinical endpoints like metastasis and disease-specific death [S1|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17574, S2|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17574]. A disadvantage of long-term follow-up is the evolution of clinical practice and treatment modalities over time [S3|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17574, S4|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17574, S6|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17574]. The study acknowledges a potential underestimation of the large cribriform pattern due to biopsy techniques used in the 1990s [S5|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17574]. While the large cribriform architecture is believed to be associated with a worse outcome than the small cribriform pattern, there is no consensus on their distinguishing features [S7|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17574]. This study defined the large cribriform pattern as structures exceeding twice the size of adjacent pre-existent glands, a definition that is easy to apply but subjective [S8|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17574, S9|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17574]. Alternative definitions for the large cribriform pattern may lead to different distributions and clinical outcomes [S10|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17574].

The study defined large cribriform pattern as structures exceeding twice the size of adjacent pre-existent glands [S8|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17574], a threshold noted to be easy to apply but subjective [S9|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17574], with alternative definitions (e.g., exact µm cut-off or number of punched-out lumina) likely yielding different distributions and outcomes [S10|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17574].

C2.summary_text: This chunk presents two methodological limitations from a study on cribriform pattern prostate carcinoma. First, interobserver variability in cribriform pattern assessment is acknowledged as a potential confounder for cross-study comparisons [S1|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17574]. Second, basal cell immunohistochemistry was not applied to every cribriform biopsy, which is necessary to differentiate invasive carcinoma from intraductal carcinoma; this omission may have impacted definitive grade group assignment in the study cohort [S2|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17574].

Based on these previous observations, allergic rhinitis and parasinusitis may not necessarily be considered direct causes of blood hypereosinophilia in the present case.

Although detailed genetic analyses were unavailable, there was no specific underlying disease accounting for blood hypereosinophilia, including leukemia, parasitic infection, and connective tissue diseases.
Accordingly, the present case appears to be clinicopathologically consistent with idiopathic rather than primary (neoplastic) or secondary (reactive) HES.
Cutaneous manifestations in HES are characterized by erythematous lesions rather than palpable purpura commonly occurring in EGPA.
Serum CRP level is generally low or within the normal range in HES, which also appears to support the diagnosis of HES in the present case, while it is high in patients with EGPA.
Neurological manifestations in HES are relatively uncommon compared to those in EGPA, and cerebral vasculitis is rare; it is reported in only 1% of patients with HES.

Recently, the term ' idiopathic eosinophilic vasculitis (EoV) or HESassociated vasculitis ' was proposed as an additional manifestation of HES, characterized clinicopathologically by an eosinophil-rich, non-granulomatous necrotizing, systemic form of vasculitis that affects vessels of various sizes in ANCA-negative, asthma-free patients.

Although it is difficult to interpret such cases, including our case, according to the CHCC2012 definitions 2 because of the ambiguous distinctions between the categories, particularly ' variable vessel vasculitis (VVV), ' ' vasculitis associated with systemic disease, ' and ' vasculitis associated with probable etiology, ' this disease concept, in agreement with the previous report, would better be added to the VVV list according to these definitions.

CNS involvement seems rare in HES-associated vasculitis, as there was no case of histopathologically proven CNS EoV among the 10 original cases in the publication, and its extensive English literature review, together with our own PubMed search, identified only two reported cases similar to EoV or HESassociated vasculitis affecting particularly the small vessels in the CNS in an ANCA-negative, asthma-free patient who showed rapid improvement in symptoms with highdose intravenous steroid administration.

C1.summary_text: In patients with asthma, eosinophils in the blood do not exceed 1.5 /C2 10 9 /L, irrespective of clinical severity or comorbid allergic rhinitis [S1]. Allergic rhinitis and parasinusitis are not necessarily direct causes of blood hypereosinophilia [S2]. While detailed genetic analyses were unavailable, no specific underlying disease like leukemia, parasitic infection, or connective tissue diseases accounted for blood hypereosinophilia [S3]. The case presented is clinicopathologically consistent with idiopathic HES rather than primary (neoplastic) or secondary (reactive) HES [S4]. Cutaneous manifestations in HES are characterized by erythematous lesions, unlike the palpable purpura commonly seen in EGPA [S5]. Serum CRP levels are typically low or normal in HES, supporting the diagnosis, whereas they are high in EGPA [S6]. Neurological manifestations are less common in HES than in EGPA, with cerebral vasculitis being rare, reported in only 1% of HES patients [S7]. Idiopathic eosinophilic vasculitis (EoV) or HES-associated vasculitis, a proposed manifestation of HES, is characterized by eosinophil-rich, non-granulomatous necrotizing systemic vasculitis affecting various vessel sizes in ANCA-negative, asthma-free patients [S8]. CNS involvement appears rare in HES-associated vasculitis, with no histopathologically proven CNS EoV cases among 10 original publication cases [S10]. Literature review identified only two reported cases of EoV or HES-associated vasculitis affecting CNS small vessels in ANCA-negative, asthma-free patients who responded well to high-dose intravenous steroids [S10].

Neurological manifestations are relatively uncommon in HES compared to EGPA, with cerebral vasculitis being rare and reported in only 1% of HES patients [S7]. The term 'idiopathic eosinophilic vasculitis (EoV) or HES-associated vasculitis' has been proposed as an additional manifestation of HES [S8]. This condition is clinicopathologically characterized by an eosinophil-rich, non-granulomatous necrotizing, systemic vasculitis affecting vessels of various sizes in ANCA-negative, asthma-free patients [S8]. This disease concept is suggested for inclusion in the Variable Vessel Vasculitis (VVV) list according to CHCC2012 definitions [S9]. CNS involvement is rare in HES-associated vasculitis, with no histopathologically proven cases among 10 original cases and only two reported literature cases of EoV/HES-associated vasculitis affecting small CNS vessels in ANCA-negative, asthma-free patients who showed rapid improvement with high-dose intravenous steroids [S10].

Blood eosinophil counts in asthma patients, even with allergic rhinitis, do not exceed 1.5×10⁹/L [S1], indicating that allergic rhinitis and parasinusitis are unlikely direct causes of blood hypereosinophilia [S2]. CNS involvement in HES-associated vasculitis is rare—no histopathologically proven CNS EoV among 10 original cases, and only 2 similar cases identified in a comprehensive literature review—with those cases showing small-vessel CNS involvement and rapid improvement with high-dose intravenous steroids [S10].

Eosinophil infiltration of the vasculitis lesion is identified as a key histopathological feature of EoV; its absence despite peripheral blood hypereosinophilia argues against EoV [S1|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10435]. HES-associated vasculitis is characterized by peripheral blood hypereosinophilia, and its absence together with raised CRP argues against clinical consistency with this diagnosis [S1|PMC9541515_NEUP-42-239|10435]. C1.sentence: The aim of this study was to assess the analytic and clinical performance of four rapid lateral flow point-of-care tests (POCTs) for identifying SARS-CoV-2-specific antibodies.

A retrospective study was conducted between 22 January and 30 March 2020 on 132 serum samples for SARS-CoV-2-specific antibody detection referred to a tertiary referral hospital laboratory in New South Wales.

Multiple sera were tested from 20 confirmed or suspected COVID-19 patients with SARS-CoV-2-specific antibodies detected by immunofluorescence (IFA) or neutralisation, and 71 SARS-CoV-2 uninfected individuals.

We measured the sensitivity and specificity for detection of SARS-CoV-2 IgM and IgG antibodies for each POCT in comparison to positive SARS-CoV-2-specific IFA and viral neutralisation, our current laboratory benchmark tests.

C1.summary_text: This chunk analyzes HER-2/neu status in gastric cancer (GC) using three molecular detection methods: FISH, SISH, and real-time PCR. HER-2/neu amplification is detected in 17.5% of samples by FISH [S2] and 21% by SISH [S2], with HER-2/neu heterogeneity identified in up to 52% of cases [S3]. FISH and SISH show concordant results in 96.4% of cases [S4]. However, six discordant cases are all positive by SISH but negative by FISH [S5]. Upon review, these discordant cases are polysomic with FISH HER-2/neu ratios between 2.06 and 2.50, and are confirmed negative for amplification by real-time PCR [S6, S7]. Setting the FISH amplification cutoff at ≥3 achieves perfect concordance between FISH and SISH [S7]. The authors conclude that dual-colour SISH represents a novel method for determining HER-2 status in GC [S8].

C1.summary_text: This chunk reports the comparative performance of FISH, dual-colour SISH, and real-time PCR (LightMix kit HER-2/neu) for HER2 status determination in gastric cancer (GC). HER2 amplification rates were 17.5% by FISH and 21% by SISH [S2]. Intratumoral heterogeneity was observed in up to 52% of cases [S3]. Overall FISH–SISH concordance was 96.4% [S4]. All six discordant cases were SISH-positive/FISH-negative [S5]; on re-review, these were found to be polysomic and were confirmed amplification-negative by real-time PCR [S6]. The HER2 ratios in these discordant cases fell between 2.06 and 2.50, and applying a cut-off of ≥3 achieved perfect concordance [S7]. The authors conclude that dual-colour SISH represents a novel method for HER2 status determination in GC [S8].

C1.sentence: Systems biology encompasses tools that hold great promise for deciphering the vulnerabilities of the tumour ecosystem as a whole.

Studies are based on the premise that multiple oncogenic events converge on a number of cellular networks that may contain essential or synthetically lethal clinically targetable hubs or factors, such as the eIF4F complex.
Nonetheless, many contemporary systems biology approaches do not consider intratumour heterogeneity.

This is relevant because key functional nodes within the metabolic, signal transduction and gene expression networks responsible for supporting the tumour phenotype are critically dependent on the heterogeneity of the tumour.

These data can also help to classify tumours according to histopathological, biochemical and genomic features and thus help to tailor the diagnosis and clinical management to a patient's biological tumour profile.

Accordingly, multidimensional molecular and gene expression data, which are associated with the response to antitumour treatments and clinical progress, are thought to facilitate the selection of patients who are more likely to respond to targeted or 'precise' therapies.

-131 The availability of systemwide data in a variety of cancers is facilitating the development of approaches that go beyond the classic, reductionist paradigms that associate single genes with cellular phenotypes and functions.
Systems biology approaches consider the interplay between multiple molecular factors that underpin phenotype development.

Accordingly, rather than a genetic disease, cancer is now perceived as a disease of 'networks', and to fully grasp the complexity of the tumour ecosystem the networks driving cancer need to be mapped and their dynamics and evolution over time deciphered.

Emerging data show that these cancer networks are constantly rewired in part by clonal interactions, changing microenvironments and the acquisition of novel molecular alterations that are largely induced by anticancer treatments.

C2.sentence: Therefore, minor subpopulations that are not readily detectable in bulk tumours or that can adapt to hostile environments may emerge following treatments that specifically target cancerdriving mutations present in the predominant tumour subpopulations.

Thus, in the coming years, systems biology implementation may be crucial for (i) detailed, clinically oriented subclassification of cancer types, (ii) mapping of oncogenic networks and identification of the critical nodes to overcome the effects of ITH and (iii) informing future preclinical research and design of Phase I clinical trials by anticipating therapy response in silico and predicting the best targets for each patient and tumour (personalised cancer therapy or precision medicine).

C1.sentence: The first patient was a 64-year-old woman with metastatic breast carcinoma on therapy, who underwent upper GI endoscopy for anaemia and post-prandial diarrhoea that revealed a single 6-mm submucosal nodule with a localised distribution in the duodenal bulb.

Histopathological examination revealed two fragments of duodenal mucosa with reactive epithelial changes, including non-specific villous blunting and gastric metaplasia, consistent with peptic duodenitis.
Additionally, one of the two fragments showed crushed blue cells in the submucosa, mimicking crushed lymphoid cells (Figure 1A -D).
Given the crush artefact, it was difficult to discern the morphology of these cells on haematoxylin and eosin-stained slides.
The second patient was a 64-year-old woman presenting with abdominal pain, and an upper GI endoscopy showed a single 6-mm mucosal nodule with localised distribution in the duodenal bulb.
Histopathological examination showed duodenal mucosa with gastric metaplasia and non-specific villous blunting, consistent with peptic duodenitis.

Additionally, a higher-powered examination showed some glands interspersed within nonneoplastic duodenal crypts remarkably similar to Brunner glands, but were identified in the superficial mucosa, a location unusual for Brunner glands.
These Brunner-like glands showed abundant frothy lightly eosinophilic cytoplasm and basally located bland nuclei (Figure 2A -D).
The presence of peptic duodenitis in both cases could have explained the 'nodular' appearance seen on endoscopy, in addition to the crushed lymphoid-like cells in the first case.

However, given the presence of these crushed blue 'lymphoid-like' cells in the submucosa (in the first case) and the aberrant location of the 'Brunner-like' glands (in the second case), ancillary stains were performed.

C2.sentence: The lesional cells in both cases were positive for synaptophysin, chromogranin A, insulinoma-associated protein 1 (INSM1) and cytokeratin (AE1/AE3), supporting the diagnosis of a NET.
The Ki67 index was assessed to be approximately 2% in both cases on this limited lesional material, favouring a grade 1 NET.
Clinical management for the first patient consisted of close observation and repeated endoscopy in 6 months, given the ongoing chemotherapy for her breast cancer.

The second patient underwent an endoscopic resection of the nodule, which was consistent with well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumour (residual 0.4 cm), with a Ki67 labelling index of 4.3%, consistent with a grade 2 tumour.
Staging scans confirmed no residual disease, and the plan was for active endoscopic surveillance.

Histopathological examination revealed two fragments of duodenal mucosa with reactive epithelial changes, including non-specific villous blunting and gastric metaplasia, consistent with peptic duodenitis [S2|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4798]. C1.summary_text: Two case presentations of duodenal lesions in women with distinct histopathological findings [S1, S5]. Both patients showed peptic duodenitis characterized by reactive epithelial changes including non-specific villous blunting and gastric metaplasia [S2, S6]. The first case revealed crushed blue cells in the submucosa mimicking lymphoid cells, with crush artefact limiting morphological assessment on H&E slides [S3, S4]. The second case demonstrated aberrantly located Brunner-like glands in the superficial duodenal mucosa with frothy lightly eosinophilic cytoplasm and basally located bland nuclei, in contrast to the normal submucosal location of true Brunner glands [S7, S8]. Peptic duodenitis itself could explain the nodular endoscopic appearance observed in both cases [S9]. The presence of these unusual histological findings (crushed lymphoid-like cells and aberrantly located Brunner-like glands) prompted the use of ancillary stains for further characterization [S10].

C1.summary_text: This chunk describes two cases of duodenal biopsies with diagnostically challenging histological findings. In the first case, histopathology of the duodenal submucosa revealed crushed blue cells mimicking lymphoid cells, with crush artefact severely limiting morphological assessment on H&E [S3–S4|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4798]. In the second case, glands morphologically similar to Brunner glands were identified in the superficial duodenal mucosa — an abnormal location — with abundant frothy eosinophilic cytoplasm and bland basally placed nuclei [S7–S8|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4798]. Both biopsies additionally showed features of peptic duodenitis (gastric metaplasia and non-specific villous blunting) [S2, S6|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4798], which could explain the nodular endoscopic appearance [S9|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4798]. The combination of submucosal crushed lymphoid-like cells and aberrantly located Brunner-like glands prompted ancillary stain evaluation [S10|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4798].

C1.sentence: This is the first study, to our knowledge, to investigate the clinicopathological characteristics of lymph nodes with dermatopathic reaction in patients infected by HTLV-1.
Although HAL-D cases showed an indolent clinical course for the most part, two of the three patients with ATLL-D showed a relatively aggressive clinical course.
The third ATLL-D case was accompanied by leukaemic atypical lymphocytes, decreased albumin and elevated LDH, possibly classified as unfavourable chronic type, suggesting a relatively poor prognosis.

Our study also showed the usefulness of abnormal T cell immunophenotype to distinguish HAL-D and ATLL-D. This method is also used in the evaluation of other T cell type neoplasms, such as S /C19 ezary syndrome.
Kobayashi et al. established a method for identifying ATLL tumour cells based on flow cytometric detection of CD3 and CD7 expression.
With disease progression, ATLL cells gradually change their immunophenotype from CD3 ( + ) /CD7 ( + ) to CD3 ( /C0 ) /CD7 ( /C0 ).
The abnormal T cell immunophenotype seems not only to distinguish neoplastic from inflammatory status, but also predicts aggressiveness of the disease.
Conversely, CD25-positive transformed lymphoid cells proliferated in all cases.
The number of CD30-positive cells varied among cases, but was unrelated to either the distinction of ATLL-D and HAL-D or the clinical course.
These cells can be regarded as activated/stimulated lymphocytes.

C1.summary_text: This study investigated clinicopathological characteristics of lymph nodes with dermatopathic reaction in HTLV-1 infected patients [S1]. While HAL-D cases generally showed an indolent clinical course, two of three ATLL-D patients had an aggressive course [S2]. One ATLL-D case with leukaemic atypical lymphocytes, decreased albumin, and elevated LDH suggested a poor prognosis [S3]. Abnormal T cell immunophenotype was useful in distinguishing HAL-D from ATLL-D and is also used for other T cell neoplasms [S4]. ATLL tumour cells can be identified by flow cytometry detecting CD3 and CD7 expression [S5]. With disease progression, ATLL cells change from CD3(+)/CD7(+) to CD3(-)/CD7(-) [S6]. Abnormal T cell immunophenotype distinguishes neoplastic from inflammatory status and predicts disease aggressiveness [S7]. CD25-positive transformed lymphoid cells proliferated in all cases [S8]. The number of CD30-positive cells varied and was unrelated to ATLL-D/HAL-D distinction or clinical course [S9]. These CD30-positive cells are considered activated/stimulated lymphocytes [S10].

HAL-D cases demonstrated an indolent clinical course [S2], whereas ATLL-D cases showed variable aggressiveness, with two of three exhibiting aggressive progression [S2] and one case presenting with leukaemic features, hypoalbuminaemia, and elevated LDH consistent with unfavourable chronic-type ATLL and poor prognosis [S3]. Abnormal T cell immunophenotype proved useful for distinguishing HAL-D from ATLL-D [S4], with ATLL cells characteristically expressing CD3+/CD7+ at presentation but gradually losing this phenotype (becoming CD3−/CD7−) with disease progression [S6]. CD25-positive transformed lymphoid cells proliferated uniformly across all cases [S8], whereas CD30-positive cell numbers varied without correlation to disease subtype distinction or clinical course [S9].

C1.summary_text: In a cohort of 1,887 prostate cancer patients, invasive cribriform and/or intraductal carcinoma (invCR/IDC) was detected in 280 men (14.8%) [S1]. The prevalence of invCR/IDC showed a striking dose-response relationship with Gleason grade group: grade group 1 (1.1%, n=1116), grade group 2 (18.2%, n=444), grade group 3 (57.1%, n=163), grade group 4 (55.4%, n=83), and grade group 5 (59.3%, n=81) [S2]. Men with invCR/IDC were significantly older (P=0.006) [S3] and had significantly higher PSA levels (P<0.001) compared to those without invCR/IDC [S3].

C1.summary_text: In a cohort of prostate carcinoma patients (PMC9321809), invasive cribriform and/or intraductal carcinoma (invCR/IDC) was observed in 280 (14.8%) men overall [S1|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17562]. The prevalence of invCR/IDC increased sharply with grade group, being lowest in grade group 1 (1.1%; 12/1116) and highest in grade groups 3–5 (57.1%, 55.4%, and 59.3%, respectively), compared with 18.2% in grade group 2 [S2|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17562]. Men harboring invCR/IDC were significantly older (P=0.006) and had significantly higher PSA levels (P<0.001) than those without [S3|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17562].

C1.summary_text: This chunk describes the performance of an in-house immunofluorescence assay (IFA) and neutralisation antibody assay as benchmark reference standards for SARS-CoV-2 serology [S1|PMC7508500_main|14254]. When samples were collected ≥14 days after symptom onset and compared against NAT-confirmed cases, IFA demonstrated a sensitivity of 91.3% (95% CI 84.9–95.6) and a specificity of 98.9% (95% CI 98.4–99.8) for detecting one or more classes of SARS-CoV-2 antibodies (IgG, IgM, or IgA) [S2|PMC7508500_main|14254]. The underlying principles of viral neutralisation and IFA were noted as previously described elsewhere [S3|PMC7508500_main|14254].

C1.summary_text: Condyloma acuminatum (CA) is an HPV-induced lesion occurring predominantly on the genitalia of young adults [S1]. Clinically, CA presents as fleshy exophytic lesions, often larger than epidermodysplasia acuminatum (EA), and can involve the glans penis, penile shaft, penile root, pubic area, groin, and perianal area — in contrast to EA, which preferentially affects the scrotum in men and the labia majora in women [S2]. Histologically, CA resembles EA by sharing acanthosis, papillomatosis, and hyperkeratosis [S3], and coarse keratohyalin granules may occasionally be observed [S4]. Key distinguishing histological features of CA include the usual absence of acantholysis and the presence of a homogenous perinuclear halo with a retracted nucleus [S5].

C1.sentence: The surgical pathology report on cancer resection specimens is fundamental to providing clinicians with the information needed for adequate patient oncology treatment.

Since the multi-institutional quality study on pathology reporting of colorectal cancer published by Zarbo in 1992, many other studies have shown that the use of checklists or synoptic reporting is superior to traditional narrative (free text) reporting.
Using electronic health records, synoptic histopathology reporting tools can be designed to be very sophisticated with discrete data fields, drop down menus, and automated SNOMED encoding.
The use of discrete data fields ('atomic data') means that it is possible to automatically search, extract, and transmit data electronically.

Despite the apparent benefits of electronic synoptic histopathology reporting, and the successful regional implementation of such a reporting system in Ontario, Canada, others have reported that the implementation and use of electronic histopathology reporting is no easy organisational task.
Similar challenges have also been reported regarding the implementation and use of a web-based synoptic reporting tool for cancer surgery.
From a management and organisational perspective, the list of possible causes for project failure with respect to information technology development, implementation and use is long.
In our opinion, a pro-active understanding and management of key organisational issues is a requirement for successful long-term synoptic histopathology cancer reporting.

The surgical pathology report on cancer resection specimens is essential for providing clinicians with necessary information for adequate oncology treatment. Studies since 1992, including a multi-institutional quality study by Zarbo, have demonstrated that synoptic reporting or checklists are superior to traditional narrative reporting for pathology of colorectal cancer. Electronic synoptic histopathology reporting tools can be sophisticated, featuring discrete data fields, drop-down menus, and automated SNOMED encoding, enabling automatic data search, extraction, and electronic transmission. Despite benefits and successful regional implementation in Ontario, Canada, electronic histopathology reporting faces significant organizational challenges. Similar challenges exist for web-based synoptic reporting tools for cancer surgery. Effective management and understanding of organizational issues are critical for successful long-term synoptic histopathology cancer reporting.

C1.summary_text: This introductory chunk establishes the clinical context and study scope for benign rete testis neoplasms. Benign neoplasms of the rete testis—specifically adenomas and Sertoliform cystadenomas—are generally recognizable but may require exclusion of malignant tumours, including metastatic carcinomas from multiple primary sites, which are significantly more frequent [S1|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15499]. Crucially, the histopathologic, immunophenotypic, and molecular characteristics of these benign tumours remain largely undescribed in the literature [S2|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15499]. To address this gap, the authors present a case series of 11 benign rete testis tumours with comprehensive morphologic, immunophenotypic, and molecular profiling [S3|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15499].

C1.sentence: Unlike Sertoliform cystadenomas, which are solid and cystic or solid, most of the remaining benign neoplasms of the rete testis are entirely cystic.
These benign cystadenomas are generally wellcircumscribed, discovered incidentally, and characterized by cystic spaces lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar epithelial cells.
A subset may contain mucinous epithelium with intraluminal mucin, and some tumours include a subpopulation of ciliated cells.

Based on morphologic findings, these tumours have often been interpreted as testicular counterparts of similar-appearing Mullerian tumours of the ovaries, but the immunophenotypic and molecular features of these lesions had not been previously studied in detail.

Mucinous or serous ovarian neoplasms may harbour KRAS or BRAF mutations, which were not identified in benign cystadenomas of the rete testis (including a case with focal epithelial proliferation consisting of stubby papillae lined by short columnar cells).
An important caveat is that, due to their nature, tumour cellularity is often low in these neoplasms, making the molecular analysis challenging.

C1.summary_text: Benign cystadenomas of the rete testis are generally well-circumscribed, incidentally discovered, and characterized by cystic spaces lined by cuboidal to columnar epithelial cells. A subset may contain mucinous epithelium with intraluminal mucin, and some include ciliated cells. Sertoliform cystadenomas are solid and cystic or solid, while most other benign neoplasms of the rete testis are entirely cystic. These tumours have been interpreted as testicular counterparts of ovarian Mullerian tumours based on morphology. KRAS or BRAF mutations, found in ovarian neoplasms, were not identified in benign cystadenomas of the rete testis. Molecular analysis can be challenging due to low tumour cellularity in these neoplasms [S1|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15510, S2|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15510, S3|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15510, S4|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15510, S5|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15510, S6|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15510].

C1.summary_text: Sertoliform cystadenomas are described as solid and cystic or solid, while most other benign neoplasms of the rete testis are entirely cystic [S1|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15510]. These benign cystadenomas are generally well-circumscribed, discovered incidentally, and characterized by cystic spaces lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar epithelial cells [S2|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15510]. A subset may contain mucinous epithelium with intraluminal mucin, and some include a subpopulation of ciliated cells [S3|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15510]. Morphologically, these tumours are often interpreted as testicular counterparts of Mullerian tumours of the ovaries, but their immunophenotypic and molecular features had not been studied in detail [S4|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15510]. Unlike mucinous or serous ovarian neoplasms which may harbour KRAS or BRAF mutations, these mutations were not identified in benign cystadenomas of the rete testis [S5|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15510]. Tumour cellularity is often low in these neoplasms, which makes molecular analysis challenging [S6|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15510].

C1.summary_text: Benign cystadenomas of the rete testis are entirely cystic, well-circumscribed neoplasms that are usually discovered incidentally and characterized by cystic spaces lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar epithelial cells [S2]. A subset may contain mucinous epithelium with intraluminal mucin, and some tumors include ciliated cells [S3]. Unlike mucinous or serous ovarian neoplasms, which may harbor KRAS or BRAF mutations [S5], these mutations were not identified in benign cystadenomas of the rete testis, even in a case with focal epithelial proliferation consisting of stubby papillae lined by short columnar cells [S5]. The low cellularity of these neoplasms presents a technical challenge for molecular analysis [S6].

C1.summary_text: This chunk characterizes benign cystadenomas of the rete testis in contrast to Sertoliform cystadenomas. Sertoliform cystadenomas have solid and cystic or purely solid architecture [S1], whereas the remaining benign rete testis neoplasms are entirely cystic [S1]. Benign cystadenomas are well-circumscribed, incidentally discovered, and lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar epithelium [S2]. A subset harbours mucinous epithelium with intraluminal mucin [S3], and some contain ciliated cells [S3]. Morphologically, these tumours have been likened to ovarian Mullerian neoplasms [S4]; however, unlike mucinous/serous ovarian tumours—which may harbour KRAS or BRAF mutations—these mutations were not identified in benign rete testis cystadenomas, including a case with focal epithelial proliferation showing stubby papillae [S5]. A key technical caveat is that low tumour cellularity in these lesions makes molecular analysis challenging [S6].

C1.summary_text: This chunk reports prognostic associations of cribriform patterns in prostate cancer. The cribriform pattern (any) was associated with significantly worse MFS (HR=3.04; 95% CI=1.93–4.78; P<0.001) and DSS (HR=4.07; 95% CI=2.51–6.62; P<0.001) compared to men without the cribriform pattern [S1|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17568]. The large cribriform pattern specifically was also independently associated with worse MFS (HR=3.17; 95% CI=1.68–5.99; P<0.001) and DSS (HR=4.13; 95% CI=2.14–7.98; P<0.001) [S2|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17568]. Importantly, patients with large cribriform structures had statistically similar MFS (P=0.77) and DSS (P=0.96) outcomes to those with the small cribriform pattern, indicating no significant prognostic difference between cribriform size subtypes [S3|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17568].

C1.summary_text: In a study of metastatic breast carcinoma patients, CTCs were detected and characterised in 38.5% of patients, with a total of 92 CTCs identified [S1|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13936]. A striking receptor status discordance was observed: at least 69.6% of CTCs exhibited an ERα and/or ErbB2 status different from the primary tumour, while only 30% of patients had CTCs with no receptor status change [S2|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13936]. Notably, CTC clusters (observed in four patients) consistently displayed uniform receptor profiling within each cluster [S3|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13936]. The authors postulate that the presence of benign cytokeratin-positive circulating cells may partially account for these findings [S4|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13936].

C1.sentence: Molecular and preneoplastic changes in the context of the adjacent tissue: field cancerisation may display premalignant histological changes such as dysplasia; furthermore, many genetic alterations occur without cytological changes.
These environmental changes can affect tumour progression by exerting evolutionary pressure on tumour cells and ultimately determining which mutations are selected.

Examples of preneoplastic histological lesions include dysplasia (cytological atypia, large hyperchromatic nuclei or nucleoli) and in-situ carcinomas (with no basement membrane invasion), which are observed in most carcinomas.
It is noteworthy that some early neoplastic lesions such as colon adenomas and skin naevi are polyclonal.
Progression to cancer probably involves the accumulation of multiple field cancerisation driver mutations among synergistically acting groups of mutations.
In this regard, molecular studies of peritumour areas in normal ducts of the breast or prostate may show a high number of genetic alterations and driver mutations.
The clinical meaning of these molecular changes remains unknown, and further large studies are needed to establish their correlation with tumour relapse.

Nonetheless, two important conclusions can be drawn: (i) the study of non-tumour tissue can be relevant in predicting prognosis and risk of second or multiple neoplasia and (ii) we must be very cautious making a diagnosis of malignancy based only on molecular data, as not all mutations in, for example, driver genes, are directly linked to cancer development.

C1.summary_text: Field cancerisation can display premalignant histological changes like dysplasia, which includes cytological atypia, large hyperchromatic nuclei, and nucleoli [S1|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828, S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. In-situ carcinomas are observed in most carcinomas [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. Many genetic alterations occur without cytological changes [S1|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. Early neoplastic lesions like colon adenomas and skin naevi can be polyclonal [S4|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. Molecular studies of peritumour areas in normal breast or prostate ducts may reveal a high number of genetic alterations and driver mutations [S6|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. The clinical significance of these molecular changes is unknown, and further studies are needed to correlate them with tumour relapse [S7|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. Studying non-tumour tissue can be relevant for predicting prognosis and the risk of second or multiple neoplasia [S8|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. However, caution is advised when diagnosing malignancy based solely on molecular data, as not all driver gene mutations are directly linked to cancer development [S8|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828].

C1.summary_text: Field cancerisation may exhibit premalignant histological changes like dysplasia [S1|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. Many genetic alterations can occur without corresponding cytological changes [S1|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. Dysplasia and in-situ carcinomas are examples of preneoplastic histological lesions, characterized by features such as cytological atypia, large hyperchromatic nuclei, and nucleoli in dysplasia, and the absence of basement membrane invasion in in-situ carcinomas; these are observed in most carcinomas [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. Early neoplastic lesions like colon adenomas and skin naevi are polyclonal [S4|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. Cancer progression likely involves the accumulation of multiple field cancerisation driver mutations [S5|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. Molecular studies of peritumour areas in normal breast or prostate ducts may reveal a high number of genetic alterations and driver mutations [S6|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. However, the clinical significance of these molecular changes remains unknown, and further large studies are required to establish their correlation with tumour relapse [S7|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. The study of non-tumour tissue can be relevant for predicting prognosis and the risk of second or multiple neoplasia [S8|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. Caution is advised when diagnosing malignancy based solely on molecular data, as not all driver gene mutations are directly linked to cancer development [S8|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828].

C1.summary_text: This chunk discusses molecular and histological features of field cancerisation and preneoplastic lesions in neoplastic development [S1|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. Field cancerisation may display premalignant histological changes including dysplasia, and genetic alterations can occur without accompanying cytological changes [S1|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. Environmental pressures affect tumour progression through selective pressure on tumour cell mutations [S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. Preneoplastic histological lesions include dysplasia (characterized by cytological atypia, large hyperchromatic nuclei or nucleoli) and in-situ carcinomas (lacking basement membrane invasion), which are observed in most carcinomas [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. Early neoplastic lesions such as colon adenomas and skin naevi display polyclonal origins [S4|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. Cancer progression likely involves accumulation of multiple field cancerisation driver mutations among synergistically acting groups [S5|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. Molecular studies of peritumour areas in normal breast and prostate ducts may reveal high numbers of genetic alterations and driver mutations [S6|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. The clinical significance of these molecular changes remains unclear, and further large studies are needed to establish correlation with tumour relapse [S7|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. Study of non-tumour tissue is relevant for predicting prognosis and risk of second or multiple neoplasia; however, caution should be exercised diagnosing malignancy based solely on molecular data, as not all driver gene mutations directly link to cancer development [S8|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828].

C1.summary_text: This chunk addresses field cancerisation and preneoplastic changes in the context of tumour-adjacent tissue [S1|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. Field cancerisation may exhibit premalignant histological changes such as dysplasia, while many genetic alterations arise without any cytological changes. Environmental shifts in the tumour microenvironment exert evolutionary pressure that shapes mutation selection and tumour progression [S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. Preneoplastic lesions include dysplasia (characterised by cytological atypia, large hyperchromatic nuclei, or nucleoli) and in-situ carcinomas (lacking basement membrane invasion), both observed across most carcinoma types [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. Notably, some early neoplastic lesions — including colon adenomas and skin naevi — are polyclonal [S4|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. Cancer progression likely requires accumulation of multiple synergistic driver mutations [S5|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. Molecular studies of peritumour normal ducts in breast and prostate tissue can reveal a high burden of genetic alterations and driver mutations [S6|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828], though the clinical significance of these changes with respect to tumour relapse remains undefined [S7|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828]. Two practical conclusions are drawn: (i) analysis of non-tumour tissue may help predict prognosis and second neoplasia risk; and (ii) not all driver gene mutations are causally linked to cancer, urging caution when diagnosing malignancy on molecular data alone [S8|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27828].

C1.summary_text: This chunk reports serology findings in the context of increased vaccination and international travel. A majority (~75%) of individuals vaccinated with Pfizer mRNA show positive anti-spike IgM at 3 weeks post-first dose [S2|PMC9012948_main|6785]. C1.summary_text: This chunk addresses the clinical and public health implications of vaccine-induced antispike IgM seropositivity in the context of travel serology screening. Up to 75% of individuals tested positive for antispike IgM at 3 weeks after the first dose of the Pfizer mRNA vaccine in the reported cohort [S2|PMC9012948_main|6785], with IgM remaining detectable for up to 8 weeks post-mRNA vaccination according to one study [S2|PMC9012948_main|6785]. To address this confound in travel screening (e.g., for entry to China), nucleocapsid-specific IgM testing has been mandated to exclude individuals whose IgM positivity is solely vaccine-induced rather than indicative of prior natural infection [S3|PMC9012948_main|6785].
