C1.sentence: The histopathologic features are acanthosis and hyperkeratosis with variable degree of papillomatosis.

Ackerman described EA 50 years ago as a combination of variously sized clear spaces around nuclei in the stratum spinosum and granulosum, amphophilic material forming indistinct cellular boundaries, markedly thickened granular zone containing keratohyalin bodies, and compact hyperkeratosis.
This pattern differs from the cytopathogenic effect of HPV, where a clear halo around the nucleus is homogenous and the nucleus is retracted.
Acantholysis is also different, as cytoplasm is eosinophilic and the nucleus is hyperchromatic.
Four histological patterns of EA have been described, which may coexist in the same lesion.
They consist of the papillomatous, cup-shaped, acanthomatous, and polypoid variants.
Ultrastructural studies have shown tonofilament alterations with agglutination of them in the cytoplasm and intracellular vacuolization, as well as premature cornification of keratinocytes [2, 7].

C1.summary_text: Epidermodysplasia actinica (EA) is characterized by histopathologic features including acanthosis, hyperkeratosis with variable papillomatosis, variously sized clear spaces around nuclei in the stratum spinosum and granulosum, amphophilic material forming indistinct cellular boundaries, markedly thickened granular zone containing keratohyalin bodies, and compact hyperkeratosis [S1|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7709, S2|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7709]. This pattern differs from the cytopathogenic effect of HPV, which presents with a homogenous clear halo around the nucleus and a retracted nucleus [S3|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7709]. Acantholysis in EA shows eosinophilic cytoplasm and a hyperchromatic nucleus [S4|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7709]. Four histological patterns of EA have been described: papillomatous, cup-shaped, acanthomatous, and polypoid variants, which may coexist within the same lesion [S5|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7709, S6|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7709]. Ultrastructural studies reveal tonofilament alterations with cytoplasmic agglutination, intracellular vacuolization, and premature cornification of keratinocytes [S7|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7709].

C1.summary_text: Epidermolytic acanthoma (EA) is characterized by acanthosis, hyperkeratosis, and variable papillomatosis [S1]. The key histopathologic features include clear spaces around nuclei in the stratum spinosum and granulosum, amphophilic material with indistinct cellular boundaries, a markedly thickened granular zone containing keratohyalin bodies, and compact hyperkeratosis [S2]. EA differs morphologically from HPV-induced cytopathogenic effects, which show homogenous halos and retracted nuclei [S3], and from acantholysis, which presents with eosinophilic cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei [S4]. Four coexisting histological patterns of EA have been identified: papillomatous, cup-shaped, acanthomatous, and polypoid variants [S5, S6]. Ultrastructural examination reveals tonofilament alterations with agglutination in the cytoplasm, intracellular vacuolization, and premature cornification of keratinocytes [S7].

C1.summary_text: This chunk describes the histopathological, ultrastructural, and differential diagnostic features of Epidermolytic Acanthoma (EA). The key histopathologic features are acanthosis, hyperkeratosis (including compact hyperkeratosis), and variable-degree papillomatosis [S1|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7709]. Ackerman's classic description includes variously sized perinuclear clear spaces in the stratum spinosum and granulosum, amphophilic material forming indistinct cellular boundaries, markedly thickened granular zone with keratohyalin bodies, and compact hyperkeratosis [S2|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7709]. These features are distinguished from HPV koilocytic effect (homogeneous perinuclear halo with retracted nucleus) [S3|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7709] and from acantholysis (eosinophilic cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nucleus) [S4|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7709]. Four histological variants — papillomatous, cup-shaped, acanthomatous, and polypoid — have been described and may coexist in the same lesion [S5–S6|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7709]. Ultrastructural studies reveal tonofilament agglutination in the cytoplasm, intracellular vacuolization, and premature cornification of keratinocytes [S7|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7709].

C1.sentence: Primary tumours have heterogeneous epithelial cell content, and form an ecosystem with the environmental cells, including stromal cells, endothelial cells, leucocytes, lymphocytes, histiocytes and their secreted factors.

In a pathological context, we can quantify and evaluate the expression of the immune checkpoints programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1) and programmed cell death-1 (PD-1) in epithelial and inflammatory parts of the tumour and use this information for clinical correlation studies.
Similar to cell signalling pathways, key components of immune checkpoints, such as PD-L1, can also have heterogeneous expression throughout the tumour.
The PDL1 protein is expressed in a wide range of cell types, including lymphocytes, macrophages and dendritic cells, and is stimulated by variable and complex mechanisms.
In contrast to other immune checkpoint components, PD-L1 is rarely expressed in normal tissue but is induced in tumour-associated tissue, is a tumour biomarker and is also an attractive drug target.
As many current treatment schemes are based on immunotherapy, pathological assessment should include immune checkpoint proteins.

Furthermore, the heterogeneous and dynamic expression of factors such as PD-L1 in basal conditions and in response to different treatments presents a challenge to predicting which patients will respond to antiPDL1 therapies.
The assessment of CD4 +, CD8 + cells, and tumour mutational burden (TMB) can also be helpful in clinical decision-making.
TMB has recently been proposed as a new biomarker to quantify the potential tumoral neoantigenicity, with the aim of predicting patients who will benefit from immunocheckpoint inhibitors.
Nevertheless, different technologies and different thresholds have been proposed to define high versus low TMB in different tissue samples.

C1.summary_text: Primary tumours exhibit heterogeneous epithelial cell content and form an ecosystem with environmental cells [S1]. Immune checkpoints like PD-L1 and PD-1 can be quantified in tumour parts, with PD-L1 showing heterogeneous expression [S2, S3]. PDL1 protein is expressed in lymphocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells, is rarely found in normal tissue but induced in tumour-associated tissue, and serves as a tumour biomarker and drug target [S4, S5]. Heterogeneous PD-L1 expression challenges prediction of response to antiPDL1 therapies [S7]. Assessment of CD4+, CD8+ cells, and TMB can aid clinical decision-making [S8]. TMB quantifies tumoral neoantigenicity and predicts benefit from immunocheckpoint inhibitors, though different technologies and thresholds exist for its definition [S9, S10].

C1.summary_text: Primary tumours exhibit heterogeneous epithelial cell content and form an ecosystem with various environmental cells, including stromal cells, endothelial cells, leucocytes, lymphocytes, histiocytes, and their secreted factors [S1|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27851]. The expression of immune checkpoints like PD-L1 and PD-1 can be quantified and evaluated in both epithelial and inflammatory parts of the tumour for clinical correlation studies [S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27851]. PD-L1, as a key immune checkpoint component, can show heterogeneous expression throughout the tumour [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27851]. The PD-L1 protein is expressed in various cell types, including lymphocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells, and its expression is stimulated by complex mechanisms [S4|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27851]. PD-L1 is rarely expressed in normal tissue but is induced in tumour-associated tissue, serving as a tumour biomarker and an attractive drug target [S5|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27851]. Given that many current treatments are immunotherapy-based, pathological assessment should incorporate immune checkpoint proteins [S6|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27851]. However, the heterogeneous and dynamic expression of PD-L1, both in basal conditions and in response to treatments, complicates the prediction of patient response to anti-PD-L1 therapies [S7|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27851]. Assessing CD4+ and CD8+ cells, along with tumour mutational burden (TMB), can aid clinical decision-making [S8|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27851]. TMB has been proposed as a biomarker to quantify tumoral neoantigenicity and predict patient benefit from immunocheckpoint inhibitors [S9|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27851]. Different technologies and thresholds are used to define high versus low TMB across various tissue samples [S10|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27851].

C1.summary_text: This chunk discusses the role of immune checkpoints, particularly PD-L1 and PD-1, in tumour pathology and their relevance to immunotherapy. Primary tumours are described as complex ecosystems containing heterogeneous epithelial cells alongside stromal and immune cells [S1|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27851]. PD-L1 and PD-1 expression can be quantified in epithelial and inflammatory tumour compartments [S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27851], with PD-L1 showing heterogeneous expression patterns throughout tumours [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27851]. The PD-L1 protein is expressed across multiple cell types including lymphocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells, driven by variable signalling mechanisms [S4|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27851]. Notably, while PD-L1 is rarely expressed in normal tissue, it is induced in tumour-associated tissue and serves as both a tumour biomarker and drug target [S5|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27851]. Pathological assessment should include immune checkpoint proteins in the context of immunotherapy [S6|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27851]. The heterogeneous and dynamic nature of PD-L1 expression presents a challenge to predicting which patients will respond to anti-PD-L1 therapies [S7|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27851]. CD4+ and CD8+ cell assessment, along with tumour mutational burden (TMB), are identified as helpful tools for clinical decision-making [S8|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27851]. TMB is proposed as a biomarker to quantify neoantigenicity and predict response to immunocheckpoint inhibitors [S9|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27851], though standardization remains challenging due to variable technologies and thresholds across tissue types [S10|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27851].

C1.summary_text: This chunk from PMC6851567 (HIS-75-4) provides a conceptual overview of immune checkpoint biology and its pathological assessment. Primary tumours exhibit heterogeneous epithelial cell content and form a complex ecosystem with stromal, endothelial, immune, and secreted-factor components [S1]. PD-L1 and PD-1 can be quantified in both epithelial and inflammatory tumour compartments for clinical correlation [S2]. PD-L1 expression is itself heterogeneous throughout the tumour [S3], is broadly expressed in lymphocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells via complex stimulatory mechanisms [S4], and — in contrast to other checkpoint components — is rarely expressed in normal tissue but is induced in tumour-associated tissue, qualifying it as both a biomarker and drug target [S5]. Given widespread immunotherapy adoption, pathological assessment should incorporate immune checkpoint proteins [S6]. The dynamic and heterogeneous nature of PD-L1 expression, both at baseline and in response to treatment, complicates response prediction for anti-PD-L1 therapies [S7]. CD4+/CD8+ assessment and tumour mutational burden (TMB) also contribute to clinical decision-making [S8]; TMB is specifically proposed as a neoantigenicity biomarker for predicting benefit from immune checkpoint inhibitors [S9], though high/low TMB thresholds remain inconsistent across technologies and tissue types [S10].

C1.summary_text: The chunk addresses the clinical and pathological characterization of ATLL-D (Adult T-cell Leukemia/Lymphoma, Dermatotropic variant). The classification status of ATLL-D as a lymphoma type remains unclear, though cases typically present with aggressive clinical course and dismal prognosis [S1]. Ohshima et al. previously described a Hodgkin-like variant as an incipient form of ATLL [S2]. Although ATLL-D exhibits morphological findings distinct from the Hodgkin-like type [S3], ATLL-D may represent another variant of incipient ATLL. Clinical evidence shows that at least one ATLL-D patient (case 18) was classified clinically as chronic type [S4], suggesting heterogeneity in disease presentation. However, further assessment of clinicopathological findings across similar cases is required to establish definitive classification patterns [S5].

C1.summary_text: This chunk discusses the clinical and morphological classification of ATLL-D in relation to established ATLL subtypes. ATLL lymphoma type is characterised by a very aggressive clinical course and dismal prognosis [S1|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21932], and it remains uncertain whether ATLL-D cases should be managed as lymphoma type. The Hodgkin-like ATLL type has been previously described as an incipient form of ATLL [S2|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21932]. Although ATLL-D has distinct morphological findings from the Hodgkin-like type [S3|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21932], it is proposed as another potential variant of incipient ATLL [S3|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21932]. The authors note that further clinicopathological assessment of similar cases is needed to confirm this classification [S5|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21932].

C1.summary_text: This chunk describes the cohort and methods for a HER2 status study on gastric adenocarcinoma (PMC3166662). A total of 166 randomly selected gastric adenocarcinomas from Spanish institutions were collected [S1]. Tissues were fixed in buffered formalin prior to paraffin embedding, though fixative concentration and duration were unknown [S3, S4]. Specimen types included 50 (30.1%) endoscopic biopsies and 116 (69.9%) surgical specimens, of which 15 (9%) were distant metastases [S5]. Per Lauren's classification, 86 (51.8%) were intestinal type, 28.3% were diffuse type, and 33 (19.9%) were indeterminate type [S6].

C1.sentence: The clinical characteristics of the reported cases are shown in Table 1.
The median age was 76 years and 14 of the 18 patients were male.
All of the patients were more than 60 years of age, which is older than the cohort in a previous study on lymph nodes with dermatopathic reaction without malignancy.
Erythema was observed in all cases, and one case showed purpura.
Most patients had enlargement of axillary or inguinal lymph nodes.
One patient (case 2) was diagnosed as smouldering ATLL based on haematological findings in peripheral blood.
Seven cases were considered to be a 'cutaneous' variant of the smouldering type based on the pathological findings in skin lesions.
Another seven cases did not show clear pathological or molecular evidence of lymphoma cell infiltration in either lymph nodes or skin, and were therefore considered as HTLV-1 carriers.

Two patients (cases 16 and 17), classified as ATLL-D, showed a progressive disease course and died 14 and 7 months respectively after diagnosis despite treatment that included mogamulizumab, an antibody therapy against CCR4.

Another case of ATLL-D (case 18) showed proliferation of atypical lymphocytes in peripheral blood ( > 40%) with a slight increase in serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and decreased serum albumin levels (data not shown), indicating a chronic type with an unfavourable prognosis as the clinical subtype.

C2.sentence: The patient with smouldering type (case 2) received oral etoposide (VP-16) treatment, whereas the remaining 14 cases, including patients regarded as HTLV-1 carriers or cutaneoustype ATLL, received topical therapy for their cutaneous lesions.

Although a precise comparison of clinical outcome between case 2 and the other HAL-D patients was difficult, because their treatment regimen was different, case 2 showed an indolent clinical course, similar to the other HAL-D cases, with no definitive transformation event.
Case 12, initially diagnosed as HAL-D, progressed to aggressive-type ATLL 30 months after lymph node biopsy and died within 1 month.
In the pathological review of the lymph node specimen of case 12, Hodgkin -Reed -Sternberg (HRS)-like cells, a hallmark finding of incipient ATLL, were not identified.
The other HAL-D cases showed no obvious transformation.
Case 5 died 6 years after a diagnosis of HAL-D, but the cause of death was unknown and no transformation was confirmed.
Case 11, diagnosed as cutaneous type, died from Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia 2 months after lymph node biopsy without transformation to aggressive ATLL.
Case 14, who exhibited proliferation of EBV-infected atypical large B cells, was aged 83 years.
This patient was seronegative for human immunodeficiency virus and no other immunosuppressive status, including immune suppressive therapy, was noted in the history.

C1.summary_text: The clinical characteristics of 18 patients are described, with a median age of 76 years and a male predominance (14/18). All patients were over 60 years old. Morphologically, all cases presented with erythema, one with purpura, and most had enlarged axillary or inguinal lymph nodes. One patient was diagnosed with smouldering ATLL based on peripheral blood findings [S6]. Seven cases were classified as a 'cutaneous' variant of the smouldering type based on skin lesion pathology [S7]. Another seven cases were identified as HTLV-1 carriers, lacking clear pathological or molecular evidence of lymphoma infiltration in lymph nodes or skin [S8]. Two patients with ATLL-D showed a progressive disease course and died within 7-14 months despite mogamulizumab treatment [S9]. Another ATLL-D case (case 18) exhibited atypical lymphocyte proliferation (>40%) in peripheral blood, a slight increase in serum LDH, and decreased serum albumin, indicating a chronic type with an unfavourable prognosis [S10].

C1.summary_text: The study cohort had a median age of 76 years, with 14 out of 18 patients being male [S2|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21923]. All patients were over 60 years old, which is older than a comparative cohort with dermatopathic reaction without malignancy [S3|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21923]. Clinically, erythema was observed in all cases, and purpura in one case [S4|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21923]. Most patients presented with enlarged axillary or inguinal lymph nodes [S5|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21923]. Seven cases were classified as a 'cutaneous' variant of the smouldering type based on skin lesion pathology [S7|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21923]. Another seven cases lacked clear pathological or molecular evidence of lymphoma cell infiltration in lymph nodes or skin and were considered HTLV-1 carriers [S8|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21923]. The chronic type of ATLL-D is associated with an unfavourable prognosis, indicated by proliferation of atypical lymphocytes in peripheral blood (>40%), increased serum LDH, and decreased serum albumin levels [S10|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21923].

C2.summary_text: This chunk describes treatment and clinical outcomes for 15 patients with HAL-D (HTLV-1-associated lymphoproliferative disorder) and related cutaneous ATLL. One smouldering-type case received oral etoposide [S1], while 14 others (including HTLV-1 carriers and cutaneous-type ATLL) received topical therapy for cutaneous lesions [S1]. The etoposide-treated case showed an indolent clinical course with no transformation [S2], consistent with typical HAL-D behavior [S5]. However, HAL-D can progress to aggressive-type ATLL (case 12 at 30 months post-diagnosis with rapid death) [S3], and the initial lymph node biopsy of this case lacked characteristic HRS-like cells [S4]. One HAL-D patient achieved 6-year survival without transformation [S6], while a cutaneous-type ATLL case died from Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia without ATLL progression [S7]. An additional case (case 14) involved proliferation of EBV-infected atypical large B cells in an 83-year-old patient [S8] who was HIV seronegative with no immunosuppressive history [S9].

C1.summary_text: This chunk describes clinical characteristics of 18 patients with ATLL/HTLV-1-associated dermatopathic lymphadenopathy [S1|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21923]. The cohort had a median age of 76 years with 14/18 (78%) males [S2|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21923], and all patients were >60 years—older than dermatopathic lymphadenopathy without malignancy cohorts in prior studies [S3|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21923]. Erythema was universal; purpura was noted in one case [S4|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21923], and most patients had axillary or inguinal lymph node enlargement [S5|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21923]. Disease subtypes were heterogeneous: 1 case was haematologically diagnosed as smouldering ATLL [S6|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21923], 7 as cutaneous-variant smouldering ATLL by skin pathology [S7|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21923], and 7 lacked pathological/molecular evidence of lymphoma infiltration (HTLV-1 carriers) [S8|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21923]. Two ATLL-D cases (cases 16 and 17) had progressive disease and died within 7–14 months despite mogamulizumab (anti-CCR4) treatment [S9|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21923]. A third ATLL-D case showed >40% peripheral blood atypical lymphocytes, elevated LDH, and low albumin, consistent with chronic-type ATLL and unfavourable prognosis [S10|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21923].

C2.summary_text: In this HAL-D case series (PMC7383570), treatment varied by disease subtype: the single smouldering-type case received oral etoposide (VP-16) [S1], while the remaining 14 cases (HTLV-1 carriers or cutaneous-type ATLL) received topical therapy for cutaneous lesions [S1]. Overall, HAL-D demonstrated an indolent clinical course with no definitive transformation in the majority of cases [S2, S5]. One exception was case 12, which progressed to aggressive-type ATLL 30 months after lymph node biopsy and died within 1 month [S3]; pathological review of this case notably failed to identify Hodgkin-Reed-Sternberg (HRS)-like cells, described as a hallmark of incipient ATLL [S4]. Case 5 died 6 years after HAL-D diagnosis from an unknown cause without confirmed transformation [S6], and case 11 (cutaneous type) died from Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia 2 months after biopsy without transformation to aggressive ATLL [S7]. Case 14 presented an unusual finding of EBV-infected atypical large B-cell proliferation [S8] in an 83-year-old patient who was HIV-seronegative and had no documented immunosuppressive status [S9].

C1.sentence: The ToGA trial was a prospective, randomized, multicentre phase III trial conducted in 24 centres.

This study looked for HER2 expression / amplification in 3807 patients with GCs, and found a positivity rate of 22% [either by fluorescence in-situ hybridization (FISH) or immunohistochemistry (IHC) 3+].
Five hundred and eighty-four HER2-positive GCs were included and randomized between cisplatin plus fluoropyrimidine (capecitabine) (Ch) or the same chemotherapy plus trastuzumab (Ch+T).

Patients treated with Ch+T showed a clinically and statistically significant improvement in terms of overall survival (13.8 months versus 11.1 months, hazard ratio 0.7, 95% confidence interval 0.6-0.9, P = 0.0046).

Secondary endpoints of the study were also met; thus Ch+T significantly improved the overall response rate and progressionfree survival, as compared with Ch alone, without any increase in toxic effects, including cardiac events.
Therefore, Ch+T chemotherapy has become the new standard treatment for HER2-positive advanced gastric cancer.

C1.summary_text: The ToGA trial [S1] was a prospective, randomized, phase III multicenter trial that screened 3,807 gastric cancer patients for HER2 expression/amplification [S2], identifying a 22% positivity rate by FISH or IHC 3+ [S2]. Among 584 HER2-positive cases [S3], patients randomized to cisplatin/fluoropyrimidine plus trastuzumab (Ch+T) demonstrated clinically and statistically significant improvements in overall survival (13.8 vs 11.1 months; HR 0.7, 95% CI 0.6–0.9; p=0.0046) [S4], overall response rate, and progression-free survival compared to chemotherapy alone [S5], without increased toxicity or cardiac events [S5]. C1.sentence: There is currently a lot of interest in circulating tumour cells (CTCs), and their potential in liquid- based tumour diagnosis.
In this context, a CTC usually refers to a circulating cell from a solid tumour, such as a carcinoma, melanoma or sarcoma, and haematological malignancies are excluded.
CTCs are not a recent discovery.
There is a description of tumour cells in post- mortem blood from 1869.
They were found in a man who had approximately 30 subcutaneous tumours.

It is quite likely that this patient actually had a haemato- lymphoid malignancy with a leukaemic component, as the malignant cells in the blood appear to have been much more numerous than our modern experience of CTCs.

There is a more reliable and more detailed description of CTCs in living patients with carcinomas, melanomas and sarcomas from the 1950s, along with a description of other rare benign circulating cells, includ ing macrophages and megakaryocytes, that can mimic CTCs.
Most recent studies have concentrated on extracting and analysing neoplastic circulating epithelial cells, with the aim of developing techniques to diagnose and characterise carcinomas.
Non- neoplastic circulating epithelial cells have received relatively little attention, partly because of their rarity and the consequent difficulty in studying them.

However, there are reports of non- neoplastic circulating cytokeratin- positive cells (NCCCs) in patients with benign diseases, including prostatitis and Crohn's disease, and after benign breast surgery.

C1.summary_text: Circulating tumour cells (CTCs) are cells from solid tumours, excluding haematological malignancies [S2]. The concept of CTCs dates back to 1869 with descriptions of tumour cells in post-mortem blood [S4], though these may have been more numerous than modern CTCs [S6]. More reliable descriptions of CTCs in living patients with carcinomas, melanomas, and sarcomas emerged in the 1950s [S7]. Other cells like macrophages and megakaryocytes can mimic CTCs [S7]. Recent research focuses on neoplastic circulating epithelial cells for carcinoma diagnosis [S8], while non-neoplastic circulating epithelial cells receive less attention due to rarity and study difficulty [S9]. However, non-neoplastic circulating cytokeratin-positive cells (NCCCs) have been reported in benign conditions like prostatitis, Crohn's disease, and after benign breast surgery [S10].

C1.summary_text: This chunk introduces the concept and history of circulating tumour cells (CTCs). CTCs are defined as circulating cells from solid tumours (carcinomas, melanomas, sarcomas), explicitly excluding haematological malignancies [S2|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13914]. The earliest historical description of tumour cells in post-mortem blood dates to 1869, though this case is now suspected to represent a haemato-lymphoid malignancy with leukaemic involvement due to the far greater abundance of malignant cells than seen in modern CTC experience [S4|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13914, S6|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13914]. A more reliable account of CTCs in living patients with carcinomas, melanomas, and sarcomas was provided in the 1950s, along with recognition that benign circulating cells—specifically macrophages and megakaryocytes—can mimic CTCs [S7|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13914]. Contemporary research has focused primarily on neoplastic circulating epithelial cells for carcinoma diagnosis and characterisation [S8|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13914]. Non-neoplastic circulating epithelial cells remain poorly studied due to their rarity [S9|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13914], though non-neoplastic circulating cytokeratin-positive cells (NCCCs) have been documented in patients with prostatitis, Crohn's disease, and following benign breast surgery [S10|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13914].

findings.claim: NCCCs (non-cultured circulating cells) are almost never detectable in healthy subjects
findings.verbatim_support: It has been thought that NCCCs are almost never detectable in healthy subjects.

C2.summary_text: A single generalizable fact is extractable from this chunk: NCCCs (non-cultured circulating cells) are considered to be almost never detectable in healthy subjects [S1|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13914]. This is presented as a prevailing assumption in the field rather than a directly measured result, hence medium confidence is assigned.

[S1|PMC7508500_main|14255] Sixty serum samples were obtained from COVID-19 NAT-confirmed patients ( n =17) or COVID-19 suspected patients without positive NAT tests ( n =3) who were symptomatic household contacts of confirmed cases.
[S2|PMC7508500_main|14255] The NAT method used was an in-house nucleic acid test targeting E gene and RdRp: the primers have been described elsewhere.

C1.sentence: Urothelial bladder carcinoma.
Different molecular classifications are currently being explored.
One of them, based on RNA genomewide studies, has characterised two main molecular groups of bladder cancer with prognostic and predictive impact.
Group 1 basal subtype includes a subgroup of claudin-low and is characterised by expression of the basal cytokeratins CK5, CK14 and CD44.
Group 2 luminal subtype has mutations of the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) gene and urothelial differentiation markers such as CK20, GATA3 and uroplakins.
The luminal subtype has a more favourable prognosis than the basal subtype.

Recently, a prospective multicentre validation study with a 12-gene signature progression score in nonmuscle-invasive bladder cancer was demonstrated to have independent prognostic power beyond clinical and histopathological risk factors, and could help in stratifying patients to optimise treatment and followup.

Other molecular alterations have also been described, such as FGFR3 mutations in 80%, PI3KCA mutations in approximately 20% and mutations in the core promoter region of the human telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) gene in up to 85% of bladder tumours.
Interestingly, FGFR3 and PIK3CA mutations have been demonstrated as biomarkers on liquid biopsy for disease surveillance for bladder cancer.
Different cell cycle genes may be altered in invasive urothelial carcinoma, mainly tumour suppressor genes, including TP53, p16 and Rb.

C2.sentence: Finally, combinations of TP53, p21, p27 and pRb proved to be more precise in classifying bladder cancer patients into risk groups.

C1.summary_text: Bladder cancer is being explored for molecular classifications, with two main groups identified based on RNA genomewide studies, impacting prognosis and prediction [S3]. Group 1 basal subtype includes a claudin-low subgroup and is characterized by basal cytokeratins CK5, CK14, and CD44 expression [S4]. Group 2 luminal subtype exhibits FGFR3 gene mutations and urothelial differentiation markers like CK20, GATA3, and uroplakins [S5]. The luminal subtype has a more favorable prognosis than the basal subtype [S6]. A 12-gene signature progression score in nonmuscle-invasive bladder cancer has independent prognostic power beyond clinical and histopathological factors, aiding patient stratification [S7]. FGFR3 mutations are found in 80%, PI3KCA mutations in approximately 20%, and TERT gene core promoter mutations in up to 85% of bladder tumors [S8]. FGFR3 and PIK3CA mutations serve as liquid biopsy biomarkers for bladder cancer surveillance [S9]. Invasive urothelial carcinoma may show alterations in tumor suppressor genes such as TP53, p16, and Rb [S10].

A 12-gene signature progression score demonstrates independent prognostic power in nonmuscle-invasive bladder cancer beyond traditional clinical and histopathological risk factors, with utility in treatment stratification [S7|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27847]. Additional molecular alterations include FGFR3 mutations (80% prevalence), PIK3CA mutations (~20% prevalence), and TERT core promoter mutations (up to 85% prevalence) in bladder tumours [S8|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27847]. FGFR3 and PIK3CA mutations have utility as liquid biopsy biomarkers for disease surveillance [S9|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27847]. C1.summary_text: This chunk covers the molecular classification of urothelial bladder carcinoma (PMC6851567). RNA genome-wide studies define two main molecular subtypes with prognostic and predictive relevance [S3]. The **basal subtype (Group 1)** includes a claudin-low subgroup and is characterised by expression of CK5, CK14, and CD44 [S4]. The **luminal subtype (Group 2)** harbours FGFR3 mutations and expresses urothelial differentiation markers CK20, GATA3, and uroplakins [S5]. Crucially, the luminal subtype carries a more favourable prognosis compared to the basal subtype [S6]. A prospective multicentre validation study showed that a 12-gene signature progression score in non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer has independent prognostic power beyond clinical and histopathological risk factors [S7]. Key molecular alterations include FGFR3 mutations (~80%), PIK3CA mutations (~20%), and TERT core promoter mutations (up to 85%) across bladder tumours [S8]; FGFR3 and PIK3CA mutations have additionally been validated as liquid biopsy biomarkers for disease surveillance [S9]. In invasive urothelial carcinoma, cell cycle tumour suppressor genes—TP53, p16, and Rb—are frequently altered [S10].

This suggests that multi-marker combinations of cell-cycle regulatory proteins provide improved prognostic stratification in bladder cancer patients.

[S4|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15513] Second, cystadenomas of the rete testis lack molecular alterations seen in most mucinous tumours of Mullerian origin arising in the ovary and may therefore not represent a true counterpart.

C1.sentence: Despite the multiple limitations of the current study, including the use of sequencing panels (rather than genome-wide or exon-wide assays) and the limited number of cases, two relevant conclusions can be drawn from its results.

First, except for the presence of tubular and/or tubulopapillary architecture, benign tumours previously considered Sertoliform cystadenomas of the rete testis and now regarded as Sertoli cell tumours, NOS with intra-rete growth by the WHO classification of urinary and male genital tumours lack the hallmark findings of Sertoli cell tumours NOS.
Hence, this assumption is likely incorrect.
Second, cystadenomas of the rete testis lack molecular alterations seen in most mucinous tumours of Mullerian origin arising in the ovary and may therefore not represent a true counterpart.

Unfortunately, the use of sequencing panels precluded identification of novel variants; additional studies are needed to determine the molecular alterations that underlie oncogenesis in these neoplasms.

C1.summary_text: This chunk reports conclusions from a molecular sequencing study of Sertoliform cystadenomas of the rete testis, now reclassified by WHO as Sertoli cell tumours, NOS with intra-rete growth [S2]. The study found that while these tumours exhibit tubular and/or tubulopapillary architecture, they lack the hallmark morphological findings of typical Sertoli cell tumours NOS, suggesting their previous categorization as Sertoliform cystadenomas may be incorrect [S2|S3]. Molecularly, cystadenomas of the rete testis lack the alterations characteristic of mucinous tumours of Mullerian origin from the ovary and therefore likely do not represent a true histological counterpart [S4]. The authors acknowledge that the use of sequencing panels rather than genome-wide assays and the limited case number constrain these conclusions [S1], and note that additional molecular studies are needed to identify the underlying genetic alterations in these neoplasms [S5].

C1.summary_text: This chunk presents two key conclusions from a study of rete testis tumours using sequencing panels. First, benign tumours previously called Sertoliform cystadenomas of the rete testis — recently reclassified by the WHO as Sertoli cell tumours NOS with intra-rete growth — lack the hallmark features of Sertoli cell tumours NOS (apart from tubular/tubulopapillary architecture), suggesting the WHO reclassification is likely incorrect [S2|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15513; S3|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15513]. Second, cystadenomas of the rete testis do not harbour the molecular alterations characteristic of mucinous Müllerian-origin tumours of the ovary, indicating they are likely not a true counterpart to such neoplasms [S4|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15513]. The authors note that sequencing panel limitations precluded identification of novel variants, and further studies are warranted [S5|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15513].

C1.summary_text: This chunk addresses molecular subtyping of colorectal carcinoma (CRC). CRC molecular subtypes are distinguished by genomic, epigenetic, and transcriptomic parameters [S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27840]. Four consensus molecular subtypes (CMS1–4) have been operationalized by IHC [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27840] using a four-protein panel — CDX2, FRMD6, HTR2B, and ZEB1 — to classify tumors as CMS4 (mesenchymal), CMS1 (immune), or CMS2/3 (epithelial) [S4|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27840]. CMS4 carries the worst prognosis among these subtypes [S4|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27840]. Across all subtypes, driver and actionable genes including RAS and BRAF must be evaluated per approved protocols [S5|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27840].

C1.summary_text: This chunk reports on circulating tumour cells (CTCs) and circulating cells in metastatic carcinoma and healthy controls. CTCs can be extracted from blood of metastatic carcinoma patients and processed into formalin-fixed cell-blocks suitable for routine paraffin processing and immunohistochemistry [S1|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13913]. However, the clinical utility is limited by a specificity constraint: circulating cytokeratin-positive cells are found in some metastatic carcinoma patients but are probably benign, and importantly, these cytokeratin-positive cells are also present in healthy volunteers [S2|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13913]. Additionally, circulating megakaryocytes are present in both carcinoma patients and healthy volunteers, suggesting they are not disease-specific [S3|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13913].

C1.summary_text: This chunk presents conclusions from a study on circulating tumour cells (CTCs) in metastatic carcinoma. CTCs could be extracted from patient blood and processed into formalin-fixed cell-blocks for routine paraffin embedding and IHC [S1|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13913]. However, assay specificity is limited because some metastatic carcinoma patients harboured circulating cytokeratin-positive cells that appeared benign, and such cells were also detected in healthy volunteers [S2|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13913]. Additionally, circulating megakaryocytes were identified in both carcinoma patients and healthy volunteers, further highlighting potential confounders in CTC detection [S3|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13913].

C1.summary_text: In this FISH-based study (PMC3166662), HER2 amplification was detected in 17.5% of samples [S2]. Among amplified cases, 55% showed double minute amplification and 45% showed cluster amplification [S2]. Intratumoral heterogeneity (focal amplification) was present in 52% of amplified cases [S3]. Interobserver agreement for FISH scoring was almost perfect [S4], with observer 1 recording a median HER2 ratio of 5.25 (range 13.26) and observer 2 a median of 5.0 (range 17.9) [S5]. HER2 amplification was strongly and significantly associated with the intestinal subtype of the Lauren classification compared to all other subtypes (86% vs 14%, P < 0.0001) [S6].

C1.summary_text: Hybrid benign peripheral nerve sheath tumors are rare and exhibit areas of more than one neural neoplasm, such as schwannoma/neurofibroma, neurofibroma/perineurioma, or schwannoma/perineurioma [S1|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9397]. C1.summary_text: Hybrid benign peripheral nerve sheath tumors (BPNST) are defined by exhibiting cell differentiation profiles of more than one neural neoplasm [S1|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9412]. Two cases of hybrid cutaneous BPNST — specifically schwannoma/perineurioma and schwannoma/neurofibroma — are reported arising in the scalp and ankle of adult men [S2|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9412]. Postoperatively, no evidence of recurrence was observed in this case series [S3|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9412]. However, as a general caveat, neural tumors with hybrid features may exceptionally recur or undergo malignant transformation [S4|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9412].

C1.summary_text: This chunk provides diagnostic guidance for pathologists evaluating duodenal mucosal and submucosal nodules. Duodenal neuroendocrine tumours (NETs) present with nodular appearance [S1] but can be mimicked by peptic duodenitis. Key diagnostic pitfalls include: (1) crush artefact in duodenal NETs with crushed tumour cells that can mimic lymphoid cells [S2], and (2) NET tumour cells that morphologically resemble Brunner glands [S3]. The presence of Brunner-like glands in the superficial mucosa or with an infiltrative pattern should raise suspicion for NET [S3].

C1.summary_text: This chunk provides diagnostic guidance on duodenal neuroendocrine tumours (NETs). First, any duodenal mucosal or submucosal nodule warrants consideration of NET even when confounders such as peptic duodenitis are present [S1|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4800]. Second, a key diagnostic pitfall is that duodenal NETs can exhibit crush artefact, causing tumour cells to morphologically resemble crushed lymphoid cells [S2|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4800]. Third, duodenal NET tumour cells may mimic Brunner glands; however, Brunner-like glands located in the superficial mucosa or displaying an infiltrative growth pattern should raise suspicion for NET [S3|PMC12326049_HIS-87-478|4800].

C1.summary_text: This chunk discusses the diagnostic utility of SARS-CoV-2 testing modalities for COVID-19, particularly in the context of pre-travel testing policy. Acute COVID-19 diagnosis relies on NAAT [S1|PMC9012948_main|6775]. A Chinese Embassy policy (from 8 November 2020) mandated a 'dual test' (NAAT + IgM serology) within 48 hours of travel from Australia to China [S2|PMC9012948_main|6775]. Two key limitations of IgM serology are highlighted: (1) IgM has low sensitivity for detecting PCR-negative but potentially infectious individuals [S3|PMC9012948_main|6775], and (2) IgM is frequently positive beyond the infectious period, rendering mandatory negative dual-test requirements unnecessary [S4|PMC9012948_main|6775].

However, independent of the formal decision procedure, a number of other organisational units and individuals will be affected by or can influence such a change.
The complex relationship between stakeholders potentially affecting, or being affected by changes within a single department is illustrated in Fig. 2.
Clinicians will clearly be affected by a move from narrative to synoptic histopathology reporting.
The hospital harbouring the pathology department may have a general policy on IT development, and there may even be regional and/or national policies on IT systems that one must adhere to.
Similarly, external organisations such as regional or national cancer registries will be affected by, and can affect, a transition from narrative to electronic synoptic reporting.
Vendors are also required to develop the IT tools needed.
Understanding and managing the needs and interests of all such stakeholders is essential for achieving the organisational changes intended.

In their study on the implementation and use of a web-based synoptic reporting tool for cancer surgery at two hospitals in Nova Scotia, Canada, Urquhart and co-workers found that implementation and early use of the synoptic tool was affected by many factors external to the individual user.
A good understanding of the multilevel organisational environment in both the planning and implementation process was deemed important for project success.

C2.sentence: In a similar study on the implementation of synoptic pathology reporting in four pathology departments in three states in the USA, Hassell and co-workers found that adaption depended both on individual user factors and organisational issues.
With respect to the latter, an asymmetric organisational balance between benefits and costs was considered a possible hindrance for implementation.

If the pathology laboratories were to carry the financial burden for implementing electronic synoptic reporting but considered the cancer registries the beneficiaries of the new reporting tool, why should the laboratories change their information systems? 6 However, even in an environment where the development of an electronic synoptic pathology tool was free of costs for pathology laboratories, local adaption varied greatly.
Some laboratories had a user rate above 90%, while other laboratories had not implemented the synoptic tool at all.

This chunk discusses implementation barriers and variability in synoptic pathology reporting adoption across pathology departments in the USA. Hassell et al. found that adaptation depended on individual user factors and organisational issues [S1|PMC4035753_pthy-46-165|5945]. Key barriers included asymmetric organisational balance between benefits and costs [S2|PMC4035753_pthy-46-165|5945], particularly when pathology laboratories bore financial burdens while cancer registries reaped benefits [S3|PMC4035753_pthy-46-165|5945]. Even when implementation was cost-free, adoption varied widely, with some laboratories achieving >90% user rates while others did not implement the tool at all [S4|PMC4035753_pthy-46-165|5945].

C1.summary_text: This chunk discusses the diagnostic utility of morphological patterns and ancillary techniques in identifying hereditary tumour syndromes and their underlying genetic alterations. Characteristic chromosomal translocations have been identified in desmoplastic round-cell tumours, clear-cell sarcoma, synovial sarcoma, and rhabdoid tumours [S1|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27822]. A simple H&E stain can reveal the presence of numerous hereditary tumours with specific genetic alterations, including medullary thyroid carcinoma, MEN, cribriform-morular variant of papillary thyroid carcinoma, familial adenomatous polyposis, medullary breast carcinoma, familial breast cancer with BRCA1 mutations, SDHB mutation-associated renal carcinoma (which shows characteristic flocculent cytoplasmic vacuoles), hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer syndrome, and sebaceous lesions associated with Muir-Torre syndrome in colon cancer [S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27822]. Additionally, immunohistochemistry has emerged as a cost-effective strategy for identifying hereditary cancer predisposition syndromes [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27822].

C1.sentence: Aims : Dermatopathic reaction is a histopathological finding of lymph nodes that usually occurs in patients with inflammatory pruritic cutaneous lesions.
However, it is sometimes seen in patients with cutaneous T cell lymphoma.
Adult T cell leukaemia/lymphoma (ATLL) is a T cell malignancy caused by infection with human T cell leukaemia virus type I (HTLV-1), which is frequently accompanied by cutaneous lesions.
However, the detailed clinicopathological characteristics of the dermatopathic reaction of lymph nodes in ATLL patients and HTLV-1 carriers, addressed in this study, remains to be clarified.
Methods and results : We retrospectively analysed 18 nodal lesions with dermatopathic reaction in HTLV-1 carriers.
Axillary and inguinal lymph nodes were the primary affected tissues.
Three cases with atypical lymphoid cell infiltration were defined as ATLL with dermatopathic reaction (ATLL-D), showing an abnormal T cell immunophenotype and T cell monoclonality.
Two of the three ATLL-D patients died 14 and 7 months after diagnosis (the third case had a very short follow-up).
The other 15 patients were indistinguishable from reactive lesions and were defined as HTLV-1-associated lymphadenitis with dermatopathic reaction (HAL-D).
They showed an indolent clinical course, with only one case eventually transforming to aggressive disease.

C1.summary_text: Dermatopathic reaction is a histopathological finding of lymph nodes usually associated with inflammatory pruritic cutaneous lesions, but can also be seen in cutaneous T cell lymphoma [S1|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21909, S2|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21909]. Adult T cell leukaemia/lymphoma (ATLL) is caused by HTLV-1 infection and frequently presents with cutaneous lesions [S3|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21909]. This study analyzed 18 nodal lesions with dermatopathic reaction in HTLV-1 carriers, primarily affecting axillary and inguinal lymph nodes [S5|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21909, S6|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21909]. Three cases were defined as ATLL with dermatopathic reaction (ATLL-D), showing atypical lymphoid cell infiltration, abnormal T cell immunophenotype, and T cell monoclonality [S7|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21909]. Two of these three ATLL-D patients died within 14 months of diagnosis [S8|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21909]. The remaining 15 patients were defined as HTLV-1-associated lymphadenitis with dermatopathic reaction (HAL-D), appearing indistinguishable from reactive lesions and generally showing an indolent clinical course, though one case transformed to aggressive disease [S9|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21909, S10|PMC7383570_HIS-77-133|21909].

C1.summary_text: This retrospective study (PMC7383570) examined 18 nodal lesions with dermatopathic reaction in HTLV-1 carriers [S5]. Dermatopathic reaction is a lymph node histopathological finding typically associated with inflammatory pruritic cutaneous lesions [S1] but also occasionally seen in cutaneous T cell lymphoma [S2]. ATLL, caused by HTLV-1, is frequently accompanied by cutaneous lesions [S3]. Axillary and inguinal lymph nodes were the primary affected tissues [S6]. Three cases (ATLL-D) showed atypical lymphoid cell infiltration, abnormal T cell immunophenotype, and T cell monoclonality [S7]; two of these patients died at 7 and 14 months post-diagnosis [S8]. The remaining 15 cases (HAL-D) were histologically indistinguishable from reactive lesions [S9] and followed an indolent clinical course, with only one case transforming to aggressive disease [S10].

C1.summary_text: This chunk discusses tumour heterogeneity at the molecular level. Cellular stress can alter gene expression and signalling pathways within tumour cells, leading to heterogeneous protein expression [S1|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27857]. Despite this heterogeneity, so-called "funnel factors" — specifically p4E-BP1 and peIF4E — are expressed evenly throughout tumours, independent of upstream oncogenic alterations or local microenvironmental changes [S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27857]. The authors highlight that identifying such uniformly expressed targets is increasingly critical as a strategy to overcome tumour heterogeneity [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27857].

[S2] The Standard Q IgM assay produced two false positives: one in a rheumatoid factor-positive patient and one in a SARS-CoV-2 uninfected individual. [S5] All nine samples had SARS-CoV-2-specific IgG detectable by IFA, but sensitivity varied markedly across IgG assays: Innovita detected none (0/9), OnSite and Standard Q each detected 3/9, and Sinocare detected 1/9. These findings highlight significant diagnostic discordance and cross-reactivity issues across different rapid serological platforms.

C1.summary_text: This chunk (PMC7508500_main, C1) reports performance characteristics of four SARS-CoV-2 rapid lateral flow assays (Sinocare, Standard Q, OnSite, and Innovita) in a comparative serology evaluation. The Sinocare test showed cross-reactivity with samples positive for Mycoplasma pneumoniae IgM and influenza A serology [S1]. The Standard Q assay produced two false positives: one attributed to rheumatoid factor interference, and one in a SARS-CoV-2-uninfected patient [S2]. A subgroup of nine samples was identified as IgA-positive by IFA but IgM-negative by IFA, OnSite, and Innovita assays [S3]; the Standard Q IgM assay captured two of these nine [S4]. All nine had detectable SARS-CoV-2-specific IgG by IFA, yet sensitivity varied markedly among rapid assays: Innovita IgG detected none (0/9), OnSite IgG and Standard Q IgG each detected 3/9, and Sinocare detected only 1/9 [S5], highlighting substantial IgG detection gaps in rapid assays for IgA-dominant seroconverters.

C1.summary_text: This chunk addresses the prevalence of non-cancerous circulating cells (NCCCs) in healthy individuals. Most studies report NCCCs to be absent in healthy volunteers [S1|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13933]. One study using CellSearch® (immunomagnetic recovery) detected one circulating epithelial cell per 7.5 mL of blood in 5.5% of 145 healthy women, with no sample exceeding a single cell [S2|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13933]. By contrast, the authors' own immunostaining method on cell-block paraffin sections identified up to three cytokeratin-positive cells on a single slide in a healthy volunteer sample [S3|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13933], suggesting potentially higher sensitivity or different detection characteristics compared to CellSearch®.

[S3|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13935] In this previous study, CTCs were detected in blood of 16 from 35 patients with ER- positive breast carcinomas, with a median of 3 CTCs/7.5 mL. [S4|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13935] No correlation was found between the intensity and/or percentage of ER staining in the primary tumour with the number and ER status of CTCs of the same patient.

C1.sentence: Some studies have found circulating epithelial cells in carcinoma patients that were discordant with the immunophenotype of the carcinoma.
In one study, ER- negative circulating epithelial cells were found in a patient with ER- positive breast carcinoma.

In this previous study, CTCs were detected in blood of 16 from 35 patients with ER- positive breast carcinomas, with a median of 3 CTCs/7.5 mL. In total, ER- negative CTCs were detected in 11/16 (69%) of the CTC- positive cases, including blood samples with only ER- negative CTCs (19%) and samples with both ER- positive and ERnegative CTCs (50%).
No correlation was found between the intensity and/or percentage of ER staining in the primary tumour with the number and ER status of CTCs of the same patient.

The authors of this study suggest that the results could be evidence of heterogeneity of the tumour cells, but an alternative explanation could be that some of the cells were not CTCs, but are benign circulating epithelial cells.

For example, ER- negative CTCs were found in a patient with ER- positive breast carcinoma [S2]. In one study, CTCs were detected in the blood of 16 out of 35 patients with ER- positive breast carcinomas, with a median of 3 CTCs/7.5 mL. ER- negative CTCs were detected in 69% (11/16) of these CTC-positive cases, including 19% with only ER- negative CTCs and 50% with both ER- positive and ER-negative CTCs [S3]. No correlation was found between the intensity and/or percentage of ER staining in the primary tumour and the number and ER status of CTCs from the same patient [S4]. The authors suggest tumour cell heterogeneity as a possible explanation, or that some cells might be benign circulating epithelial cells rather than CTCs [S5].

C1.summary_text: This chunk reports findings on CTC immunophenotype discordance in breast carcinoma patients [S1|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13935]. In a cohort of 35 patients with ER-positive breast carcinoma, CTCs were detected in 16 (46%), with a median of 3 CTCs per 7.5 mL blood [S3|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13935]. Strikingly, ER-negative CTCs were identified in 11/16 (69%) of CTC-positive cases, including samples with only ER-negative CTCs (19%) and samples with mixed ER-positive and ER-negative CTCs (50%) [S3|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13935]. No correlation was observed between the intensity or percentage of ER staining in the primary tumour and the number or ER status of CTCs from the same patient [S4|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13935]. Authors proposed two interpretations: (1) these findings reflect intratumoral heterogeneity, or (2) some ER-negative circulating epithelial cells may be benign rather than true CTCs [S5|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13935].

C1.sentence: Hybrid BPNST with neurofibromatous and schwannomatous differentiation (hybrid neurofibroma/schwannoma) as in our second case has also been described.
Feany et al. reported the largest series of hybrid neurofibroma/schwannoma, including a total of 9 tumors arising in 9 patients.

These tumors were reported to arise sometimes in the setting of a neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1) or schwannomatosis, but are not confined to this type of patients, as they were also reported in patients with no stigmata for these syndromes [8, 9].
The cases reported by Feany et al. were described to arise in dermal, subcutaneous, or subfascial areas.

They often showed a predominance of neurofibromatous loose myxoid areas in plexiform arrangement, delimited at the periphery by a perineurium and including in their center a well-defined nodule of a schwannomatous differentiation.

Interestingly, plexiform neurofibromas are considered pathognomonic for NF1; however, in our case and in 5 out of the 9 patients with hybrid plexiform neurofibroma including schwannomatous nodules reported by Feany et al., the clinical examination failed to demonstrate stigmata of neurofibromatosis.
In this report, one patient with nonplexiform hybrid tumors was diagnosed with NF1.
Mitoses were rarely found in the schwannomatous component but not in the neurofibromatous one.
Recurrence was reported in only 1 out of the 9 cases reported by Feany et al., and it occurred 44 years after the initial excision.

C1.summary_text: Hybrid BPNST with neurofibromatous and schwannomatous differentiation (hybrid neurofibroma/schwannoma) has been described, often showing a plexiform arrangement [S1]. The largest series reported 9 tumors in 9 patients [S2]. These tumors can arise in the setting of NF1 or schwannomatosis, but also in patients without these syndromes [S3]. They occur in dermal, subcutaneous, or subfascial areas [S4] and often show a predominance of neurofibromatous loose myxoid areas in plexiform arrangement, delimited by perineurium and including a central schwannomatous nodule [S5]. While plexiform neurofibromas are pathognomonic for NF1, 5 out of 9 patients with hybrid plexiform neurofibroma lacked stigmata of neurofibromatosis [S6]. One patient with nonplexiform hybrid tumors was diagnosed with NF1 [S7]. Mitoses were rarely found in the schwannomatous component but absent in the neurofibromatous component [S8]. Recurrence was reported in 1 out of 9 cases, occurring 44 years after excision [S9].

C1.summary_text: Hybrid BPNST can exhibit both neurofibromatous and schwannomatous differentiation [S1|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9409]. A series by Feany et al. included 9 hybrid neurofibroma/schwannoma tumors from 9 patients [S2|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9409]. These tumors can be associated with neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1) or schwannomatosis, but are not exclusively confined to such patients, also arising in individuals without stigmata for these syndromes [S3|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9409]. Tumors in the Feany et al. series originated in dermal, subcutaneous, or subfascial areas [S4|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9409]. Morphologically, they often show a predominance of plexiform neurofibromatous loose myxoid areas, delimited by perineurium, and a central well-defined nodule of schwannomatous differentiation [S5|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9409]. While plexiform neurofibromas are pathognomonic for NF1, clinical examination in 5 out of 9 patients with hybrid plexiform neurofibroma (Feany et al. series) failed to show neurofibromatosis stigmata [S6|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9409]. One patient with nonplexiform hybrid tumors was diagnosed with NF1 [S7|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9409]. Mitoses were rarely found in the schwannomatous component and absent in the neurofibromatous component [S8|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9409]. Recurrence was reported in 1 out of 9 cases from the Feany et al. series, occurring 44 years post-excision [S9|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9409].

C1.summary_text: Hybrid BPNST exhibits neurofibromatous and schwannomatous differentiation [S1|PMC5803675|9409]. The largest series of hybrid neurofibroma/schwannoma tumors reported by Feany et al. included 9 tumors arising in 9 patients [S2|PMC5803675|9409]. These tumors can arise sometimes in the setting of neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1) or schwannomatosis but also occur in patients without stigmata for these syndromes [S3|PMC5803675|9409]. The tumors arise in dermal, subcutaneous, or subfascial areas [S4|PMC5803675|9409]. They often show a predominance of neurofibromatous loose myxoid areas in plexiform arrangement with well-defined schwannomatous nodules at the center [S5|PMC5803675|9409]. Plexiform neurofibromas are considered pathognomonic for NF1, but 5 out of 9 patients with hybrid plexiform neurofibroma including schwannomatous nodules had no clinical stigmata of neurofibromatosis [S6|PMC5803675|9409]. One patient with nonplexiform hybrid tumors was diagnosed with NF1 [S7|PMC5803675|9409]. Mitoses were rarely found in the schwannomatous component but absent in the neurofibromatous component [S8|PMC5803675|9409]. Recurrence was reported in only 1 out of 9 cases, occurring 44 years after initial excision [S9|PMC5803675|9409].

C1.summary_text: This chunk describes the clinicopathological features of hybrid benign peripheral nerve sheath tumors (BPNST) with combined neurofibromatous and schwannomatous differentiation [S1]. The largest documented series by Feany et al. comprises 9 cases [S2]. These tumors may arise in the context of neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1) or schwannomatosis, but importantly, they also occur sporadically in patients without syndromic stigmata [S3]. Anatomically, they present in dermal, subcutaneous, or subfascial locations [S4]. Morphologically, they characteristically demonstrate neurofibromatous loose myxoid areas in plexiform arrangement with perineurial delimitation at the periphery and a well-defined schwannomatous nodule centrally [S5]. Although plexiform neurofibromas are pathognomonic for NF1 [S6], notably 5 of 9 reported hybrid cases with plexiform architecture lacked clinical evidence of neurofibromatosis [S6], and a nonplexiform hybrid case was found to have NF1 [S7]. Mitotic activity is rare in the schwannomatous component but absent in the neurofibromatous component [S8]. Recurrence is uncommon, occurring in only 1 of 9 cases, and this occurred 44 years after initial surgical excision [S9].

C1.summary_text: Eccrine angiomatous hamartoma (EA), first described by Shapiro and Baraf (1970), is a distinctive lesion occurring predominantly in elderly adults during the fifth to seventh decade of life [S1|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7708]. It preferentially arises on the trunk, extremities, scrotum, and vulva [S1|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7708], and presents clinically as small white or fleshy papules of 1–2 mm [S2|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7708]. Lesions may be solitary or multiple [S3|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7708], and the disseminated form most frequently involves genital skin [S4|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7708]. EA lesions are often asymptomatic but can be pruritic; the chronic form may progress to lichenification [S5|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7708].

[S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27820] Grouping together the evidence for these theories, it has been demonstrated that (i) many spontaneous somatic mutations accumulate in cells during their lifetime, (ii) oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes play a critical role in cancer development and (iii) environmental factors trigger cancer onset and progression.
[S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27820] Regarding field cancerisation, some authors have proposed that cancer is a tissue disorder with similarities to abnormal embryonic development, while others propose that cancer is a consortium of clones and local factors.
[S4|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27820] It is understood that a single clone cannot harbour all the genetic alterations required for the invasive and metastatic tumour phenotype and that several clones acquire malignant properties that, synergistically, allow cells to grow, invade and metastasise.
[S5|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27820] This consortium of tumour cell clones and microenvironment cells includes leucocytes, lymphocytes, fibroblasts and endothelial cells.
[S6|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27820] A minimum number of cells is also required for a clone to be biologically viable -a phenomenon known as the Allee effect.
[S7|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27820] This clonal cooperation has been proposed in pancreatic and breast cancer and melanoma and for circulating tumour cell (CTC) clusters.

C1.sentence: Other theories include the tissue organisation field theory (TOFT), which postulates that neoplasia arises from a local tissue disorder and may be due to a defect in interaction between cells and other tissue components, -27 where epigenetic or genetic changes affect both epithelial and stromal cells in multiple locations.

Grouping together the evidence for these theories, it has been demonstrated that (i) many spontaneous somatic mutations accumulate in cells during their lifetime, (ii) oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes play a critical role in cancer development and (iii) environmental factors trigger cancer onset and progression.

Regarding field cancerisation, some authors have proposed that cancer is a tissue disorder with similarities to abnormal embryonic development, while others propose that cancer is a consortium of clones and local factors.

It is understood that a single clone cannot harbour all the genetic alterations required for the invasive and metastatic tumour phenotype and that several clones acquire malignant properties that, synergistically, allow cells to grow, invade and metastasise.

C1.summary_text: This chunk reviews theoretical frameworks underpinning cancer development with a focus on field cancerisation and clonal evolution. The Tissue Organisation Field Theory (TOFT) proposes that neoplasia arises from local tissue disorder through defective cell–tissue interactions, with epigenetic/genetic changes affecting both epithelial and stromal cells at multiple locations [S1]. Consolidating evidence across theories confirms that: (i) spontaneous somatic mutations accumulate lifelong, (ii) oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes are critical drivers of cancer, and (iii) environmental factors trigger cancer onset and progression [S2]. Field cancerisation is conceptualised either as a tissue disorder resembling abnormal embryonic development or as a consortium of clones influenced by local factors [S3]. Crucially, no single clone contains all genetic alterations needed for invasion and metastasis; multiple clones synergistically cooperate to achieve the malignant phenotype [S4]. The tumour consortium encompasses not only tumour cell clones but also microenvironmental cells including leucocytes, lymphocytes, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells [S5]. Clonal viability requires a minimum cell number, described as the Allee effect [S6]. Clonal cooperation has been documented in pancreatic cancer, breast cancer, melanoma, and CTC clusters [S7].

C1.sentence: EMPSGC is more common in women than men, and the median age at presentation is 70 years (range years).

For a long time, EMPSGC was considered to pertain exclusively to the eyelid region (around the eye, peri-ocular) but, albeit rarely, cases in extraeyelid localizations have been reported, for example, by Tsai J.H. et al. and Raquena L. and Sangueza O. in their book 'Cutaneous Adnexal Neoplasms'; in particular, while the former case was discussed as it was localized in the areolar region, the case presented in was localized at the level of a man's scalp, casting doubt on the possible extra-eyelid localization.

Various authors, and even the WHO classification, recognize that EMPSGC may be a precursor of primary mucinous carcinoma of the skin (PCMC), and, therefore, it should be discussed in the differential diagnosis.
Histologically, EMPSGCs appear as rather well-circumscribed uni/multi-nodular tumors with solid, cystic, and papillary areas.

The nodular areas usually show a solid growth pattern with small, scattered cysts, and, in addition, in some areas, a cribriform arrangement is present, in which the tumor cells grow on a lacelike network and/or a pseudo-rosette pattern.

C1.summary_text: This chunk describes the epidemiology, localization, precursor potential, and histomorphology of ectopic meibomian-type primary sebaceous gland carcinoma (EMPSGC). Demographically, EMPSGC is more common in women than men with a median age at presentation of 70 years [S1|PMC10529628_dermatopathology-10-00035|1755]. Although classically restricted to the eyelid/peri-ocular region, rare extra-eyelid cases have been reported in sites such as the areolar region and scalp [S2|PMC10529628_dermatopathology-10-00035|1755]. The WHO classification and multiple authors recognize EMPSGC as a potential precursor of primary mucinous carcinoma of the skin (PCMC), which should be included in its differential diagnosis [S3|PMC10529628_dermatopathology-10-00035|1755]. Histologically, EMPSGCs are well-circumscribed uni/multinodular tumors showing solid, cystic, and papillary areas [S4|PMC10529628_dermatopathology-10-00035|1755]. The nodular areas display a solid growth pattern with small scattered cysts and, focally, a cribriform arrangement with tumor cells growing on a lacelike network and/or pseudo-rosette pattern [S5|PMC10529628_dermatopathology-10-00035|1755].

C1.summary_text: Analysis of 60 samples from 20 confirmed or suspected COVID-19 patients revealed high frequency of SARS-CoV-2-specific antibody detection. [S1] IgG was detected in 55/60 samples (92%), and in all 55 of these samples, IgM and/or IgA were also detected. [S2] An additional 6/60 samples (10%) showed IgG alone without concurrent IgM or IgA. [S4] Serial testing in a subset of patients demonstrated antibody seroconversion with diagnostic significance: three patients exhibited SARS-CoV-2-specific antibody seroconversion with a four-fold rise in IgG, and a further three patients had a four-fold IgG rise, consistent with acute or recent infection.

C1.summary_text: In a cohort of 20 confirmed or suspected COVID-19 patients assessed across 60 serial samples [S1|PMC7508500_main|14263], SARS-CoV-2-specific IgG was detected in 55/60 (91.7%) samples, all of which co-expressed IgM and/or IgA [S1|PMC7508500_main|14263]. In 6/60 samples, IgG alone was detected without co-detection of IgM or IgA [S2|PMC7508500_main|14263]. The majority of samples (48%) were collected more than two weeks after symptom onset [S3|PMC7508500_main|14263]. On serial testing, three patients demonstrated SARS-CoV-2-specific antibody seroconversion alongside a four-fold rise in IgG, and an additional three patients exhibited a four-fold IgG rise [S4|PMC7508500_main|14263].

C1.summary_text: Glioblastomas are classified into four molecular subtypes based on gene expression profile (proneural, mesenchymal, mixed, and unknown) and up to six subtypes based on methylation arrays, recurrent driver genes, and transcriptomics [S2]. These molecular subtypes are utilized in current clinical oncology guides [S3]. The most recent WHO classification categorizes grade IV gliomas as IDH-mutant GB, IDH-wt GB, and midline glioma with H3 K27M mutation [S4]. To differentiate between subtypes, analyses of IDH1/IDH2, ATRX, TP53, FGFR, NF1, H3.1, and H3.3 mutations, EGFR and PDGFR amplifications, BRAF V600 mutation, translocations, and CDKN2A/CDKN2B deletion can be performed using IHC, FISH, or PCR [S5].

C1.sentence: Molecular classification based on mRNA expression profiling of gene groups is a frequent approach to identify and classify molecular subtypes of tumours.
One of the major achievements of molecular classification has been the subcategorisation according to prognosis, and it is instrumental for the identification of new genetic alterations.
However, mRNA-based expression studies are often limited by a low reproducibility, depending on mRNA stability.
Furthermore, single-cell sequencing approaches are not feasible in routine diagnostics.
Currently, samples are sequenced as the bulk of tumour cells and therefore do not provide information on ITH.

In addition to these technical issues, monitoring gene expression at the mRNA level does not necessarily correlate with the function of a protein within a cell, as many post-transcriptional modifications determine whether or not mRNA finally gives rise to a functional protein.

Importantly, however, the different molecular subtypes based on enormous mRNA expression matrices can be validated according to protein or gene expression using just a few in-situ hybridisation or IHC probes in most molecular cancer subtypes (see Table 2).

C1.summary_text: Molecular classification using mRNA expression profiling is a common method for identifying and classifying tumour subtypes and new genetic alterations [S1|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838, S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838]. However, mRNA-based studies face challenges such as low reproducibility due to mRNA stability [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838], and single-cell sequencing is not feasible for routine diagnostics [S4|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838]. Bulk tumour cell sequencing does not provide information on intratumoural heterogeneity (ITH) [S5|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838]. Furthermore, mRNA expression does not always correlate with protein function due to post-transcriptional modifications [S6|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838]. Despite these limitations, molecular subtypes identified by mRNA expression can often be validated using protein or gene expression with IHC probes in most molecular cancer subtypes [S7|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838].

C1.summary_text: Molecular classification using mRNA expression profiling is a common method to identify and classify molecular tumour subtypes [S1|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838]. This classification enables subcategorisation of tumours according to prognosis [S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838]. However, mRNA-based expression studies often suffer from low reproducibility due to mRNA stability issues [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838]. Single-cell sequencing approaches are currently not feasible in routine diagnostics [S4|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838]. Bulk sequencing of tumour cells does not provide information on intratumoural heterogeneity (ITH) [S5|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838]. Moreover, mRNA expression does not necessarily correlate with protein function because of post-transcriptional modifications [S6|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838]. Importantly, molecular subtypes defined by mRNA expression can be validated by protein or gene expression using a few in-situ hybridisation or IHC probes in most molecular cancer subtypes [S7|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838].

C1.summary_text: This chunk discusses molecular classification approaches for tumour subtyping and their limitations. Molecular classification based on mRNA expression profiling is a frequent approach for identifying and classifying tumour molecular subtypes [S1|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838]. A major achievement of molecular classification is subcategorisation of tumours according to prognosis and identification of new genetic alterations [S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838]. However, mRNA-based expression studies face limitations due to low reproducibility dependent on mRNA stability [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838]. Single-cell sequencing approaches are not feasible in routine diagnostics [S4|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838], and bulk tumour cell sequencing does not provide information on intratumoural heterogeneity [S5|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838]. Importantly, mRNA expression levels do not necessarily correlate with protein function because post-transcriptional modifications determine whether mRNA produces a functional protein [S6|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838]. Despite these technical limitations, molecular subtypes derived from mRNA expression matrices can be validated using a small number of in-situ hybridisation or IHC probes in most molecular cancer subtypes [S7|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838].

C1.summary_text: This chunk discusses the methodological landscape of mRNA-based molecular classification in oncology. While molecular subtyping based on mRNA expression profiling enables prognostic subcategorisation and identification of new genetic alterations [S1–S2|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838], it carries several technical limitations: mRNA studies have low reproducibility due to mRNA instability [S3|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838], single-cell sequencing is not feasible in routine diagnostics [S4|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838], and bulk sequencing fails to capture intra-tumour heterogeneity (ITH) [S5|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838]. Furthermore, mRNA expression levels do not necessarily reflect protein function, owing to post-transcriptional modifications [S6|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838]. Despite these limitations, molecular subtypes defined by large mRNA expression matrices can generally be validated using a small number of IHC or in-situ hybridisation probes across most molecular cancer subtypes [S7|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27838].

A weak trend toward lower HER2 ratios with FISH compared to brightfield ISH was observed [S2], which may matter if ratios carry predictive value, as demonstrated in the neoadjuvant breast carcinoma setting [S3]. Critically, the HERA trial failed to confirm that HER2 amplification degree predicts adjuvant trastuzumab benefit [S4], though this conclusion is limited by central FISH data being available in only 61% of randomized patients across two laboratories [S5]. Looking forward, automated hybridization assays capable of producing rapid (<24 h), reliable, and permanent ISH results are proposed as valuable tools for large clinical trials [S6].

C1.summary_text: This chunk (PMC9541515) describes clinical and laboratory findings from a case with multisystem involvement. Serological workup was negative for ANCA, proteinase 3-ANCA, and rheumatoid factor, with CRP within normal range [S1]. Hepatic and renal functions were normal [S2], and cerebrospinal fluid examination was unremarkable [S3]. Imaging revealed nasal mucosal thickening and paranasal sinus fluid retention on head CT/MRI [S5], and multiple bilateral small pulmonary nodules on chest CT [S6]. Multiple foci of erythema were noted in the bilateral hips and thighs, with one lesion biopsied [S4]. Corticosteroid administration led to resolution of erythema, rhinitis, parasinusitis, and pulmonary lesions, with no enhancing brain lesion on follow-up MRI; however, erythema recurred three weeks later [S7]. No peripheral neuropathy was noted [S8].

ALK translocation affects anaplastic large-cell lymphoma, lung adenocarcinoma, and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour [S1]. EWSR1-CREB1 translocation characterises both clear-cell sarcoma and angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma [S1]. BRAF mutations and translocations are present in benign nevi, malignant melanoma, colon adenocarcinoma, glioblastomas, and pilocytic astrocytoma [S1]. These findings demonstrate that identical molecular aberrations can be associated with tumours having markedly different histological and clinical phenotypes.
