C1.summary_text: This chunk (S1|PMC6851567_HIS-75-4|27823) highlights that certain recurrent molecular alterations are shared across morphologically distinct tumour types. Specifically: (1) the ETV6-NTRK3 translocation is found in infantile fibrosarcoma, cellular mesoblastic nephroma, and secretory breast carcinoma; (2) ALK gene translocations occur in anaplastic large-cell lymphoma, lung adenocarcinoma, and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour; (3) the EWSR1-CREB1 translocation is present in clear-cell sarcoma and angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma; and (4) BRAF mutations and translocations are detected across benign nevi, malignant melanoma, colon adenocarcinoma, glioblastomas, and pilocytic astrocytoma. The overarching observation is that shared molecular drivers can underlie tumours with strikingly different morphological characteristics.

C1.summary_text: This chunk reports validation of an automated dual-colour SISH (Silver In Situ Hybridization) method for HER2 testing in gastric cancer (GC) [S2]. The method demonstrates excellent concordance with no false-negative cases [S2], establishing its reliability. A comparison with FISH revealed only a few discrepant results, which were attributed to polysomy [S3]. To mitigate this limitation, raising the amplification cut-off threshold to ≥3 is proposed as a solution [S4]. The authors emphasize the need for standardized consensus guidelines at global and national levels for both analytical and interpretative aspects of HER2 testing [S5], noting that implementations should be informed by GC-specific data while learning from prior lessons in breast cancer HER2 testing [S6].

C1.summary_text: This chunk summarises a comparison of two ISH approaches (FISH and automated dual-colour SISH) for HER2 testing in gastric cancer (GC). The novel SISH method demonstrated excellent concordance with FISH and produced no false-negative results, validating its use [S2|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|19011]. The few discrepant cases between the two methods were attributable to polysomy [S3|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|19011], and raising the amplification cut-off to ≥3 is proposed as a mitigation strategy [S4|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|19011]. The authors advocate for global and national consensus on analytical and interpretative standards for HER2 testing in GC [S5|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|19011], and recommend that new GC-specific methodology take into account prior experience from breast cancer HER2 testing [S6|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|19011].

Prevalence of this pattern increased markedly with grade group: 1.1% in GG1 (n=1116), 17.8% in GG2 (n=444), 47.2% in GG3 (n=163), 37.3% in GG4 (n=83), and 42.0% in GG5 (n=81), confirming its association with higher-grade disease [S2|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17564]. Notably, all GG1 cases exhibiting the small cribriform/IDC pattern showed pure IDC without any coinciding invasive cribriform growth [S3|PMC9321809_HIS-80-1041|17564].

C1.summary_text: This methodological chunk describes the technical parameters for ISH-based HER2 assessment. FISH nuclei were scored from two areas using an epifluorescence microscope (Olympus BX61) with DAPI/Spectrum Orange/Spectrum Green filters and a ×100 oil immersion lens [S1|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|18995], while SISH scoring used a brightfield microscope (Olympus BX41) at ×40 [S2|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|18995]. Chromosome 17 polysomy was defined as ≥3 CEP17 signals per cell on average [S4|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|18995]. Amplification patterns (clusters vs double minutes) were classified per published criteria [S5|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|18995].

C1.summary_text: The chunk discusses advantages of SISH (Silver In Situ Hybridization) over FISH for gastric HER2 assessment [S3]. Implementation of FISH in US hospitals with <300 beds remains limited at approximately 4% adoption [S1], making interpretation by unfamiliar pathologists likely [S2]. SISH provides three main advantages: creation of permanent records, brightfield post-analytical capabilities, and fully automated analysis [S3]. In gastric carcinomas specifically, SISH enables easier low-power screening, which is particularly important given that approximately 8-13% of gastric cancers exhibit HER2 genetic-protein discordances between ISH and IHC [S3]. Additionally, straightforward co-localization of ISH and IHC findings is facilitated by brightfield assays [S3]. Notably, gastric cancer patients with IHC 0 or 1+ and FISH-positive HER2 status do not appear to benefit from trastuzumab treatment, highlighting the clinical significance of accurate HER2 assessment [S3].

C1.summary_text: This chunk from PMC3166662 addresses HER2 assessment methodologies in gastric cancer (GC), comparing SISH and FISH. A CAP survey found FISH implementation in local laboratories to be below expectations, with only ~4% of hospitals with fewer than 300 beds adopting it [S1|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|19010]. As a result, gastric HER2 SISH interpretation is likely to fall to pathologists unfamiliar with FISH [S2|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|19010]. SISH offers three key advantages over FISH — permanent record, brightfield post-analytical phase, and fully automated analytical phase — which are particularly relevant to gastric HER2 assessment [S3|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|19010]. Specific advantages include: (1) easier low-power screening (important given HER2 heterogeneity); (2) straightforward co-localization of ISH and IHC findings in brightfield, relevant because ~8–13% of GCs exhibit HER2 genetic-protein discordances; and (3) a fully automated SISH workflow enabling rapid subgroup mining of the ToGA trial database, which is of interest for understanding why IHC 0 or 1+ / FISH-positive patients do not appear to benefit from trastuzumab [S3|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|19010].

C1.summary_text: The study recruited 50 patients with metastatic carcinoma and 50 healthy volunteers. Blood was collected, with initial samples from 15 carcinoma patients yielding 10 mL, while subsequent samples from other carcinoma patients and all healthy volunteers involved 20 mL. This increase in volume was due to the discovery of probable NCCCs and megakaryocytes in early samples, necessitating additional blood for Parsortix™ extraction and cytology. Samples were processed using a Parsortix™ PR1 device following the manufacturer's PX2_ANG_002_SH_90 protocol. Two Parsortix devices allowed for parallel extraction. The extract from one tube was used for cell-block formation, and the extract from the other was used for cytology. C1.summary_text: The study cohort consisted of 50 patients with metastatic carcinoma and 50 healthy volunteers [S1|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13917]. Blood samples were drawn from all subjects, with the first 15 carcinoma patients having 10 mL collected in a single EDTA Vacutainer tube, and the remaining carcinoma patients and all healthy volunteers having 20 mL collected in two tubes [S3|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13917]. Probable circulating carcinoma cells (NCCCs) and megakaryocytes were discovered in early blood samples from carcinoma patients, prompting the increase in blood volume collected [S4|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13917]. Samples were processed through a Parsortix™ PR1 device within one day, with two devices used in parallel to extract two tubes of blood simultaneously [S5|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13917; S7|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13917]. Extracts from one tube were used to form cell-blocks, and extracts from the other tube were used for cytology [S8|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13917].

C1.summary_text: This methodological chunk describes a study recruiting 50 metastatic carcinoma patients and 50 healthy volunteers [S1|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13917]. Blood sampling protocols were adapted during the study: the first 15 carcinoma patients provided 10 mL in a single EDTA Vacutainer tube, while the remaining 35 carcinoma patients and all 50 healthy controls provided 20 mL in two tubes [S3|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13917]. This protocol modification was driven by the discovery of probable nucleated circulating carcinoma cells (NCCCs) and megakaryocytes in early samples, necessitating additional blood volume for Parsortix extraction and cytological examination [S4|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13917]. Samples were processed through Parsortix™ PR1 devices using the manufacturer's standard protocol [S5|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13917, S6|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13917], with parallel extraction of two tubes for cell-block and cytology preparations [S8|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13917].

C1.summary_text: This chunk describes the study design and blood processing methodology for a cohort of 50 metastatic carcinoma patients and 50 healthy volunteers [S1]. Blood collection was initially 10 mL (single EDTA Vacutainer) for the first 15 carcinoma patients, then increased to 20 mL (two tubes) for remaining patients and all healthy volunteers [S3]. The protocol change was driven by the discovery of probable non-conventional circulating cells (NCCCs) and megakaryocytes in early samples, prompting additional volume for Parsortix™ extraction and cytological examination [S4]. All samples were processed through a Parsortix™ PR1 device as promptly as possible (same or next day) [S5], using the manufacturer's protocol [S6], with two devices run in parallel [S7]. Extracts from the two blood tubes were allocated separately — one for cell-block formation and the other for cytological examination [S8].

C1.sentence: For the remaining 11 cases with cytokeratin- positive cells, it was not possible to be certain that these cells were the same as those in the patient's carcinoma.
In some cases, this was because there were only scanty cells and this constrained the reliability of the interpretation of the immunostains.
However, for some cases the circulating cytokeratin- positive cells appeared to be distinctly different from the primary carcinoma.
Their immunoprofile was inconsistent with the carcinoma from the diagnostic specimen, and their morphology was also different.
In some cases, the morphology suggested that the cells were probably benign epithelial cells, as they had small regular nuclei.
In Case 9, the cell- block showed MNF116- positive cells that were also positive for CK7, CK20 and WT1 (Figure 3).
The latter three markers were negative in the patient's clear cell renal carcinoma, and the morphology was different to that of the renal carcinoma.

This suggests that the circulating cells were NCCCs, but it is also notable that there is no normal organ that has cells that co- express these markers, further suggesting that there may have been two different types of NCCCs.
There also appears to be a mismatch between circulating cells and the carcinoma for cases 4, and 32.
For Case 37, the patient had squamous carcinoma, diagnosed without immunohistochemistry, but the circulating cells were positive for CK7 and CK20 which is not typical of squamous carcinoma.

C1.summary_text: In 11 cases, cytokeratin-positive cells were identified, but their reliability was constrained by scanty cell numbers [S1|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13927]. In some instances, these circulating cells appeared distinctly different from the primary carcinoma, with an inconsistent immunoprofile and different morphology [S3|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13927, S4|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13927]. The morphology suggested benign epithelial cells in some cases [S5|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13927]. Case 9 exhibited MNF116-positive cells, also positive for CK7, CK20, and WT1, which were negative in the patient's clear cell renal carcinoma, and the morphology differed [S6|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13927, S7|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13927]. These circulating cells were suggested to be NCCCs, with the possibility of two types, as no normal organ co-expresses these markers [S8|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13927]. A mismatch between circulating cells and carcinoma was noted in cases 4 and 32 [S9|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13927]. For Case 37, circulating cells were positive for CK7 and CK20, which is atypical for squamous carcinoma [S10|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13927].

C1.summary_text: In 11 cases with cytokeratin-positive cells, it was not possible to definitively confirm their identity with the patient's carcinoma cells [S1|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13927]. This uncertainty was sometimes due to scanty cells, which constrained the reliability of immunostain interpretation [S2|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13927]. In some instances, circulating cytokeratin-positive cells appeared distinctly different from the primary carcinoma, showing inconsistent immunoprofiles and different morphology [S3|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13927, S4|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13927]. Some circulating cells exhibited morphology suggestive of benign epithelial cells, characterized by small regular nuclei [S5|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13927]. In one case (Case 9), MNF116-positive cells were also positive for CK7, CK20, and WT1 [S6|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13927]. These three markers (CK7, CK20, WT1) were negative in the patient's clear cell renal carcinoma, and the morphology of the circulating cells differed from the renal carcinoma [S7|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13927]. This suggested the circulating cells were NCCCs, and it was noted that no normal organ co-expresses these specific markers, potentially indicating two different types of NCCCs [S8|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13927]. Mismatches between circulating cells and carcinoma were also observed in cases 4 and 32 [S9|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13927]. For Case 37, a patient with squamous carcinoma, circulating cells were positive for CK7 and CK20, which is not typical for squamous carcinoma [S10|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13927].

C1.summary_text: Among 11 cases with cytokeratin-positive circulating cells, discordance was frequently observed between circulating cell immunoprofile/morphology and the patient's primary carcinoma [S3|S4|S5]. In Case 9, circulating cells expressed MNF116, CK7, CK20, and WT1 [S6], whereas the patient's clear cell renal carcinoma was negative for CK7, CK20, and WT1 [S7], with distinct morphology [S7]. The co-expression of these three markers was notable for lack of correspondence to any normal organ tissue [S8]. Cases 4 and 32 also demonstrated mismatches between circulating cells and primary carcinoma [S9]. In Case 37, circulating cells showed CK7 and CK20 positivity, which is atypical for the patient's squamous carcinoma diagnosis [S10]. These findings suggest that in some cases, cytokeratin-positive circulating cells may represent non-malignant circulating cells rather than circulating tumor cells derived from the primary carcinoma.

C1.summary_text: This chunk (PMC6899935_CYT-30-620, C1) reports observations from a case series in which circulating cytokeratin-positive cells were found to be discordant with the patients' primary carcinomas in 11 cases [S1|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13927]. Scanty cell yield in some cases limited reliable immunostain interpretation [S2|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13927]. In several cases, circulating cells were morphologically and immunophenotypically distinct from the primary tumour, with some displaying small regular nuclei suggestive of benign epithelial origin [S3–S5|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13927]. Notably, in Case 9 (clear cell renal carcinoma), circulating cells were MNF116/CK7/CK20/WT1-positive [S6|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13927], while the primary tumour was negative for CK7, CK20, and WT1 [S7|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13927]; morphological discordance further indicated these were non-carcinoma circulating cells (NCCCs), possibly of two distinct subtypes given the absence of any known normal tissue co-expressing these markers [S8|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13927]. Mismatches were also noted in Cases 4 and 32 [S9|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13927]. In Case 37, circulating cells were CK7/CK20-positive despite the primary diagnosis of squamous carcinoma — an immunoprofile atypical for squamous carcinoma [S10|PMC6899935_CYT-30-620|13927].

C1.summary_text: Histological examination of a dermal lesion revealed a multilobular, well-circumscribed, plexiform architecture with a biphasic proliferation. The lesion comprised lobules of myxoid hypocellular areas and a distinct cellular nodular component in the center of one lobule, with an abrupt transition between the two components. The peripheral areas were consistent with a neurofibroma, composed of spindle cells with heterogenous cytology in a myxoid stroma, intermingled with collagen bundles and mast cells. These neurofibroma cells expressed CD34 and partially S100 protein by immunohistochemistry. A slender capsule positive for EMA was identified at the periphery of the lobules. The central nodular area was consistent with a schwannoma, characterized by a plump spindle cell population with palisading disposition (Verocay bodies), and expressed S100 protein diffusely by immunohistochemistry, but was negative for EMA and CD34. [S1-S7|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9404]

The peripheral areas of the lesion were consistent with a neurofibroma, featuring spindle cells with heterogeneous cytology arranged in a myxoid stroma, intermingled with collagen bundles and mast cells [S4|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9404]. These spindle cells expressed CD34 and partially expressed S100 protein by immunohistochemistry [S5|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9404]. A slender capsule positive for EMA was observed at the periphery of the lobules [S6|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9404]. The central nodular area was consistent with a schwannoma, characterized by a plump spindle cell population with palisading disposition (Verocay bodies), diffusely expressing S100 protein, but negative for EMA and CD34 by immunohistochemistry [S7|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9404].

C1.summary_text: Histological examination of a dermal lesion revealed a multilobular, well-circumscribed, plexiform architecture with a distinctive biphasic composition [S1]. The peripheral component (S1, S4) was consistent with a neurofibroma composed of spindle cells with heterogenous cytology arranged in a myxoid stroma interspersed with collagen bundles and mast cells [S4]. These peripheral neurofibroma cells expressed CD34 by immunohistochemistry and showed partial S100 protein expression [S5]. A slender EMA-positive capsule was identified at the periphery of the lobules [S6]. The central nodular component represented a schwannoma characterized by plump spindle cells arranged in palisading disposition with Verocay bodies [S7], diffusely expressing S100 protein but negative for both EMA and CD34 by immunohistochemistry [S7]. The two components—neurofibroma and schwannoma—were clearly separated with an abrupt transition [S3], representing a composite benign nerve sheath tumor.

C1.summary_text: This chunk describes histological and immunohistochemical findings of a biphasic plexiform dermal lesion [S1|PMC5803675_dpa-0004-0001|9404]. The lesion is multilobular and well-circumscribed, predominantly composed of myxoid hypocellular lobules [S1]. A second distinct cellular nodular component is located centrally within a lobule [S2], with an abrupt transition between the two components [S3]. The peripheral areas are consistent with a neurofibroma, showing spindle cells of heterogeneous cytology in a myxoid stroma with collagen bundles and mast cells [S4]; these cells express CD34 and focally/partially S100 protein by IHC [S5]. A slender EMA-positive capsule demarcates the lobular periphery [S6]. The central nodular area is consistent with a schwannoma, featuring plump spindle cells in palisading arrangements (Verocay bodies) with diffuse S100 positivity but negativity for both EMA and CD34 [S7]. The IHC profile thus differentiates the schwannoma component (S100+, EMA−, CD34−) from the neurofibroma component (S100 partial, CD34+) within the same lesion.

C1.sentence: Of the 224 travellers to China, 15/190 (8%) were found to have positive Abbott IgM results with one of these also positive on the Roche assay and having confirmed infection overseas 6 months prior.
This patient was eventually cleared for travel when a negative IgM result by IFA was obtained.
Of the remaining 14, were cleared to travel following reporting of the subsequent reflex Roche Total result which returned negative results for all of these samples.

The remaining four that did not undergo reflex testing were reported as positive with further discussion with the Chinese Embassy allowing clearance due to negative PCR and recent vaccination in the previous 6 weeks considered the likely cause of the positive Abbott IgM result.
Retrospective reflex testing found these four samples to also be negative on the Roche assay excluding recent infection.
The remaining 34 travellers who were tested by the Roche Total alone were all negative.
Since review of this dataset, an additional asymptomatic traveller to China was found to be positive by both Abbott IgM and Roche Total during the Delta outbreak in Sydney.
He had not been vaccinated and, while PCR was negative, he was judged to have had recent infection.

Travel was deferred and he was required to undergo repeat PCR testing (result on day 2 and day 22 negative), chest imaging (result normal) and repeat serology (3 weeks later: rising IgM and IgG levels) and travel was further delayed until his ' dual test ' was negative.

C1.summary_text: A study of 224 travellers to China found that 15/190 (8%) had positive Abbott IgM results, with one also positive on the Roche assay and confirmed infection overseas 6 months prior [S1]. This patient was cleared for travel after a negative IFA IgM result [S2]. Of the remaining 14, reflex Roche Total testing returned negative results, clearing them for travel [S3]. Four samples not undergoing reflex testing were positive, but clearance was granted due to negative PCR and recent vaccination [S4]. Retrospective testing showed these four samples were negative on the Roche assay, excluding recent infection [S5]. The remaining 34 travellers tested by Roche Total alone were all negative [S6]. An additional asymptomatic traveller tested positive by both Abbott IgM and Roche Total during the Delta outbreak; they had not been vaccinated and, despite negative PCR, were judged to have recent infection [S7, S8]. Travel was deferred pending repeat PCR (negative), chest imaging (normal), and repeat serology showing rising IgM and IgG levels, with travel delayed until a 'dual test' was negative [S9].

C1.summary_text: Among 224 travellers to China, 190 were tested with the Abbott IgM assay, of whom 15/190 (8%) were positive [S1|PMC9012948_main|6782]. One of these had concurrent Roche Total positivity and confirmed prior infection 6 months earlier; that individual was cleared only after a negative IgM by IFA [S1–S2|PMC9012948_main|6782]. The remaining 14 Abbott IgM-positive travellers all tested negative on reflex Roche Total, permitting travel clearance [S3|PMC9012948_main|6782]. Four Abbott IgM-positive travellers who did not undergo reflex testing were cleared after discussion with the Chinese Embassy (negative PCR; recent vaccination within 6 weeks deemed the likely cause of false-positivity); retrospective reflex Roche Total was also negative for all four, excluding recent infection [S4–S5|PMC9012948_main|6782]. The 34 travellers tested by Roche Total alone were all negative [S6|PMC9012948_main|6782]. An additional asymptomatic, unvaccinated traveller was found positive by both Abbott IgM and Roche Total during Sydney's Delta outbreak; despite a negative PCR, recent infection was suspected [S7–S8|PMC9012948_main|6782]. Travel was deferred; repeat PCR on day 2 and day 22 was negative, chest imaging was normal, and repeat serology at 3 weeks showed rising IgM and IgG levels, with travel further delayed until the dual test was negative [S9|PMC9012948_main|6782].

C1.summary_text: The expanded paracortex can contain interdigitating dendritic cells and pigmented macrophages [S1]. Dermatopathic reaction is characterized by a polymorphous cellular context including transformed lymphocytes, activated macrophages, and dendritic cells [S4]. C1.summary_text: This chunk describes dermatopathic lymphadenopathy (DL) and its relation to cutaneous T cell lymphoma (CTCL). DL is characterised morphologically by an expanded paracortex containing interdigitating dendritic cells and pigmented macrophages [S1]. It typically occurs in the context of pruritic cutaneous lesions without malignancy [S2]. However, in CTCL such as mycosis fungoides, nodal dermatopathic lesions may harbour tumour cell infiltration, which has prognostic implications [S3]. Differentiating true lymphomatous involvement from reactive dermatopathic changes is diagnostically challenging because the latter features a polymorphous cellular milieu—including numerous transformed lymphocytes, activated macrophages, and dendritic cells—that can mimic lymphoma [S4].

C1.sentence: The remaining seven tumours were entirely cystic and classified as benign cystadenomas.

The lining epithelium contained mucinous cells in two tumours (Figure 4A), a mixture of mucinous and ciliated columnar cells in one tumour (Figure 4B); and cuboidal to short columnar cells in the remaining four tumours.
Based on their microscopic appearance, the cysts seemed unilocular/simple (i.e. they lacked internal septations) and were lined by a single layer of epithelial cells.
Focal stubby, branching papillae were seen in one neoplasm that did not contain mucinous cells (Figure 5A,B).
Some lesions showed inflammatory cells (within the mucin) and/ or evidence of reaction to extravasated mucin.
True stratification was not seen, although pseudostratification occurred focally, including in the tumour with stubby papillae.
Of note, in the latter, the epithelium lining the papillae showed more significant nuclear atypia, with conspicuous nucleoli, than the remaining neoplasms in this group (Figure 5B).
Very focal areas with ovarian-like stroma were seen in only two tumours (Figures 5 and 6).
Mitotic activity was consistently low (below one mitotic figure per 10 high-power fields), and necrosis, invasive growth, or lymphovascular invasion were not seen.
All lesions were tested de-novo for PAX8, WT1, and CDX2.

C1.summary_text: This case series analyzed seven benign cystadenomas with comprehensive morphological characterization [S1]. All lesions were entirely cystic with unilocular/simple architecture lacking internal septations, lined by a single layer of epithelial cells [S3]. Some lesions contained inflammatory cells and evidence of mucin extravasation [S5]. True epithelial stratification was absent, though pseudostratification occurred focally [S6]. Very focal areas with ovarian-like stroma were identified in only two tumours [S8]. All cases showed consistently low mitotic activity (below one mitotic figure per 10 high-power fields) with absent necrosis, invasive growth, and lymphovascular invasion [S9]. Immunohistochemical testing for PAX8, WT1, and CDX2 was performed de novo on all lesions [S10].

C1.summary_text: This chunk describes the histopathological features of seven entirely cystic benign cystadenomas [S1|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15506]. The lining epithelium was heterogeneous: mucinous cells in two tumours, a mixed mucinous/ciliated columnar pattern in one, and cuboidal-to-short columnar cells in four [S2|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15506]. All cysts appeared unilocular/simple, lacking internal septations, and were lined by a single epithelial layer [S3|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15506]. One non-mucinous tumour harboured focal stubby, branching papillae [S4|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15506] and displayed greater nuclear atypia with conspicuous nucleoli compared to the remaining group [S7|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15506]. Some lesions contained inflammatory cells within mucin and/or evidence of extravasated mucin reaction [S5|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15506]. True stratification was universally absent, though focal pseudostratification occurred [S6|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15506]. Ovarian-like stroma was seen only focally in two of the seven tumours [S8|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15506]. Benign features were consistent: mitotic activity was uniformly low (<1/10 HPF), and necrosis, invasive growth, and lymphovascular invasion were all absent [S9|PMC12129600_HIS-87-35|15506]. C1.summary_text: This chunk establishes foundational context for HER2 biology and therapeutics. In 1987, Slamon et al. first described HER2 gene amplification in breast carcinomas [S1|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|18983]. Subsequently, the development of trastuzumab (an HER2-targeted antibody) represented a major clinical success in solid tumour oncology [S2|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|18983]. Recognizing that HER2 amplification is not limited to breast cancer, researchers attempted to extend trastuzumab-based approaches to other malignancies including gastric, bladder, and lung carcinomas [S3|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|18983]. By 2009, the ToGA trial presented results evaluating treatment outcomes in patients with advanced gastric carcinoma [S4|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|18983].

C1.summary_text: This introductory chunk establishes the historical context of HER2 amplification in oncology. HER2 gene amplification was first described in a subset of breast carcinomas in 1987 [S1|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|18983]. The targeted antibody trastuzumab was subsequently developed as a specific treatment for this alteration, representing a landmark success in solid tumour oncology [S2|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|18983]. HER2 amplification was also recognised in other carcinoma types, including gastric, bladder, and lung carcinomas [S3|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|18983]. The ToGA trial, reporting results in 2009, extended these therapeutic strategies to patients with advanced gastric carcinoma [S4|PMC3166662_his0059-0008|18983].

C1.summary_text: This chunk describes clinical findings in a 78-year-old patient with lipoprotein lipase deficiency. The literature establishes that lipoprotein lipase deficiency carries a substantial risk for pancreatitis, affecting 50–80% of affected patients (S2|PMC9012948_main|6805). The discovery of hypertriglyceridaemia at age 56 following a transient ischaemic attack (S3|PMC9012948_main|6805) represents a common associated metabolic abnormality in lipoprotein lipase deficiency.
